p: Marginalia is a self-hosted writing tool for long-form fiction co-written with large language models. You write the instructions for each part of the story, the model writes the prose, and Marginalia keeps everything around it in order: the branching story, the world lore, the summaries that keep long books within the model's context, and the prompt settings that shape the style.

It runs in your browser - as a desktop app on your own computer, or as a small server for you and your friends - and works with any OpenAI-compatible API: OpenAI, OpenRouter, LiteLLM, llama.cpp, LM Studio, Ollama, vLLM, and others.
The story editor
Books with branching stories – regenerate or swipe a part, branch from any point, move around the story tree, edit the generated text. See Books.
Lorebooks – world and character notes put into the prompt only when they matter: by book tags, text or regex filters, nested lorebooks. SillyTavern world info can be imported. See Lorebooks.
Templates and macros - prompts are Handlebars templates with SillyTavern-compatible macros, so imported lore keeps working. See Templates & macros.
Summaries – older parts are condensed so long books fit into the context window. See Summaries.
Any OpenAI-compatible model - including reasoning models, with per-model limits and switchable generation settings. See Inference providers and Protocols.
Backups - per-book backups with restore and copy, and full database backups on a schedule. See Book backups and Database backups.
Multiple users – each with their own books, lore, and models; administrators manage users, backups, and cleanup. See Administration.
Published books – a read-only reading view you can share. See Publishing & viewer.

Search and replace, commands - search and replace in the story and the lorebooks, and a command line next to the story menu with commands that read and change the book. See Commands and Regular expressions.
Agents - a model that works on a book on its own through the commands, on a copy: you watch it, talk to it in a console and review its changes before they reach the book. See Agents.
Extensions - plugins add features at runtime: chapter markers, lorebook history, AI reviews, side questions to the model. See Extensions.

Marginalia is open source under the MIT License. Pictures used in the screenshots of this manual are credited on the Credits page. Releases are on GitHub; bugs and ideas go to the issue tracker.

This part of the manual is for people who write with Marginalia and for those who run it for others. It explains every screen and setting, from installing Marginalia and connecting a model to branching a story, building a lorebook and backing up the database. You don't need to know anything about programming; a few pages about templates go deeper for those who want to fine-tune what is sent to the model.
If you are new, start with Getting started – it takes you from installation to the first generated part of a book in a few minutes.

Installation

Marginalia has no model of its own. It needs an OpenAI-compatible API to write text: a cloud service (OpenAI, OpenRouter...) or a model running on your own computer (llama.cpp, LM Studio, Ollama, vLLM...). Have the API address and an API key ready (a local server that doesn't need one works without a key, see Adding a provider).
Marginalia runs in your browser. You can install it in two ways:
One person on one computer
Port 8080, normally behind a reverse proxy with HTTPS
Server (Docker)
Several users, or access from other devices
Install Marginalia: desktop app or server.
Create the administrator account on the first start.
Follow the quick start: connect a model, create a protocol and write the first part of a book.
The desktop app is a self-contained version of Marginalia for one computer. It brings its own Java runtime and server, listens only on your computer and opens in your default browser.
Download the archive for your system from the releases page. Two variants are published for every system:
Archive
Contents
marginalia-version-os-arch-app
The app: Marginalia.app on macOS, Marginalia.exe on Windows, bin/Marginalia on Linux
marginalia-version-os-arch
A portable folder started with a script, with command line options

Builds are available for Windows x64, macOS (Apple Silicon and Intel) and Linux (x64 and arm64). arch in the file name is x86_64 for 64-bit Intel and AMD processors (Windows, macOS Intel, Linux) and aarch64 for ARM (Apple Silicon, Linux arm64).
Extract the archive and move Marginalia.app to Applications.
Open it. The app is not signed yet, so the first time macOS refuses to open it. Right-click the app and choose Open, or run:
Extract the archive.
Run Marginalia\Marginalia.exe.
SmartScreen may warn about an unknown publisher. Click More info → Run anyway.
Run Marginalia/bin/Marginalia.
Run bin/marginalia (bin\marginalia.bat on Windows).
Starting takes a few seconds. Marginalia then opens in your browser at http://127.0.0.1:8765 and shows the first start dialog.
c: xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/Marginalia.app

p: While it runs, Marginalia shows an M icon in the system tray (in the menu bar on macOS). Its menu has two items:
Open Marginalia - opens Marginalia in the browser again, for example after you closed the tab.
Quit Marginalia - stops the server. Closing the browser tab does not stop Marginalia.
Starting the app a second time while it already runs only opens it in the browser.

To move Marginalia to another computer, quit it and copy the .marginalia folder (with secret.key, which decrypts the saved API keys). Before larger changes, make a database backup.
The portable launcher accepts these options:
With --host 0.0.0.0 (or another address) Marginalia is reachable from your network over plain HTTP. For access from other devices use the server behind HTTPS instead.

c:
marginalia --port 8765        # port to listen on; a free one is picked when 8765 is taken
marginalia --host 127.0.0.1   # address to listen on
marginalia --home /path       # directory that holds the .marginalia folder (default: your home directory)
marginalia --no-browser       # don't open the browser
marginalia --no-tray          # no tray icon; stop with Ctrl+C
marginalia --help

p: Quit Marginalia, replace the app (or the portable folder) with the new version and start it again. Your data stays in .marginalia and is upgraded automatically on the first start; before the structure of the database changes, Marginalia saves a copy of it in db-backups. Extensions are built for one Marginalia version, so update them at the same time (see Managing extensions).
Delete the app or the folder. To remove your data as well, delete the .marginalia folder.
Run Marginalia as a server when several people use it, or when you want to open it from other devices. Every user gets their own books, lorebooks, inference providers and protocols.
Docker with Docker Compose
About 1 GB of memory for Marginalia
For access over the internet: a domain and a reverse proxy with HTTPS (see below)

The first docker compose up builds the image from source, which takes a few minutes. Marginalia then listens on port 8080. Open http://server:8080 and create the administrator account (see First start).

c:
git clone https://github.com/Enerccio/Marginalia.git
cd Marginalia
docker compose up -d

p: Instead of building from source you can use the image published with each release (linux/amd64 and linux/arm64). In docker-compose.yml, replace the build: block with image::
latest is the newest release, edge the development version, and 1.1.0 (or 1.1) pins a release. The rest of the file stays the same.

c:
services:
  marginalia:
    image: ghcr.io/enerccio/marginalia:latest

p: Everything is set in docker-compose.yml:
Setting
What it does
ports
8080:8080 publishes Marginalia on port 8080 of the host. Use 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 when only a reverse proxy on the same host should reach it.
volumes

./data holds the database, backups and extensions. Keep it, and include it in your server backups. It is created on the first start if it doesn't exist; on start the container makes it owned by the user Marginalia runs as inside the container (jetty), so the files in it belong to that user's ID on the host.
-Xmx1g
Maximum memory. Raise it (for example -Xmx2g) for many users or very large books.
After changing the file, apply it with docker compose up -d.

c:
services:
  marginalia:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: Dockerfile
    container_name: marginalia-app
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    volumes:
      - ./data:/var/marginalia/.marginalia
    environment:
      - JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS=-Duser.home=/var/marginalia -Xms256m -Xmx1g -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/var/marginalia/.marginalia/heapdump.hprof

p: ~/.marginalia (/var/marginalia/.marginalia in the image)
Default
empty
en
false hides Save login.
Folder of the database, backups, extensions and the key that encrypts API keys. Change it only with a matching volume (./data:/your/folder); the container fixes the owner of this folder on start.
How long a saved login lasts, in seconds (30 days).
Language of the login page and of users who have not chosen one (en or ja; the language of an extension can't be used here).
MARGINALIA_ALLOW_PERSISTENT_LOGIN
MARGINALIA_DATA
MARGINALIA_DEFAULT_LANGUAGE
MARGINALIA_PERSISTENT_LOGIN_TTL
MARGINALIA_TRUSTED_PROXIES
Marginalia's own settings are environment variables of the service, next to JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS:
Reverse proxies whose X-Forwarded-For header is believed, see below. Replaces -DtrustedProxies.

The same settings can be given as Java options, -Dmarginalia.default-language=ja, which take precedence over the variables. A value that does not fit (text for the number of seconds, an unknown language) stops Marginalia from starting; the reason is in the log.
true
Variable
What it does

c:
environment:
      - JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS=-Duser.home=/var/marginalia -Xms256m -Xmx1g
      - MARGINALIA_DEFAULT_LANGUAGE=ja
      - MARGINALIA_PERSISTENT_LOGIN_TTL=604800
      - MARGINALIA_TRUSTED_PROXIES=172.16.0.0/12

p: Passwords and login cookies are sent with every request. Over plain HTTP anyone on the way can read them. Put Marginalia behind a reverse proxy with HTTPS.
The Save login option on the login screen also needs HTTPS: its cookies are marked secure, so browsers keep them only on HTTPS connections.
Marginalia updates the page over a WebSocket connection, so the proxy must forward WebSocket upgrades. Examples for marginalia.example.com:
Caddy gets the certificate and forwards WebSockets automatically.

Failed logins are throttled per user and per client address (after 30 failures from one address, logins from it are refused for a growing time, up to 15 minutes). Marginalia only believes the X-Forwarded-For header of a proxy you name: without it, all users appear to come from the proxy's address and 30 failures from anyone block everybody for a while. Keep the header in the proxy configuration (as above) and set MARGINALIA_TRUSTED_PROXIES=address or range of the proxy in the environment of docker-compose.yml. A proxy on the Docker host reaches the container from the Docker network, normally 172.16.0.0/12; several entries are separated by commas. The throttling is kept in memory, restarting Marginalia clears it.
c: marginalia.example.com { reverse_proxy localhost:8080 }

server { listen 443 ssl; server_name marginalia.example.com; ssl_certificate /etc/letsencrypt/live/marginalia.example.com/fullchain.pem; ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/marginalia.example.com/privkey.pem; client_max_body_size 100m; # uploads of backups and extensions location / { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8080; proxy_http_version 1.1; proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade; proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade"; proxy_set_header Host $host; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme; proxy_read_timeout 1h; # long generations keep the connection open } }

p: Inside the container, localhost is the container itself, not the server. To use a model server that runs on the Docker host (llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio...), use the address http://host.docker.internal:port/v1 in the inference provider. On Linux, add this to the service in docker-compose.yml:
The model server must also listen on an address the container can reach, not only on 127.0.0.1.

c:
extra_hosts:
      - "host.docker.internal:host-gateway"

p: With the prebuilt image use docker compose pull and docker compose up -d instead.
The database is upgraded automatically when the new version starts. Marginalia saves a copy of the database before it changes its structure, but make a database backup of your own first as well.

c:
git pull
docker compose up -d --build

p: rebuild.sh (Linux, macOS) and rebuild.bat (Windows) in the repository root do the update for you; run them from the root, for example from a cron job or a scheduled task. They fetch the remote branch and do nothing when there is nothing new (--force rebuilds and restarts anyway, for example after changing docker-compose.yml). Otherwise they stop the container, git pull, rebuild the bundled plugins and copy their JARs into data/extensions (replacing the installed ones), and start the container again with docker compose up -d --build. If any step fails, the script stops with a message.

The Docker image doesn't contain the extensions, and they have to be built from the same source as the application. You don't need Java or Maven for that: marginalia/plugins/docker-compose.yml builds all of them in a container, which builds the application first and then every plugin, and copies the JARs into marginalia/plugins/build:

The first build takes several minutes (it downloads the dependencies of the application). Then copy the JARs into data/extensions and restart Marginalia, or load them in Admin → Extensions (see Extensions). rebuild.sh / rebuild.bat do the copying for you, so on a server that uses them the plugins are always updated together with the application.

c:
docker compose -f marginalia/plugins/docker-compose.yml build
docker compose -f marginalia/plugins/docker-compose.yml run --rm plugins

p: The image has a Docker health check: docker ps shows (health: starting) while Marginalia starts (up to two minutes), then (healthy). It is unhealthy when http://localhost:8080/health stops answering with 200. Docker does not restart an unhealthy container by itself; use the status for your monitoring or an auto-heal tool.

/health needs no login, so a monitoring tool or a load balancer can use it too (through the proxy: https://marginalia.example.com/health). It answers 200 and {status:UP} when Marginalia runs and its database answers, and 503 with {status:DOWN,...} while it is starting or when something is wrong. It shows nothing else (no version, no details); the log has the reason.

c: docker compose logs -f marginalia

p: When Marginalia starts with an empty database, it asks for the first account instead of showing the login screen. This account is the administrator: it can manage users, database backups, cleanup and extensions.
Creating the administrator account
Fill in:
Field
Username
The login name.
Full Name
The name shown in the application.
Password, Repeat password
Both must match. Marginalia also accepts an empty password - never leave it empty on a server, anyone could then log in as administrator with just the user name.
Administrator is checked and cannot be changed for the first account. Click OK. The page reloads and shows the login screen.
Remember the password. There is no password reset by e-mail. Other administrators can set a new password for a user in Admin → Users.
Log in with the new account. With Save login checked, the browser stays logged in for 30 days. This works only over HTTPS or on 127.0.0.1 with the desktop app (see Server).

From a fresh installation to the first generated part of a story. It assumes Marginalia is installed and you are logged in as the administrator.
Open the Inference Providers tab and click Add Inference Provider.
Enter a Name, for example OpenRouter - Claude.
In General Settings, set Max Context Size to the context size of the model, for example 32000, and Max Response Tokens to the longest part you want, for example 2000.
In Per Type Settings, enter the OpenAI URL (it ends with /v1) and the Api Key (leave it empty for a local server that has no key), click Refresh and pick the Model.
Click OK.
The fields are described in Inference providers, with URLs for common services.
Open the Protocols tab and click Add Protocol.
Enter a Name, for example Default.
Leave Max Context Tokens and Max Reply Tokens empty - the limits of the inference provider are used.
Click OK.
See Protocols.
Open the Settings tab and pick the new provider as Default Model and the new protocol as Default Protocol. Click Save. New books then start with both, so you don't have to select them every time.
Default model and protocol in Settings
Open the Books tab and click Add Book.
Enter the name of the book. The book opens.
On the About tab, check that Model and Protocols are set (they come from your defaults), and add a Description of the story if you want to.
Open the Story tab.
Click + in the bottom right corner. The New Turn Instructions panel opens.
Describe what should happen in Instructions, for example:
A lighthouse keeper on a remote island finds a message in a bottle addressed to her, dated fifty years in the future. Introduce her and the island. About 800 words.
Scene Setting, POV Character and Present Characters are optional; fill them in to give the model more direction.
Click Generate. The text appears while the model writes it. The red Stop button (in place of +) interrupts the generation.

Click + again for the next part. Each part can be edited, regenerated or swiped for an alternative version from its menu (☰); see Story editor and Branches & story tree.

Marginalia has a layout made for phones. You write, edit and regenerate parts, read and tweak lorebooks and manage your models from the phone browser, but the phone layout is not a copy of the desktop one: it is simpler, a few things are missing and not every extension works in it. This page lists the differences.
For reading a book on a phone, there is also the viewer, which is made for it.

l: When the phone layout is used
p: Marginalia looks at the width of the browser window when the page loads. Narrower than 768 pixels gives you the phone layout, anything wider the normal workspace.
Tablets and phones in landscape mode are usually wider than 768 pixels and get the desktop layout.

The layout is not switched while you work. If you turn the phone or tablet on its side, or resize the window, the layout stays as it was until you reload the page. So to get the larger desktop layout on a tablet or a turned phone, turn it and reload; to go back to the phone layout, turn it back and reload again.
A narrow desktop browser window gets the phone layout too, which is handy to try it.
Like the desktop, the phone layout can be added to the home screen like an app (Install app / Add to Home Screen in the browser menu).

The tabs on the left are replaced by a drawer. Tap the menu button in the top bar to open it, tap a tab to switch to it. The tab you are on fills the whole screen and its name is shown in the top bar.
The phone workspace with the drawer open

The drawer has the same tabs as the desktop - Books, Lorebooks, Settings, Protocols, Inference Providers, Agents (only for users who may use agents), Resources and Trash - and the Language selector, Change Password and Logout at the bottom. Extensions may add buttons, but only to the places they know on the phone, see Extensions.
While the Settings tab has unsaved changes, the drawer is locked as on the desktop: save or discard first.

The book list is one column. Above it are the name filter, the tag filter and the sort buttons (Last Modified, Created, Name; tap the active one again to reverse the order), then Add Book, the magnifier (the advanced search: tags to include and exclude, dates, number of parts and text) and refresh. Each book has buttons: the star makes it a favorite, Move to folder puts it into a folder, the pencil opens it and the trash deletes it (into the Trash).
The book list on a phone

The list shows one folder at a time, as on the desktop: the path of the folder you are in as buttons to go back on, the check box Include subfolders, then the folders above the books (tap one to go in; it shows how many books are beneath it) and, at the top level, the virtual Favorites folder. The name and tag filters search the current folder, or everything below it with Include subfolders. Add Book and the imports put the new book into the folder you are in. The folder you are in is remembered.
Folders on a phone

A folder can't be made, renamed or deleted on the phone, and there is no Organise window or mass change; do that on a computer. The language of a book can be inherited from a folder here too, and the Prompts tab shows where each value comes from.

The phone shows a reduced lorebook editor. You can pick a lorebook, enable or disable it and its entries, and edit the content of an entry. Everything else is shown as text only: name, order, tags, filtering and insertion mode, negative tags and note. You cannot create, delete, import or export lorebooks, or add entries. Use the desktop for that, see Lorebooks.

The same reduced editor is used in the Lorebook tab of a book. When the lorebook of the book has sub lorebooks, the box Shown lorebook under it switches the tab to any of them, and back, without changing the lorebook of the book.
A lorebook on a phone
The button next to the Enabled check box opens Search and replace for the entries of the lorebook, see Entries.

Settings are the same as on the desktop, only laid out in a narrow column. The one thing missing is Import Backup as New Book. To bring a backup file back on the phone, create a book, use Import Backup in its Backups tab and restore it there, or import it as a new book on the desktop.

An inference provider is a connection to a model: the API address, the API key, the model and its limits. Every book uses one provider. You can have as many as you like, for example a large cloud model for the story and a small local one for experiments, and switch a book between them at any time.
Providers belong to your account. Other users don't see them or their API keys. API keys are stored encrypted (see The data folder).

Adding a provider needs the permission Create own models, which an administrator gives you (administrators always have it, see Permissions). Without it you can only use the providers the administrators share with you; the Add Inference Provider button is not shown.

How long to wait for the API to answer, and for more text once it started writing. The default is 300. Reasoning models may need minutes before the first text; a request that hears nothing for this long fails with a timeout message (the thinking of a model counts as text, so a model that keeps thinking is not cut). How often a request is repeated when the API answers with a rate limit (429) or a server error (5xx), or cannot be reached. The wait between attempts grows, and a Retry-After header of the API is respected. The default is 2, 0 turns retrying off. Marginalia fills the context only up to Max Context Size minus Max Response Tokens. If the finished prompt is still bigger than that (for example because an extension added text, or the token count was off), a warning shows the estimated sizes before the request is sent. The request is sent anyway; the API may reject it or cut the prompt.
The warning about a prompt that may not fit

Reasoning models think before they answer. With Enable Reasoning checked, Marginalia sends the chosen Reasoning Effort (None, Low, Medium or High) to the API as reasoning_effort. More effort usually means better planned text, but slower and more expensive responses. Not every API supports the parameter; if requests fail with reasoning enabled, turn it off.

When the model returns its reasoning (as reasoning_content or reasoning, depending on the server), it is shown above the generated part under View Reasoning. The reasoning is not part of the story and is not sent back to the model.
Reasoning of a generated part
Reasoning counts toward the response: give reasoning models a larger Max Response Tokens, or the text may be cut off after a long reasoning.
Marginalia counts tokens to decide how much of the story fits into the prompt. It asks the provider when it can, and tries these methods in order:
the OpenAI token counting endpoint (/v1/responses/input_tokens),
the /tokenize endpoint of llama.cpp,
the /tokenize endpoint of LiteLLM,
the /v1/messages/count_tokens endpoint of LiteLLM (for Anthropic models),
a local estimate with the OpenAI tokenizer.

The first method that works is used from then on. The local estimate is close for most models but not exact, which is another reason to keep Max Context Size a little below the real limit. Providers of the type Extension count as their extension says; the Google Gemini and Anthropic Claude ones ask the provider to count.

Every request Marginalia makes for a kind of work (a new part, an annotation, a redraft, a summary...) carries the header X-Session-ID, a hash that is the same for the same user and kind. A server or proxy that keeps a prompt cache can use it to find the cache of the previous request of that kind. A server that doesn't know it ignores it. See Prompt cache and session id, with an example for one slot of llama.cpp kept on disk.

On an installation with several users, an administrator can share a provider: check Shared with all users in the provider's dialog (the checkbox is only there for administrators). Every user then finds it in the Model list of their books and in their Inference Providers tab, marked Shared Yes. They can use it, but they can't open it, see its address or API key, change it or delete it; only its owner can. Books, backups and restores that refer to a shared provider keep working for everybody who can see it.
A shared provider in the Inference Providers tab of a regular user
Sharing a provider lets the other users spend the owner's quota with the service. To stop users from adding providers of their own, so that they can only use the shared ones, see Users and providers.

A token limit has a reset (daily, weekly from Monday, or monthly; calendar periods in the time zone of the server) and three limits that can each be left empty for no limit: the tokens sent, the tokens generated, and both together (in total). Whichever is reached first stops the user until the next reset. If all three are set, the sent plus the generated limit must not be below the total (the total could then never be reached), otherwise the dialog refuses to save. For example a total of 100,000 with 100,000 sent and 20,000 generated is fine, a total of 100,000 with 20,000 sent and 10,000 generated is not.
Adding a limit

An administrator can limit what each user may do with a shared provider. In the Inference Providers tab, the administrator who owns a shared provider has a Limits button (a user with a lock) in its row, which opens a table with the limits that were set. Add limit creates a new one: pick the user and a limit type.

Every user sees the shared providers in their tab as read-only rows. The info button (the circle with an i) of a shared provider shows their own limit: what they used in this period, the limits and when they reset. When a limit is reached, the story editor, summaries and extensions show an error instead of sending the request.
Limit type
Meaning
No limit (the same as having none).
Not available

Nothing is reset on a timer: the tokens used start from zero when the user uses the provider (or looks at their limits) for the first time in a new period. The size of a request is known before it is sent, so a request whose prompt would take the user over the sent or in total limit is refused (the prompt is measured with Marginalia's own estimate, which can differ a little from the service's count). The tokens generated are not known in advance: they are counted when the request ends, so the user is stopped only once the limit is reached and the last response can go over it. Users without a limit in the table are not limited.
The limits a user sees, with what was used in this period
The limits of a shared provider
The user can not use the provider; anything that would send a request to it fails.
The user can use up to the given number of tokens per period.

To keep the generated tokens from going over, check Hard limit (only available with a limit of the generated tokens). A request reserves room for the largest response it allows (the Max Response Size of the provider, or the lower one of the protocol), and with a hard limit it is refused when that reserve does not fit into what is left of the generated limit. So a hard limit lower than the response size of the provider refuses every request; the table and the user's info show hard next to such a limit. The hard limit only covers the generated tokens, the in total limit can still be gone over by the last response.
Token limit
Unlimited

The Inference Providers tab shows, per provider, the Tokens sent (the prompt, "prefill") and Tokens generated (the response, reasoning included) you have used with it, added up over all your books, summaries and extensions. A shared provider has a count of its own for each user, so you see only your part.
Administrators also get a Usage per user button on the tab, which opens a table with what every user has used of every provider (tokens sent, tokens generated, requests and the time of the last one).
Usage per user

The numbers are what the service reports. A service that doesn't report them (or a request you stop in the middle) is counted with the local estimate described in Token counting, so those numbers are approximate. A request that fails before any text arrived isn't counted. Unless an administrator has set a limit for you on a shared provider, the counts are only informational.

Marginalia asks the service to report the token counts (stream_options with include_usage). To change that for a provider, put your own stream_options into its Additional Parameters, for example {stream_options: {include_usage: false}}: it replaces what Marginalia sends, and the local estimate is used.

Model servers keep the prompt they have just read (the prompt cache), so that the next request that starts with the same text doesn't have to read it again. For a long story that is the difference between waiting a few seconds and waiting minutes. A cache only helps as far as the new prompt starts like the old one (see Why a cache may not help). Marginalia can also tell the server what kind of work a request is, so that a server, or a proxy in front of it, can keep a cache for each kind.

l: Why a cache may not help
p: A server reuses the part of the cache where the new prompt is the same as the old one from the very first token; the first difference ends it, and everything after it is read again, however much of it is unchanged. Look at the llama-server line printed when a request starts:

f_keep is the share of the cached prompt the new request keeps. Near 1 the cache is used; here only 15 % is, so the prompt differs from the cached one early on, whether the cache was restored from disk or never left the slot.

Models with a sliding window (Gemma, for one) and hybrid models can not drop the end of their cache and go on from the middle. As far as the llama.cpp source says, llama-server can only continue from a cached prompt when the new prompt extends it exactly, or when a context checkpoint exists at or before the place where the two differ. It makes checkpoints only at the start of user messages (at least 8192 tokens apart) and shortly before the end of the prompt, and keeps them in the slot file (INFO lines appended N context checkpoint(s) and restored N context checkpoint(s) tell when it does). Without a usable checkpoint it reads the whole prompt again, whatever the f_keep says, and it reports that only at trace level (-lv 4: forcing full prompt re-processing due to lack of cache data). That is why the story of a generation, of an annotation and of a redraft is sent as a chain of messages, each part as an answer of the model after a message of the user: the last message of the user is checkpointed, which is where the next request starts to differ, and a new part only adds messages at the end. Reading a cold prefill off the log: the first prompt processing, n_tokens = 4096 line comes after about 7 s here; if a prefix had been reused it would come after a second or two.

The prompt starts with the system message, and the story comes after it, so what is in the system message must stay the same from one request to the next. In the default master template the system message holds, in this order, the lore block, the summaries and the author's notes (annotations). When any of them changes between two requests, which is usual (the new text activates other lore entries, a summary is added, a note is added or resolved), the cache is valid only up to that point and the whole story behind it is read again. The oldest parts leave the prompt first when the story no longer fits, which moves the start of the story by one part on every turn. What helps:

Give the entries that change from part to part the insertion mode Before User Prompt (Order and insertion): they go to the end of the prompt, behind the story, and do not disturb the cache. Keep what is always true in the lore block.
Leave the blocks you do not use out of the master template (the author's notes, for example, if you do not give notes to the model), so that the system message stays the same.

Open Compare Prompt in the menu of a part to see where the cache ends: it compares the prompt of the part with the one of an earlier part (the nearest one by default; the box lists the parts before it and its swipes) and marks the first message that differs. See Compare Prompt.

c: selected slot by LCP similarity, sim_best = 0.163, f_keep = 0.151

p: Compare Prompt in the menu of a part (desktop and phone) answers why was the cache not used for this part? It lists the messages of the two prompts (the system message, then a user message and a model answer per part, then the user message of the turn) with a status for each: the same, changed, added or deleted. The first message that differs is highlighted and the ones after it are marked Read again, because a server reads everything after the first difference again. Above the table:
where the first difference is (message and character) and how much of the prompt, in characters and about in tokens, is the same from the start;

a reading of the difference: the system message differs (the jailbreak, the template, the lore, the summaries or the notes changed between the two requests: the usual cause), a part in the middle of the story differs (it was edited, regenerated or replaced by a summary), the start of the story moved (the oldest parts were left out or summarised), or the difference is only the last message of the earlier prompt, the user message of that turn, which the story does not repeat. That last case is the most a next part or a swipe can reuse; if the server still did not use its cache, the prompt is not the cause (check the slot, the model and the session id).

Selecting a message shows the two texts side by side, from just before the first difference. Only the messages are compared: the model, the tools of the request and the server slot are not part of the stored prompt. The part needs a stored prompt (parts typed by the author and parts generated before the prompts were kept have none).
The request kinds below matter for what is kept when you switch between them; the prompt decides how much of it is used.

l: Using it: one slot on disk with llama.cpp
p: A model the router unloaded without the hook knowing (a wrong models_max, another client) has an empty slot while the hook still thinks the last session is in it. A request for the same session simply reads its prompt again; a request for another one saves the empty slot over that session's file first, so its cache is lost too. Both only cost a prefill.
A restart of the proxy forgets which session is in the slot; the first request after it restores its file over the slot, and what the slot held is lost.
After you change the model of a route, delete its files in the folder (their names start with the route): a state saved by other weights does not fit the new model.

and switch it on in the LiteLLM config.yaml: the callback, and slot_cache in the model_info of the route that goes to the llama-server. One wildcard entry is enough, no model has to be listed in LiteLLM (the server knows them, and the client names the one it wants):

Every switch costs a save and a restore. With automatic annotation on, a part is followed by an annotation and a redraft, so one turn can swap three or four times. Measure a turn before you rely on it.

If nothing happens, look at the log of the proxy (docker logs litellm-proxy 21 | grep slot_cache): with the hook at work there is a line for every call, and a request of Marginalia for a route without slot_cache is reported once (not used for route: no model_info.slot_cache). No slot_cache line at all means the hook did not run: the container still has an older file or config. A single file mounted into a container (./slot_cache.py:/app/slot_cache.py) keeps showing the version it had when the container was created if an editor replaced the file; docker compose up -d --force-recreate picks the new one up (a plain restart does not). docker exec litellm-proxy grep -c save_idle_seconds /app/slot_cache.py prints 0 for a file that is too old.

In Docker the proxy and llama-server are two containers, so the folder of --slot-save-path is a directory of the host that both mount (the proxy needs to write there: it deletes old files and renews the age of the used ones), the hook file goes next to the LiteLLM config, and api_base is an address the proxy can reach, with the host name of the certificate when the server uses TLS:

Limits. Without a limit the folder grows with the number of routes, users and kinds. Set max_files (a number of files) and/or max_gib (their total size) in the slot_cache of a route (or LLAMA_CACHE_MAX_FILES and LLAMA_CACHE_MAX_GIB in the environment of the proxy for all routes) and the hook deletes the caches of that route that were used the longest ago after each save: restoring a cache counts as using it. It never deletes the cache it has just saved or the one it is about to restore (so a route with two sessions in turn keeps at least two files, whatever the limit), and it only touches the files of the route, so other routes and other files in the folder are safe. A single cache that is bigger than max_gib stays (with a warning in the log). Deleting needs the folder: set save_path (or LLAMA_SLOT_SAVE_PATH) to the --slot-save-path folder as the proxy sees it; with llama-server in a container, that is a volume both containers mount. Without it nothing is deleted. A deleted cache only means that its session reads its prompt again once. The limits are optional: a cron job on the host does as well when you do not need a cap on the size, for example find /srv/ai/slots -name '*.bin' -mtime +2 -delete (a cache that is in use is saved again whenever its session is swapped out, so its age keeps starting over). Files deleted from outside are harmless to the hook; a missing one is a miss.

llama-server does not log a plain save or restore (it logs the context checkpoints it appends or restores, and errors). What it did is in its answer, and the log of the proxy (with LITELLM_LOG=INFO) has it, with a line for every call the hook makes, for example slot_cache: https://… restore file (openai/model): ok (21920 tokens, 2580 MB, 3.1 s), … save file …: ok (…) or … restore … miss (400); the miss of the first request of a session is normal (llama-server logs it as "Unable to restore slot, no available space in KV cache or invalid slot save file"). Real problems are warnings: a certificate that does not match the address, a refused api key, a server that does not answer.

llama-server in router mode (many models behind one address, loaded on demand) works: every model is an instance of its own with its own slots, so the hook keeps the state per server, model and slot, and names the model in the body of its slot calls (the name the client used, without LiteLLM's openai/; the setting model gives another one, for a route whose name is not the model). It needs a llama.cpp from February 2026 or later, which forwards /slots to the instance (before it answered 400 Invalid action).

Requirement: a llama-server from 2026-10-08 or later (llama.cpp PR #26004, preserve context checkpoints across slot save/restore). An older one writes and restores the memory of the slot but not its context checkpoints, so a model with a sliding window (Gemma, for one) or a hybrid model reads the whole prompt again after every restore, however much of it is unchanged. Check the build with llama-server --version; a container image with a moving tag (full, server...) is not updated until you pull it.

Size. A file is as big as the memory of the slot holds: for a long story and a large model hundreds of megabytes to several gigabytes. There is one file per route, user and kind, and each is overwritten in place, so the folder stays as small as that. Check that restoring one is faster than reading the prompt (a fast SSD usually is, by a lot, for a long story: a few seconds against a minute of prefill). A measured example: a 31 B model on an AMD Radeon AI PRO R9700 with a prompt of about 9,000 tokens made files of 850-930 MB; a restore took 2-3.5 s and a save 3-10 s (the hook logs both), while reading that prompt again took 18-20 s at about 440 tokens per second. A swap costs a save and a restore, so it still wins by a wide margin, and the longer the story the more it wins, as a prefill grows with the prompt and a restore only with the size of the cache.

The details: when a request arrives from another session than the one in the slot, the hook saves the slot under the name of the session that was in it, restores the file of the new one (or empties the slot when there is no file yet), and lets the request go on. The files are kept per route (the model_name): a saved state fits only the model that wrote it, so the file is named after the route and the session, and two routes never share one, also when they use the same server and folder. The server then reads only what differs from the restored prompt. A cache that can't be restored, a file that is gone or a server that doesn't answer only means that the prompt is read again; the request itself never fails because of the hook.

The hook needs no address of its own: it uses the api_base and api_key of the route the request goes to (the slots are at the root of the server, so a trailing /v1 is dropped). Only the routes with slot_cache are touched; a request for any other model, a cloud one for instance, passes through even though it carries the header. Several servers work side by side, each with its own slot. With the wildcard the route is the model the client asked for, so the files are kept per model (qwen3-32b), and you can still list some models by name next to it if they need other settings. LiteLLM reads the part of a model name before a / as the provider, so for names that contain one (org/model, as in a router preset) use the route model_name: openai/* and give Marginalia the model as openai/org/model: the hook removes the openai/, and the files and the slot calls use the name the server knows. The routes and their model_info come from the model_list: a proxy started without one (only litellm --model ...) has neither, and the hook does nothing there. The one wildcard entry is the replacement.

The hook uses CustomLogger.async_pre_call_deployment_hook, which LiteLLM calls after it chose the deployment and before it sends the request (version 1.106.5 was checked with a real router and a stand-in server); check it against the version you run. A proxy that swaps models behind one address by restarting a single server (llama-swap) is not supported: the slot calls would reach whichever model is loaded. None of this was run against a real llama-server router; the tests use a stand-in that checks the calls the hook makes.

The value is for you if the server runs out of memory for caches. A local llama-server with enough memory for several slots can keep a cache for each kind of work and needs nothing more. With memory for one slot, every other kind of work throws the cache of the story away: the annotation of a part, the redraft after it and the next generation read their prompts again each time.

The way out is to keep the cache of every kind on disk and swap it into the one slot when a request of that kind arrives. llama-server can save a slot to a file and restore it; a proxy in front of it knows which kind a request is from the header. The example below is a hook for LiteLLM.
Things to know:

When the router may hold only some of its models (--models-max, 4 by default), asking for another one makes it unload the model used longest ago, and the slot of that model, with the cache in it, is gone. The hook follows the same order (set models_max in slot_cache, or LLAMA_MODELS_MAX, to the same number as --models-max; 0 for no limit) and saves that slot before the request that makes the router unload it. For that the proxy must be the only client of the router: a request that reaches it another way is not seen. A save never loads a model the router has unloaded. What it does: the cache of a session is written to disk when the slot is needed for another one (a request of another kind, another model, or the router unloading the model), not after every request: a 3 GB write after each generation would only slow the server down. So a file shows up after the first switch, for example generate, annotate, generate: the annotation first saves the generation. With save_idle_seconds in the slot_cache (or LLAMA_SAVE_IDLE_SECONDS) the cache is also written when no request came for that long, so the folder has it soon after you stop working; a request starts the wait over, and a cache that is on disk already is not written again at the next switch. The hook sends a save, restore or erase only when the slot is idle (it asks GET /slots, is_processing; without that endpoint it sends at once): llama-server parks such a call while a request runs and releases only one parked call each time a request ends, so a request of another client that arrived behind it could wait there for good. The server does nothing else while a save writes.

Where the prompt differs. For every request after the first of a session the log has a line that says how far the prompt is the same as the last one of that session, for example slot_cache: route_session prompt: 14 messages, the last one had 12: the first 11 are the same, message 12 (user) is the same for its first 2150 of 9031 characters. A server can reuse its cache only up to there (a message is about three or four characters per token), so this is the line to read when a second request reads almost everything again: the message it names is the one whose start changed. The line also compares the last message of the two prompts, which holds what changes (the lore, the part, the task): when the story grew by a part, the old last message is not at the same place any more, and the number of characters the two last messages share is how far the lore, for one, is the same in both.

"""LiteLLM hook: keeps the prompt cache of llama-server on disk, one file per X-Session-ID.

llama-server runs with ONE slot (-np 1) and --slot-save-path. Marginalia sends the header X-Session-ID, a hash of the
user and the kind of work (generation, annotate, redraft...). When a request for another session arrives, the hook saves
the slot under the name of the session that was in it and restores the file of the new one (or empties the slot when
there is none yet), so every kind of work finds its own cache and only one is in memory.

A saved state fits only the model that wrote it, so the files are kept per route: the name is the route (the model_name
of the LiteLLM config) and the session, and the limits below count the files of one route. Routes never share a file,
also when they point at the same server or share a folder. After you change the model behind a route, delete its files.

The server is the one the request is going to (its api_base and api_key in the LiteLLM config); only deployments that
ask for it are touched, with `model_info` in config.yaml. One wildcard entry covers a llama-server in router mode, no
model has to be listed (the route is then the model the client asked for):

    model_list:
      - model_name: "*"
        litellm_params: {model: "openai/*", api_base: "http://llama-server:8080/v1", api_key: none}
        model_info:
          slot_cache: true              # or the settings below, each one optional:
          # slot_cache: {slot: 0, save_path: /var/cache/llama-slots, max_files: 8, max_gib: 20, model: qwen}

In router mode every model is an instance of its own with its own slots: the slot calls name the model (the model of the
request without the `openai/` of LiteLLM, or `model` of the settings), so the state is kept per server, model and slot.
This needs a llama.cpp that routes /slots (PR 19854, 2026-02).

  slot        the slot to use, default 0 (environment LLAMA_SLOT)
  model       the model the router knows, when it is not the one in the request
  save_idle_seconds
              also save the cache of the session in the slot when no request came for this long (default 0: only
              when the slot is needed for another session or model; environment LLAMA_SAVE_IDLE_SECONDS). A save
              is sent when the slot is idle, and the server does nothing else while it writes.
  models_max  the --models-max of the router, default 4 (environment LLAMA_MODELS_MAX), 0 for no limit. The router
              unloads the model used longest ago when a request needs more than that; its slot is gone with it. The hook
              follows the same order and saves that slot BEFORE the request that makes the router unload it. Requests
              that reach the router without this proxy are not seen, so it must be the only client of the router.
  save_path   the folder of --slot-save-path as THIS process sees it; without it the files are never deleted
              (environment LLAMA_SLOT_SAVE_PATH)
  max_files   keep at most this many saved caches of the route, default no limit (environment LLAMA_CACHE_MAX_FILES)
  max_gib     keep at most this many GiB of saved caches of the route, default no limit (environment LLAMA_CACHE_MAX_GIB)
When a limit is passed, the caches that were used the longest ago are deleted first.

A save, restore or erase is only sent when the slot is idle (GET /slots, is_processing): llama-server parks such a call
while a request runs, and only one parked call is released each time a request ends, so a request of another client that
arrived behind it could wait there indefinitely. Without /slots the calls are sent at once.
"""
import asyncio
import collections
import hashlib
import logging
import os
import re

import httpx
from litellm.integrations.custom_logger import CustomLogger

try:
    # the logger of the proxy: its INFO lines show with LITELLM_LOG=INFO
    from litellm._logging import verbose_proxy_logger as log
except ImportError:
    log = logging.getLogger("slot_cache")

SLOT = int(os.environ.get("LLAMA_SLOT", "0"))
SAVE_PATH = os.environ.get("LLAMA_SLOT_SAVE_PATH")
MAX_FILES = int(os.environ.get("LLAMA_CACHE_MAX_FILES", "0"))
MAX_GIB = float(os.environ.get("LLAMA_CACHE_MAX_GIB", "0"))
# --models-max of llama-server in router mode (its default is 4, 0 is no limit)
MODELS_MAX = int(os.environ.get("LLAMA_MODELS_MAX", "4"))
SAVE_IDLE_SECONDS = float(os.environ.get("LLAMA_SAVE_IDLE_SECONDS", "0"))
IDLE_POLL_SECONDS = 1.0         # how often a busy slot is looked at ...
IDLE_WAIT_MAX_SECONDS = 3600    # ... and for how long at most
# the header is client input and becomes a file name: only what Marginalia sends is accepted
SESSION_ID = re.compile(r"^[0-9a-f]{32}$")


def route_tag(route):
    """The part of a file name that is the route: readable, safe as a file name, and told apart by a hash of the name."""
    return re.sub(r"[^A-Za-z0-9_-]", "_", route)[:40] + "-" + hashlib.sha256(route.encode()).hexdigest()[:8]


class CacheFolder:
    """The saved caches of one route in the folder of llama-server; deletes the least recently used ones beyond the
    limits (0 is no limit). The files of other routes are not touched and not counted."""

    def __init__(self, path, max_files=0, max_bytes=0, tag=""):
        self.path = path
        self.max_files = max_files
        self.max_bytes = max_bytes
        self.files = re.compile("^" + re.escape(tag) + r"_[0-9a-f]{32}\.bin$")

    def has(self, session):
        return bool(self.path) and os.path.exists(os.path.join(self.path, session + ".bin"))

    def touch(self, session):
        """A cache that was restored was just used: it is the last one to go."""
        if self.path:
            try:
                os.utime(os.path.join(self.path, session + ".bin"))
            except OSError:
                pass

    def evict(self, keep=()):
        """Deletes the oldest caches until the limits hold, never those of the sessions in `keep`."""
        if not self.path or not (self.max_files or self.max_bytes):
            return []
        try:
            entries = []
            for name in os.listdir(self.path):
                if self.files.match(name):
                    stat = os.stat(os.path.join(self.path, name))
                    entries.append((stat.st_mtime, name, stat.st_size))
        except OSError as e:
            log.warning("Cannot list %s: %s", self.path, e)
            return []
        entries.sort()
        count = len(entries)
        size = sum(entry[2] for entry in entries)
        removed = []
        for _, name, length in entries:
            if (not self.max_files or count <= self.max_files) and (not self.max_bytes or size <= self.max_bytes):
                break
            if name[:-len(".bin")] in keep:
                continue
            try:
                os.remove(os.path.join(self.path, name))
            except OSError as e:
                log.warning("Cannot delete %s: %s", name, e)
                continue
            count -= 1
            size -= length
            removed.append(name)
        if self.max_bytes and size > self.max_bytes:
            log.warning("The cache of one session alone is over the limit of %d bytes", self.max_bytes)
        return removed


class SlotSwitcher:
    """One slot of one llama-server and the cache (route and session) that is in it."""

    def __init__(self, base_url, slot=SLOT, client=None, model=None):
        self.base_url = base_url.rstrip("/")
        self.slot = slot
        # a router sends the call to the instance of this model (the body is read by the router)
        self.model = model
        # a swap waits for the slot to be idle, which can be as long as a generation takes
        self.client = client or httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=None)
        self.headers = {}
        self.current = None
        self.folder = None
        self.version = 0            # counts the requests: what the slot holds changed since the last save
        self.saved_version = 0
        self._idle = None
        self._lock = asyncio.Lock()

    async def _busy(self):
        """Whether the slot is processing a request. False when the server does not tell."""
        try:
            response = await self.client.get(f"{self.base_url}/slots", headers=self.headers, timeout=15,
                                             params={"model": self.model} if self.model else None)
            slots = response.json() if response.is_success else None
            return isinstance(slots, list) and any(
                slot.get("is_processing") for slot in slots
                if isinstance(slot, dict) and slot.get("id", self.slot) == self.slot)
        except (httpx.HTTPError, ValueError):
            return False

    async def _wait_idle(self):
        deadline = asyncio.get_running_loop().time() + IDLE_WAIT_MAX_SECONDS
        while await self._busy() and asyncio.get_running_loop().time() < deadline:
            await asyncio.sleep(IDLE_POLL_SECONDS)

    async def _action(self, action, key=None):
        body = {}
        if self.model:
            body["model"] = self.model
        if key:
            body["filename"] = key + ".bin"
        # nothing to save in a model the router has unloaded: it must not be loaded for that
        query = f"action={action}" + ("&autoload=false" if action == "save" else "")
        try:
            response = await self.client.post(f"{self.base_url}/slots/{self.slot}?{query}", json=body or None,
                                              headers=self.headers)
            if response.status_code in (401, 403):
                log.warning("slot_cache: %s %s: the server refused the api key (%d)", self.base_url, action,
                            response.status_code)
            detail = ""
            if response.is_success:
                try:
                    detail = describe(response.json())
                except ValueError:
                    pass
            log.info("slot_cache: %s %s %s (%s%s): %s", self.base_url, action, key or "", self.model or "-",
                     "" if self.slot == 0 else f", slot {self.slot}",
                     "ok" + detail if response.is_success else
                     (f"miss ({response.status_code})" if action == "restore" else f"failed ({response.status_code})"))
            return response.is_success
        except httpx.HTTPError as e:
            # a cache that is not there is only slower, never an error of the request
            log.warning("slot_cache: %s %s: %s", self.base_url, action, e)
            return False

    async def switch(self, key, api_key=None, folder=None, idle=SAVE_IDLE_SECONDS):
        """Puts the cache `key` (the file name without .bin) in the slot; `folder` has the limits of its route.
        With `idle` the cache is saved when no request came for that many seconds."""
        folder = folder or CacheFolder(SAVE_PATH, MAX_FILES, int(MAX_GIB * 1024 ** 3))
        await self._switch(key, api_key, folder)
        self.version += 1
        if idle:
            if self._idle and not self._idle.done():
                self._idle.cancel()
            self._idle = asyncio.create_task(self._save_when_idle(idle))

    async def _save_when_idle(self, seconds):
        await asyncio.sleep(seconds)
        version = self.version
        await self._wait_idle()         # a new request cancels this task, also while it waits
        async with self._lock:
            if self.current is None or version == self.saved_version:
                return
            if await self._action("save", self.current):
                self.saved_version = version
                if self.folder:
                    await asyncio.to_thread(self.folder.evict, {self.current})

    async def _switch(self, key, api_key, folder):
        async with self._lock:
            if key == self.current:
                return
            # the key of the deployment that asks now (a placeholder is not a key)
            self.headers = {"Authorization": "Bearer " + api_key} if api_key and api_key != "none" else {}
            self.folder = folder
            await self._wait_idle()
            # a cache that was saved after its last request (the idle save) is on disk already
            unchanged = self.saved_version == self.version and self.current is not None and folder.has(self.current)
            if self.current is not None and (unchanged or await self._action("save", self.current)):
                # not the cache that was just saved, and not the one that is about to be restored
                await asyncio.to_thread(folder.evict, {self.current, key})
                self.saved_version = self.version
            if await self._action("restore", key):
                await asyncio.to_thread(folder.touch, key)
            else:
                await self._action("erase")
            self.current = key

    async def release(self, api_key=None):
        """The model is about to be unloaded by the router: its slot goes, so the cache in it is saved first."""
        async with self._lock:
            if self.current is None:
                return
            self.headers = {"Authorization": "Bearer " + api_key} if api_key and api_key != "none" else {}
            await self._wait_idle()
            if await self._action("save", self.current) and self.folder:
                await asyncio.to_thread(self.folder.evict, {self.current})
            if self._idle and not self._idle.done():
                self._idle.cancel()
            self.current = None


def describe(body):
    """What llama-server says about a slot call that worked: it logs nothing itself, the numbers are in the answer."""
    if not isinstance(body, dict):
        return ""
    timings = body.get("timings") if isinstance(body.get("timings"), dict) else {}
    try:
        if "n_restored" in body:
            return f" ({body['n_restored']} tokens, {body.get('n_read', 0) / 1e6:.0f} MB, {timings.get('restore_ms', 0) / 1000:.1f} s)"
        if "n_saved" in body:
            return f" ({body['n_saved']} tokens, {body.get('n_written', 0) / 1e6:.0f} MB, {timings.get('save_ms', 0) / 1000:.1f} s)"
        if "n_erased" in body:
            return f" ({body['n_erased']} tokens dropped)"
    except (TypeError, ValueError):
        pass
    return ""


def text_of(message):
    """The text of a chat message: a string, or the text parts of a list."""
    content = message.get("content") if isinstance(message, dict) else None
    if isinstance(content, str):
        return content
    if isinstance(content, list):
        return "".join(part.get("text", "") for part in content if isinstance(part, dict))
    return ""


def compare(previous, messages):
    """Says where a prompt first differs from the last one of its session: a server can reuse its cache up to there, and not
    after it, however much of the rest is the same. `previous` and `messages` are lists of (role, text). The last message is
    compared with the last one of the other prompt as well: it holds what changes, and when a story grew by a message it is not
    at the same place."""
    shared = 0
    while shared < min(len(previous), len(messages)) and previous[shared] == messages[shared]:
        shared += 1
    if shared == len(previous) == len(messages):
        return f"the same as the last one ({len(messages)} messages)"
    if shared == len(previous) or shared == len(messages):
        said = (f"{len(messages)} messages, the last one had {len(previous)}: the first {shared} are the same, "
                f"{'new messages follow' if shared == len(previous) else 'the end is cut'}")
    else:
        role, text = messages[shared]
        same = len(os.path.commonprefix([previous[shared][1], text]))
        said = (f"{len(messages)} messages, the last one had {len(previous)}: the first {shared} are the same, message {shared + 1} "
                f"({role}) is the same for its first {same} of {len(text)} characters (the last one: {len(previous[shared][1])})")
    last_now, last_before = messages[-1][1], previous[-1][1]
    return (said + f"; the last message is the same as the last one's last message for its first "
            f"{len(os.path.commonprefix([last_before, last_now]))} of {len(last_now)} characters (the last one: {len(last_before)})")


def upstream_model(model):
    """The name the server knows the model by: LiteLLM's name is `openai/<name>`."""
    return model[len("openai/"):] if model and model.startswith("openai/") else model


def server_root(api_base):
    """The slots are at the root of llama-server, the API address of the model ends in /v1."""
    base = api_base.rstrip("/")
    return base[:-len("/v1")] if base.endswith("/v1") else base


class SlotCacheHook(CustomLogger):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.switchers = {}
        self.loaded = {}            # per server: the models the router has loaded, the one used longest ago first
        self.skipped = set()        # the routes that were reported as not used
        self.last = {}              # the messages of the last prompt of each session, to say where the next one differs
        self.client = httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=None)

    def explain(self, key, messages):
        if not isinstance(messages, list):
            return
        current = [(m.get("role"), text_of(m)) for m in messages if isinstance(m, dict)]
        previous = self.last.get(key)
        self.last[key] = current
        if previous is not None:
            log.info("slot_cache: %s prompt: %s", key, compare(previous, current))

    async def make_room(self, root, model, models_max, api_key):
        """Follows the models the router has loaded; the ones it unloads for `model` get their slot saved first."""
        if not models_max or not model:
            return
        loaded = self.loaded.setdefault(root, collections.OrderedDict())
        loaded[model] = None
        loaded.move_to_end(model)
        while len(loaded) > models_max:
            gone, _ = loaded.popitem(last=False)
            for (r, m, _slot), switcher in list(self.switchers.items()):
                if r == root and m == gone:
                    await switcher.release(api_key)

    # runs after the router chose the deployment (so its api_base is known) and before the request is sent
    async def async_pre_call_deployment_hook(self, kwargs, call_type):
        headers = (kwargs.get("proxy_server_request") or {}).get("headers") or {}
        session = headers.get("x-session-id")
        options = (kwargs.get("model_info") or {}).get("slot_cache")
        api_base = kwargs.get("api_base")
        # the route the client asked for; without one the files of the models could not be told apart
        route = (kwargs.get("metadata") or {}).get("model_group") or kwargs.get("model")
        if not (session and SESSION_ID.match(session)):
            return None
        if not (options and api_base and route):
            # a request of Marginalia that is passed through: say why, once per route
            why = "no model_info.slot_cache" if not options else "no api_base" if not api_base else "no route"
            if (route, why) not in self.skipped:
                self.skipped.add((route, why))
                log.info("slot_cache: not used for %s: %s", route, why)
            return None
        options = options if isinstance(options, dict) else {}
        tag = route_tag(route)
        folder = CacheFolder(options.get("save_path", SAVE_PATH), int(options.get("max_files", MAX_FILES)),
                             int(float(options.get("max_gib", MAX_GIB)) * 1024 ** 3), tag)
        slot = int(options.get("slot", SLOT))
        model = options.get("model") or upstream_model(kwargs.get("model"))
        where = (server_root(api_base), model, slot)
        self.explain(f"{tag}_{session}", kwargs.get("messages"))
        await self.make_room(where[0], model, int(options.get("models_max", MODELS_MAX)), kwargs.get("api_key"))
        if where not in self.switchers:
            self.switchers[where] = SlotSwitcher(where[0], slot, self.client, model)
        await self.switchers[where].switch(f"{tag}_{session}", kwargs.get("api_key"), folder,
                                           float(options.get("save_idle_seconds", SAVE_IDLE_SECONDS)))
        return None

p: A protocol is a set of generation settings: the sampling parameters (temperature, top P and penalties) and, optionally, its own context and reply limits. The inference provider says which model writes; the protocol says how.

Protocols are separate from providers, so you can keep a few of them, such as a cautious one and a creative one, and switch a book between them without touching the connection. Like providers, protocols belong to your account.
The Protocols tab
Every sampling parameter has an Enable checkbox. A parameter that is not enabled is not set by Marginalia, and the model uses its own default. Enable only what you want to change.
Field
Frequency Penalty
Max Context Tokens
Max Reply Tokens
Name
Nucleus sampling: the model picks only from the most likely words whose probabilities add up to this value (0-1). 0.9-0.95 is a common choice.

Open the Protocols tab and click Add Protocol. Existing protocols are edited with the pen button and deleted with the trash button. The clone button (two sheets) makes a copy of a protocol, with all its settings, under a name you confirm (the original's with (Copy)), handy for trying other sampling settings without losing the ones that work.
Optional. The longest response. Empty uses the provider's Max Response Tokens.
Optional. Total tokens for prompt and response of books using this protocol. Empty uses the provider's Max Context Size.
Penalizes words by how often they already appeared, which reduces repetition. Usually 0-1.
Penalizes words that already appeared at all, which pushes the model to new topics. Usually 0-1.
Presence Penalty
Randomness of the text. Lower (around 0.7) is more focused and predictable, higher (1.0 and more) is more varied and surprising.
Temperature
The protocol dialog
The request format. Currently only Chat Completion.
Top P
Type
Your name for the protocol, e.g. Creative or Long context.
The limits of the inference provider always apply. A protocol can lower them, each one separately, but never raise them above the provider's:
Protocol value set
Protocol value empty
Context
Max Context Tokens, or the provider's Max Context Size if that is smaller
provider's Max Context Size
Response
Max Reply Tokens, or the provider's Max Response Tokens if that is smaller
provider's Max Response Tokens
A protocol with Max Context Tokens 128 000 used with a provider of 32 000 gets 32 000: the provider is what the service (or the administrator who shares it) allows.

Marginalia keeps room for the response free and fills the rest of the context with the prompt: templates, lorebook entries, summaries and as much of the story as fits. With a context of 32 000 tokens and responses of up to 2 000 tokens, the prompt gets 30 000 tokens. The response limit is also sent to the API (max_completion_tokens).

Use the protocol limits to keep prompts shorter than the model allows, for example to make long books cheaper and faster with a large-context cloud model, or to keep responses shorter for some books. The protocol limits are also used for summaries of books with this protocol.
Leave both empty unless you need them: the provider's values then apply, and when you change the provider of a book, its limits come along.

A book is one story. You give it instructions part by part, the model writes the text, and the book keeps everything that goes with it: the story tree with all its branches, the prompts that shape the style, the lorebook with the world and characters, summaries and backups.
A book in the story editor
A book is made of parts. Each part is one answer of the model, written from the instructions you gave for it (scene, point of view character, characters present and what should happen).

Parts form a tree. Usually you just continue the story, but you can also write another version of the last part, or go back and continue differently from any earlier part. Each path from the beginning to an end is a branch. The branch you are working on is the active branch; the story editor shows it, and only its parts are sent to the model. See Branches & story tree.
A book without parts opens on About, a book with parts on Story. All changes are saved right away; there is no Save button. Exit closes the book.

Tag books (next to Add Book) opens a window that puts one tag on many books, or takes it off them, without opening each. Pick the Tag (or type a new one and press Enter) and the list shows every book with its tags; the books that have the picked tag come first and show it highlighted. Each row has a + button that applies the tag to that book and a - button that removes it. To do the same for several books, tick their check boxes (the box in the header ticks all) and use Apply the tag to the checked or Remove the tag from the checked at the bottom. A book an agent works on is grayed out: it is locked, so it can not be ticked or changed until the run is paused or stopped. The same window tags lorebooks and their entries.

l: Changing the model and protocol of many books
p: The Mass changes menu (next to Tag books) has the item Mass Change Model/Protocol. It opens a window that puts one Model and/or one Protocol on many books without opening each. Leave a box empty (it shows Do not replace) and that part of the books stays as it is: pick only a model to change the models and keep the protocols. The table lists the books of the current folder by name with the model and protocol they have now; Include subfolders adds the books below it. Type in the filter under Name to narrow the list, tick the books to change (the box in the header ticks all the books that are shown) and press Replace and exit. Books that the filter hides are unticked, so only what you see is changed. A book an agent works on is grayed out: it is locked, so it can not be ticked or changed until the run is paused or stopped.

The item Mass Change Language of the same menu works the same way for the Language of the books: pick the language, filter and tick the books, press Replace and exit. The table shows the language each book has now, with what it inherits from its folders (see Language).
Changing the language of many books
Tag books and the item Tag folders work on the books, or on the folders, of the current folder in the same way.
Click Add Book.
Enter the name and confirm.

The new book is put into the folder the list shows, and so are the books you import from an archive or from SillyTavern. It opens right away. It starts with your Default Model and Default Protocol from the Settings tab (see Account & settings), if you have set them; otherwise select them on the About tab before generating.

To start a book from a folder of text files, use the import button (file icon, Import from archive) next to Add Book: upload a .zip of .md files and the new book, named after the archive, gets a part for each file, see Importing text files.
Importing a zip of text files as a new book

To continue a roleplay or story you started in SillyTavern, use the import button with the speech bubbles (Import from SillyTavern) next to Add Book. In SillyTavern, export the chat (Manage chat files, or take the .jsonl files from data/user/chats/character/), then:
Upload one or more .jsonl chats. A file that is not a SillyTavern chat is refused, the others stay.
Give the book a name (it is filled from the character of the first chat).

Tick Merge user and assistant messages into one part if you want one part per turn: the message of the user (several messages in a row are joined with an empty line) becomes the instructions of the part and the answer after it its text. Without it every message is a part of its own, with its text as the text of the part, so the book reads like the chat did.
Click Import. A progress window with Stop shows the parts being stored; stopping keeps what was stored.
Importing a SillyTavern chat

SillyTavern copies the chat when you create a branch or a checkpoint, so the chats of one story share their beginning. Upload them together and Marginalia finds the common messages and stores them once: the chats become the branches of one tree, which you can walk in the tree view. The swipes (alternative answers) of a message become sibling parts, and the book opens at the end of the chat written last (by the date of its last message). Chats that don't begin with the same message become separate first parts. Hidden (system) messages are skipped, and so are swipes that are empty. The reasoning and the model name of an answer are kept with the part.
To start a book from a backup file, use Import Backup as New Book in the Settings tab, see Book backups.

Folders sort your books the way folders on a disk sort files. A folder holds books and other folders, as deep as you like, and the books list shows one folder at a time. A folder can also hold settings (language, point of view, tense, style, the templates and the prompts): the books in it, and in the folders below it, write with them unless they have their own. That is the main reason to use folders: set the style of a series once, and every book of the series has it.
The Books tab with folders

Above the books the list shows the folders of the current one, in the order of the sorted columns. Click the name of a folder to open it. The path of buttons above the list (Books / Sci-fi / Expanse) shows where you are; click a part of it to go back there.

The check box Include subfolders lists every book below the current folder, at any depth (at the top level that is all your books), and adds a Folder column with the place of each. The current folder and the check box are remembered, also when you reload the page.

A folder row shows how many books are beneath it, at any depth. A book row shows the words and tokens of its active branch. The Name and Tags filters work on folders as well as books (folders have tags, see Tagging folders), in the current folder, or below it with Include subfolders.

A folder's Last Modified follows its books: when a book in it, or in a folder below it, changes (or one of its parts does), the folder is touched too. Sort by it to see where you wrote last. Opening a book, or moving it, does not count.
