l: Where the settings of a book come from
p: A book uses, for every one of these settings, the first of these that is not empty:
the book itself (its About and Prompts tabs),
the folder the book is in,
the folder above that one, and so on up to the top,
your user settings (Settings → Templates, see Account & settings),
the built-in default.

A blank text counts as not set. This is looked up when it is needed (when a part is generated, a summary made, a part redrafted...), nothing is copied into the book when you put it into a folder: moving a book to another folder changes how it writes, and changing a setting of a folder changes every book below it that does not set its own.
The Prompts tab of a book shows it: under each field is where its value comes from (Inherited from the folder "Sci-fi", Inherited from your settings or Built-in default).

The Language box of a book (the About tab) and of a folder can be left empty, which means inherit: the book takes the language of the nearest folder above it that sets one, else English. An empty box shows which language that is and where it comes from. The box has a clear button; clearing it inherits again (it used to turn into English). Everything that shows or uses the language of a book uses the one it has with its folders: the hyphenation of the text, the export and the Mass Change Language table.
The trash button of a folder asks what to do:
an empty folder is deleted after a confirmation;

a folder with books or folders in it offers Move its content to the folder above (the default) or Delete everything in it as well. The second asks again, with the numbers of books and folders, and sends the books to the Trash, where you can bring them back. A deleted folder itself is not listed in the Trash.

If a folder inside has the name of a folder in the folder above, moving the content up is refused (names are unique): rename one of them first. A folder with a book that an agent works on can't be deleted or moved, as the settings of that book would change under the run.

An annotation is a note for you about a passage of a part: weak scene, timeline is wrong, revisit. It works like a comment in a word processor: the text of the story stays clean, the passage is only marked, and the note lives next to it. Notes can also come from a model or from an extension that checks the story.
An annotation is for the author. It is not sent to the model unless you say so for that note, see Giving a note to the model.
Passage
The words the note is about, or the whole part.
Note
What you want to remember.
Type
An optional word you choose (continuity, style, pacing...).
Source
Who wrote it: you, a model (AI), an agent or an extension. The mark in the text has a different colour for each.
Status
Open, Resolved, Dismissed or Orphaned. Only open notes are marked in the text.
A part can have any number of annotations, also on overlapping passages.

On a passage. Select the words in the text of the part (they can have formatting, the selection does not have to be exact), then right click it (a long press on a phone) and choose Annotate selection, or press its key (a). The window shows the passage; write the note, an optional type, and whether the model gets the note, and Save. The menu (☰) of the part has no such item: opening it takes the selection away. The right click menu has Annotate selection, Redraft selection and Copy, and replaces the one of the browser on the text of a part, so it has Copy too. While the part is being edited, the selection in the editor is used: the edit is saved first.
On the whole part. Choose Annotate part in the menu of the part.
With a model. Choose Annotate with AI, see below.

A speech bubble with a number in the header of a part counts the notes of the part that need a look. Click it to see them all, also the ones about the whole part and the ones that lost their passage.

Brings a closed note back.
Changes the note and the type.

For a note without a passage: select text in the part, then click it.
Give to the model with the part

In the margin (the cogs menu of the story, Annotations in the margin; desktop only, and remembered for you) the notes of every part stand in a column left of its text, in the order of their passages, instead of in the popover. The note under the pointer and its underlined passage light up together, and a click on a passage brings its note into view. The notes are the same ones (resolve, edit...); resolved and dismissed notes are not shown there, as they are not underlined.
See below.
The Annotations tab

The Annotations tab lists the notes of the whole book, grouped by part in the order of the story, with a filter (Need a look, Closed, All). Show in story (or the number of the part) takes you to the part.
The note is not worth dealing with. Same.
The note of an underlined passage, opened at the mark
The notes in the margin of a part
The problem is dealt with. The note leaves the text and stays in the list.
You do not have to care where a note is when you edit. Marginalia keeps the passage of each note with the words it was about:
text added or removed before the passage moves it;
an edit inside the passage makes it longer or shorter;
words you type right at the start or end of the passage are outside of it;
fixing a typo in a one word passage keeps the note on that word.

When the passage is deleted or rewritten so that it can't be found, the note becomes Orphaned. It is kept: attach it to another passage (Attach to selection), dismiss it, or delete it. If you bring the words back (undo), the note finds its passage again.

When a part is generated again the text is new, so the notes find their passages again by the words they quoted; the ones whose words are gone are orphaned. When two parts are merged, the notes of the later one move to the merged part. A branch of a part copies its notes. Notes are part of backups, copies of a book and exports of a backup.

Annotate with AI in the menu of a part asks a model to review it. You say what to look for (flag continuity errors, weak dialogue, contradicts the lore; empty uses the task of the prompt), choose the model, and Annotate.

The model reads the part like the redraft does: the part, the story before it (older story as summaries), as much of the story after it as fits, the lore and the style of the book, and the notes the part already has so it does not repeat them. It never gives positions: it quotes the passage, and Marginalia finds the quote in the text. A quote that is not found is not lost: the note is proposed as a note about the whole part, marked not found in the text.
Nothing is added to the book until you accept. The notes the model proposes are listed with a check box each (all checked); uncheck the ones you do not want and choose Add the selected annotations.
Option
Model
The model that reviews. Empty is the Default model for annotating from your settings, else the model of the book. Reviewing is analysis, so this is often not the model that writes the prose.
Answer format

Automatic (structured, when the model can answer in JSON), Structured (JSON), Text blocks (for models that do not keep to a format) or Free critique, then extraction (the model writes a free review, a second model, usually a cheaper one, turns it into notes: choose it under Model that extracts the notes).
The notes a model proposes for a part

A range of parts (batch). Annotate with AI in the menu of a part reviews that part only. To review several, open the settings menu (⚙) of the story and choose Annotate a range of parts with AI (on a phone too). It is the same window with From part and To part to choose (both are required, Annotate waits for them; it does not matter which is the earlier; only parts with a text are listed). Annotate then reviews the parts of the range one after another, with the same instructions, answer format and model, each read with the story around it like a single part. The proposals are listed under the number of their part, all checked, and Add the selected annotations adds each to its own part. Stop stops the part in progress and starts no more; what was found until then stays in the list. A part whose answer can't be read or that does not fit the context of the model is skipped (the window says which) and the run goes on; a failure of the model ends the run. Every part is a request to the model, so a long range costs as many requests (and tokens).
Annotating a range of parts: the proposals are listed under the number of their part
If an answer can't be read, Marginalia asks once more; if it still can't be read, the model's answer is shown so the work is not lost. The prompt is the annotate prompt.
Add the annotations without asking
Annotate every generated part automatically
Apply the redraft without asking

Closing a window ends the whole run. If you close or stop the annotation window, nothing is added and no redraft follows; if you close the redraft window, the part keeps its text. A model that finds nothing closes its window (with a message) and nothing follows, since there is nothing to redraft. A window that stays open (no automatic add, an answer that could not be read, a stopped run) waits for you; closing it ends the run.

Every generated part costs at least one more request to the model (two with the redraft). If you generate with a local server that keeps only one prompt in its cache, the review replaces the story in it and the next generation has to read the story again: choose another Model for the review, or a second server.
Model, Protocol

Only with the one above. After the notes were added the redraft window opens and starts at once, with Deal with the open annotations of the part checked and no instructions of its own. It writes with the model of the book and does not offer to revalidate summaries: the part is new, no summary describes it.

Only with the redraft. When the model is done the redraft replaces the text of the part, the notes it dealt with are marked resolved and the window closes. Without it the window stays open for you to look at the result.
Option

The automatic redraft window has two tabs: Redrafted text (the text as the model writes it, its reasoning and the differences against the part) and Original text with annotations (the part as it was, with the passages of the open notes marked as in the story, and the notes under it). Look at the original to see what the model was asked to deal with, and stop the redraft or close the window if it is not going the way you want; the part keeps its text.
The instructions, as in Annotate with AI. Empty uses the task of the prompt.
The model that reviews. Empty is the model of the book (not the Default model for annotating of your settings, which the window you open yourself starts with).

The settings menu (⚙) of the story has Automatic annotation (on a phone too; a check mark shows that it is on). It makes the book review each part right after it was generated, and optionally redraft it. The settings are stored with the book:
The settings of the automatic annotation
Then redraft the part to address the annotations
Turns it on. After a part was generated (a new part, a swipe or a regeneration; not one that was stopped or failed) the annotation window opens and starts at once.
What to look for
When the model is done, the notes it found are added and the window closes. Without it the window stays open with the proposals, as when you start it yourself.

l: Giving a note to the model
p: Check Give to the model with the part on a note and it becomes a note to the model too: the notes of the parts that are in the prompt go into the master template as {{annotations}} (the built-in template has a block Author's notes on the story; a template of your own has to use the variable). Only open notes with this check are given, and only for the parts that fit into the prompt. Use it for what the model should keep in mind while it continues (this character is hiding the letter), not for editing remarks.

When a part has open notes, the redraft window has a check box Deal with the open annotations of the part. Checked, the model gets the notes (the passage and the note) together with your instructions and rewrites the part to deal with them; when you Apply the redraft, those notes are marked resolved. In the redraft of a selection only the notes whose passage overlaps the selection are given.

/list-annotations, /get-annotation, /create-annotation, /update-annotation, /resolve-annotation, /reattach-annotation and /delete-annotation work with the notes from the command line. Extensions can use the same commands. /generate-annotation part is Annotate with AI as a command: the model reviews the part with the model of the book (an agent uses its own model when Write the book with the model of the agent is on; profile picks another model profile of the agent), with the instructions, answer format and prompt of the book, and every note it finds is added at once, since there is nobody to pick them. It is one request to the model, so it runs alone and costs tokens.

An agent reads and writes annotations with the same commands: it can annotate a whole book (continuity, style...), resolve notes it dealt with, edit or delete them. It works on a copy of the book, so nothing reaches your notes until you review the result:

A note the agent made is a line Annotation - Added, one it resolved, dismissed or rewrote is Changed (with the note, type, status and give to the model as the fields, each with its own Take this change box), one it deleted is Deleted. The notes of a part the agent deleted go with the part and have no lines.

The line says in which part the note is (3: and the start of the note); Show in the copy opens the part in the agent's copy. A note on a part the agent wrote needs that part: ticking the note ticks the part too.

Only annotations above the list ticks the notes alone. The passage of a taken note is the same one when the text of the part is the same; when you take the agent's new text of the part, or your own text differs, the note finds its words again in the text of your book and, when it can't, becomes a note about the whole part.

A note you wrote while the agent was paused comes into its copy when it resumes (and a note you resolved is resolved there), so it knows about it; a note you and the agent both changed is a conflict like any other.
A read only look at the lore of the book, see The lorebook tab.
Annotations (left, next to the Outline)
Area
Bottom bar
Lorebook (left, next to the Outline)

One entry per part, #1, #2... with the part's database ID. Click an entry to scroll to the part (the parts before it are loaded first when it is not loaded yet). The header shows how many parts the branch has. The Chapter Marker extension shows chapter titles here.
Outline (left)
Story (center)
The notes on passages of the story, for the whole book.

The story always opens at the bottom, at the newest part. A long book is not drawn all at once: only the last parts are loaded, and the earlier ones are added above as you scroll up, without moving the part you are reading. The parts at the other end are dropped again, so no more than the Parts loaded at once in the story setting of your account stay loaded (empty loads all of them). If you scroll faster than the parts arrive, a Loading earlier parts (or later parts) mark at the edge says that there is more. Clicking a part in the outline, or finding one with the search, loads the parts around it, and starting a new part brings you back to the end of the story.
The story editor
The Story tab of a book is where you write. It shows the parts of the active branch from the beginning to the end.
The Summaries button (list icon) and the settings menu (⚙) on the left, the command line, and the + button on the right.
The text of each part, with its menu (☰) and its metadata on the right, and under it the bottom bar.

This is how a new book looks. All of these are tabs you can arrange as you like, the story included, see Arranging the tabs. The divider between the sidebar and the story can be dragged, and Marginalia remembers where you left it (saved with the book) and returns to it when you open the book again.
This page describes the desktop layout. On a phone the story is one column with the outline in a drawer, see Using Marginalia on a phone.

Above the outline there is a search field for the text of the branch you are on (the search of the story tree searches all branches). Because a long book is not loaded all at once, the search of the browser (Ctrl+F) cannot find text in the parts that are not loaded; this one can.

Type what you look for; the search starts when you stop typing. Several words must all be in the same part, a phrase goes in double quotes (old key) and * stands for any characters (light*house). The case does not matter.

Every place where a word stands is a match, and they are numbered through the whole branch. Below the field you see Match 3 of 27, in part #5 and a bar with how far you are. The story scrolls to the match and loads the parts around it when they are not loaded.
The up and down buttons go to the previous and the next match (after the last one it goes round to the first). Enter in the field does the same as the down button, Shift+Enter as the up button.
All the matches in the loaded parts are highlighted in the text, the match you are at in a stronger colour. Clear the field to remove the highlight.
On the phone the search is in the outline drawer; the drawer closes when it shows a match, open it again for the next one.

The Lorebook tab of the sidebar shows the lore of the book's lorebook without leaving the story, so you do not have to swap tabs to check what an entry says. It is a preview: nothing can be changed here, change the lore in the book's Lorebook tab. It is read again every time you come back to the Story tab, so changes you made there show at once.

Every entry is a row with its name; the arrow opens it to show its content (rendered as Markdown) and the text that activates it (the Filtering Text/Pattern, with a note when it is a regular expression).

Include sub lorebooks shows the lorebook and each of its sub lorebooks (and theirs, however deep) as rows of their own, with their entries under them; click the arrow of a lorebook to hide its entries. Without it only the entries of the book's lorebook are listed.
Entries and lorebooks that are switched off (they are not used for the story) are shown dimmed.
A book without a lorebook shows a note instead.
The Lorebook tab with two entries opened
Like every tab of the editor it can be dragged out into a panel of its own, see below.

The editor is a set of tabs: the Story itself (the parts and the bottom bar under them), the Outline, the Lorebook, and the tabs extensions add (Characters, Arcs, Side Query...). Drag a tab by its header to rearrange them (desktop only, the phone keeps one column with the outline in a drawer). A new book has the Outline and the Lorebook in a panel on the left and the Story in a column of its own on the right; you can put the story anywhere, for example in the middle with the outline on one side and the lore on the other, or above the outline:

Drop it on one of the dashed strips that appear above, between and under the panels of a column to detach it into a panel of its own in that column; the panels of a column are stacked under each other.

Drop it on one of the tall strips at the left, right or between the columns to detach it to the side: it gets a column of its own, next to the others. Widen the editor with the dividers to make room for more columns.
The panels and the columns are separated by splitters: drag them to give each panel the room you need. The sizes are saved with the arrangement.
The sidebar with Characters in a column of its own and Side Query under it

Drop it on the tab header or on the body of another panel to join that panel (dropping on a tab puts it before that tab, dropping on the body puts it last). A panel that loses its last tab disappears, and so does a column without panels.

The arrangement and the sizes are saved with the book, so it is the same the next time you open it and in every browser; the tab each panel shows is remembered with the rest of your workspace. A tab of an extension that is not loaded keeps its place for when the extension is back.

The story is always somewhere: its tab can't be closed, and a tab that lives in a panel together with other tabs is hidden while another one is selected. Whatever shows a part brings the story back: clicking an entry of the outline, a hit of the search, choosing a branch in the story tree, and starting a generation select the Story tab first. While a generation runs the other tabs are disabled and only the story stays usable, so you can stop it.

Every tab but the story has a small – button next to its name. It minimizes the tab: the tab leaves its panel (a panel whose tabs are all minimized disappears for the time being) and a round icon of it, a circle with one or two letters (Ch for the outline, Lo for the lorebook, An for the annotations, SQ for Side Query, and so on), shows up in a bar at the edge of the editor. Hover over the icon to see which tab it is. Nothing is closed, the tab keeps what it was showing. Click the icon and the tab comes back to the panel and the place among the tabs where it was, and is shown.

The bar is there while some tab is minimized. The button at its top (the circling arrows) sends the bar to the next side of the editor, clockwise: left, top, right, bottom. The story can't be minimized, so there is always something on the screen.
Minimized tabs in the bar at the edge of the editor
Which tabs are minimized and where the bar is are saved with the book, together with the arrangement and the sizes.

A new book opens with the standard arrangement (the outline, the lorebook and the annotations on the left, the story on the right). To make your own arrangement the standard one, set the tabs as you like them (panels, sizes, minimized tabs, the side of the bar) and choose Save layout as my default in the settings menu (⚙) of the story. Every book that has no arrangement of its own (a book you have not rearranged) then opens with it; a book you have arranged keeps its arrangement. The default is kept in your user settings.

To go back to the default arrangement, choose Restore default layout in the settings menu (⚙) of the story and confirm. This is the one you saved, or the standard one when you saved none. It only moves the tabs back (and forgets the sizes and what is minimized): your texts, the tab each panel shows and the tabs of extensions stay, the latter in the first panel.
Click + in the bottom right corner. The New Turn Instructions panel opens.
Click Generate.

Fill in the fields. All of them are optional, but the model needs at least some direction:

How the fields get into the prompt is set by the book's User Prompt. With the default user prompt, the model gets them as Current Location & Time, Point of View Character, Characters Currently Present / State and Plot Specifications for the Next Part.
Instructions
POV Character
Present Characters

Scene Setting, POV Character and Present Characters are filled in from the last part, so you only change what is different. Instructions starts empty each time.
The new part appears at the end and fills in as the model writes it. For reasoning models the reasoning appears first under View Reasoning.
The New Turn Instructions panel
The text is written in Markdown: *italics*, **bold**, # Heading and so on are shown formatted. A part with a # heading is a chapter for the Chapter Marker extension.
What should happen in this part.

When the model returns an error (server not reachable, wrong API key, context too long...), the error is shown. If no text arrived yet, the story stays as it was: a new part or swipe is removed and a regenerated part gets its previous text back. Text that already arrived before the error is kept, like with Stop. Fix the problem and generate again.
Where and when the part takes place, e.g. The lighthouse, a stormy night in late autumn.

While a part is being generated, the + button turns into a red Stop button. Stopping keeps the text written so far as the part. The rest of the book window is disabled until the generation finishes or is stopped.
Who is in the scene, and in what state.
Whose point of view the part is written from.
Do not know what should happen next? Draft Instructions under the Instructions field of the panel lets the model write the instructions in your place, the way you would. A window opens with:
Guidance

What the part should be about: a rough idea, a direction ("she confronts him about the letter"), or nothing at all, and the model continues the story where it leads. It starts as what you already typed into Instructions.
Plan of the Story
Only when something gives one. The Arc Outline does, with the data of the current chapter. Read only; the model follows it.

Draft Instructions starts the model and streams the answer into Drafted Instructions, which you can change or empty before you go on; Draft Again tries once more, Stop keeps what has arrived. Nothing is changed until you click Use as Instructions: the text then replaces the Instructions of the panel (the other fields are not touched) and the panel opens again, ready for Generate.

The model gets the story so far (the older story as summaries, as in a generation), the scene setting, POV and present characters that are in the panel, the lore of the last part, your latest instructions as examples of how you write them, your guidance and the plan. It does not see your lorebook entries that a new turn would activate. The request is the impersonate prompt. The model is the one of the book; drafting costs tokens like any request.
Drafting the instructions of the next turn
The same is the command /impersonate, which returns the text. Agents do not get it, they write the story with instructions of their own.

Turn Details opens the Scene Setting, POV Character, Present Characters and Instructions the part was written from. For the last part they can be changed (changes are saved right away) and are used by Regenerate and Swipe. For earlier parts they are read-only.

Editing a part that a summary covers makes that summary outdated; Marginalia notices it at the next generation and drops the summary.

A key without Ctrl, Alt or Meta (such as +, s, r, e, a, /) works only when no text field has the focus, so it never gets in the way of typing. The shortcuts work in the story tab of the open book and not while another window is open above it. The buttons show their key in the tooltip, and the menu of the last part shows it after Edit, Regenerate and Swipe. On a Mac Cmd works where a key says Ctrl (unless you gave that Cmd key to another action). You can change every key in Settings → Keyboard shortcuts.

On a computer (the phone layout has none) the writing loop works with the keyboard:
Opens the editor of the last part.
Opens the New Turn Instructions panel with the cursor in Instructions.

Saves the part that is being edited (also while the cursor is in its text).
Shows the next / previous tab, going through the tabs of all sheets in the order of the layout and round again.

Swipe / Regenerate the last part.

Delete removes the part from the story. The parts that followed it stay and continue from the part before it, so deleting a part in the middle of the story just takes it out. Deleting the last part makes the part before it the new end of the branch.

The settings menu (⚙) has Mass delete. Turning it on puts a check box at the left of every part and shows a bar under the story with the number of ticked parts and a Delete button. Tick the parts you want to get rid of (the ticks are kept while you scroll, the story loads only a window of the parts); Shift + click on a check box ticks (or clears) all the parts between it and the one you clicked before; a ticked part is tinted red. Then press Delete: after a confirmation the parts are deleted one by one behind a progress bar that can't be stopped. They are deleted as a single part is: the parts that followed a deleted part continue from the part before it, and the deleted parts go to the trash. Then the story is shown again and the mass delete is off. Cancel in the bar, or choosing Mass delete again, turns it off without deleting anything. Starting a generation also turns it off.
Mass delete with some parts ticked

Regenerate and Swipe work on the last part only and write it from scratch. Redraft works on any part, also an old one in the middle of the story, and keeps what you do not ask to change. Choose Redraft in the menu of the part:

Write what should change in Instructions for the redraft: add more dialogue between the two, make the fight longer, remove the explanation of the map, keep the ending as it is. Empty instructions write the part again with the same events.

Choose Redraft. The text streams into Redrafted text; Stop ends it early. Choose Redraft again for another try, with other instructions if you like. Differences shows what changed against the part, word by word. When the part has open annotations, Deal with the open annotations of the part (checked at first) gives them to the model as well, and Apply marks them resolved.

The redrafted text is a field you can still edit (its corner icon makes it grow to fit the whole text), and Differences follows your edits. Apply replaces the text of the part with it; Close throws it away. Nothing in the book changes before Apply.
The redraft window: the instructions, the new text and the differences

The model gets the redraft prompts: the part, your instructions, the story before the part (the older story as summaries where there are valid ones, the rest as text, the newest part first when it does not all fit), as much of the story after the part as fits (up to a quarter of the room), the lore the part was written with, the point of view, tense and style of the book, and the scene setting, point of view character, present characters and instructions of the turn the part came from. The story after the part is there so the new text still leads into it: events the following parts rely on should stay.

The part keeps its place, its summary, its pictures and how it was generated; the text, its words and tokens are replaced and the part counts as edited. Applying the redraft is an edit like Save in the editor, so summaries that describe the old text become outdated, and Marginalia tells how many. A summary on the part itself is one of them.

When a summary describes the part (the part has one, or a newer part of the branch does), the window has the checkbox Revalidate the summaries this redraft makes outdated, unchecked at first. Check it when the summaries still say the right thing (the redraft changed the wording, not what happens): Apply then works out their hash again and they stay valid. Leave it unchecked when the events changed, and make the summaries again.

To rewrite a few sentences and leave the rest of the part alone, select them in the text of the part and right click (a long press on a phone): the menu has Redraft selection. (The menu ☰ of the part is not offered for this, opening it can lose the selection in some browsers.) The window works as above with two differences: it shows the Selected text, and the redraft is only the text that replaces it. The model gets the whole part with the selection marked, and the story and lore around it, so the new passage joins the sentences before and after it. Differences compares the selection with the redrafted text; Apply puts the redrafted text in the place of the selection and keeps the rest of the part, including the space or line break at the edges of the selection. With open annotations the check box offers only the ones whose passage overlaps the selection. If the part was changed after you selected the text (in another window), Apply refuses and you select it again. While the part is edited the selection in the editor is used, and the edit is saved first.

l: Merging a part into the previous one
p: A model that stopped in the middle of a sentence (the response limit, a cut connection) cannot be told to "continue" the same text reliably. Write the next part instead (continue from where the last part stopped) and join the two with Merge into previous part in the menu of the second one. A review opens:

Join the texts with: an empty line, a line break, a space or nothing. It is preselected from the end of the previous text: a paragraph after a text that ended a sentence, a space after one that was cut.

The scene setting, POV character, present characters and instructions of both turns, combined in fields you can edit. What the two turns have in common at the start is kept once ("Write the duel. Keep it short" and "Write the duel. Add rain" give the first, and "Add rain" on the next line).

Data: what the two parts keep, value by value (for example the variables of the story and the data of extensions), with whether the value is the same, different or only on one of the parts. The merged part keeps the value of the later part (it is where the story stands now) unless you choose the value of the previous part for it, or leave the value out. Values that are the same are hidden unless you ask for them.
The review before a part is merged into the previous one

The previous part keeps its place, its summary and how it was generated (prompt, model, times); it gets the joined text, the joined reasoning and pictures, and its words and tokens are counted again. The part you merged is deleted (it is in the Trash) and what followed it continues from the previous part. Summaries that cover the two parts become outdated, as after an edit. The part cannot be merged when it is the first part of the book, or when the part before it has other continuations (swipes of the part): delete them or make them a branch first.
A part can have pictures: a map, a character portrait, an illustration. Choose Images in the part menu to open the list of the pictures of the part.
The Images dialog of a part
Add image (or drop a file on it) uploads a PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP picture of up to 10 MB. WebP pictures are converted to PNG when they are uploaded, because Word and PDF files can't contain WebP.
Caption is shown under the picture. It can be empty.
The trash button removes the picture from the part.
The pictures are shown under the text of the part and in the same order in every export.
A part with a picture

Pictures are not part of the text. The model never sees them, they are not in the prompt, they do not count as tokens and they do not change the summaries. They are also not Markdown: a ![](...) link written in the text is not a picture of the part, use Images instead.
Good to know:

Regenerate keeps the pictures of the part, also when the generation fails. Swipe writes a new part (a new version next to the old one), which starts without pictures. Branch Story copies the pictures to the new part.
Pictures belong to your account. In the viewer only you see them; readers of a published book see the text only. A book is published as it is: pictures are not made public with it.
A backup remembers which pictures a part has, but not the picture files. Restoring a backup into another account or another installation gives parts without their pictures.

Removing a picture from a part only takes it off the part. The file stays and is still listed in Resources, where you can download, replace or delete it. Deleting it there removes it from every part that uses it. The file itself stays in the data folder.

The Summaries button in the bottom bar (left of the settings menu ⚙) opens the overview of the summaries of the branch, where they can be edited, deleted and merged into meta summaries. The tooltip of the button shows how many tokens the summaries in use take in the prompt. See Summaries.

l: How much of the context the story takes
p: The settings menu (⚙) has Branch Tokens. It shows, before you generate anything, what the story of the active branch takes of the prompt: a bar for the story without summaries (all the parts) and with summaries (the summaries and the parts after the newest one), and a table with the parts, the tokens and the share of the prompt budget (the context of the book's model minus the room for the response). Only summaries that still describe the story count; the ones that no longer match are named, they are dropped when a part is generated. The lore, the system template and the instructions of the turn take room from the same budget. Without a model with a context size the table has no shares.
Branch Tokens

The settings menu (⚙) in the bottom bar has Change Styles For Text. It switches the text of the parts between the normal look of the application and a book-like reading style (the one the viewer uses). The setting is saved per book.

In this style paragraphs are justified and long words are hyphenated automatically, using the dictionary of the book's Language (set on the About tab). Hyphenation is done by the browser; for a few rare languages it has no dictionary and the text is simply not hyphenated.

The settings menu (⚙) also has the checkable Highlight Generated Text. While it is on, the text that is still the way the model wrote it is highlighted in every part, so what you added or rewrote stands out. Marginalia keeps the original text of each part and compares it with the current one word by word. A part you never edited is highlighted whole; a part you wrote yourself has nothing highlighted. The switch is not saved: it is off again when the page is opened anew.
Parts that existed before this feature count wholly as generated, because the original text was not kept for them. The highlight is available in the desktop view only, not in the phone view.
Highlighted generated text and the settings menu

Next to the menu below the story there is a command line: type / to see the commands, pick one and press Enter (or the play button) to run it. What a command returns is shown in a small window above the line. See Commands for how to write arguments, what the help shows and how to stop a command that takes a while. The command line is only in the story tab of the desktop layout so far.

A replace in the text a summary describes would make the summary outdated. With Revalidate all summaries on, Marginalia works out again the check value of every summary of the book (those of all branches too, those the replace did not touch, and those that were outdated before), so all of them are valid afterwards. That also turns an outdated summary valid without its text being looked at, so use it when you know the summaries still say the right thing.
A text is found only in the case you typed it (John does not find john). Off: the case does not matter. Locked while Search by regex is on.

The settings menu (⚙) also has Search and replace, which changes a word, a name or a phrase in the whole story at once. The window has a Search for and a Replace with field and these options:
The settings menu with Search and replace
The summaries are searched and changed too.

The table lists every part of the story and every summary that has a match, with its type and id. Open a row to see the matches in it: the text around the match as it is and as it will be after the replacement. A match or a replacement that is too long to show is written as [searched text] or [replace text].
The warning about summaries that would become outdated

When the search is done, the fields and options are locked and the Replace button is enabled. Search again forgets what was found and unlocks the window, so you can change the search. Replace changes the story: the window is frozen completely (even Stop does not work) until it is done, and then it is empty again. Replaced parts are marked as edited, as if you had edited them yourself.

With a regular expression the case is always taken as typed, start it with (?i) to ignore it. Press Search (the button on the right of the fields; on the phone below them). The progress bar shows how far it is and Stop next to it interrupts it. Nothing is changed by a search.

With the option off only the summaries the search covers are brought up to date. Those it does not cover (summaries of branches that are not searched, which share their earlier parts with the active branch; or all of them when summaries are not searched) become outdated. If there are such summaries, Marginalia tells you how many and asks whether to go on. A summary that was outdated already stays so.

The settings menu (⚙) has Import from archive. Upload a .zip of .md (Markdown) files and every file is added as a part at the end of the story: the first one after the last part of the active branch (the first part of an empty book), each next one after the one before. The files are taken in the order of their names, numbers inside the names compared as numbers (2.md before 10.md), also in folders of the archive. Folders, hidden files (.name), the __MACOSX folder and files that are not .md are skipped. The file is the text of the part as it is, it is not sent to the model and not changed; the parts count as written by you. The summaries are not made, do that in the summaries window.

The import shows a progress bar with the number of files done. Stop ends it after the part that is being stored: the parts that were already added stay in the story (the import is not undone), and a message tells how many of the files were imported.
The import button of the Books tab does the same into a new book, see Managing books. The same import into a lorebook is described in Import & export.
The settings menu (⚙) also has Export story, which saves the active branch as a text, Markdown, HTML, Word, PDF or EPUB file. See Exporting a book.
For each new part Marginalia sends:
The master template as the system message: role, lorebook entries, point of view, tense, style and summaries. The jailbreak prompt of the inference provider, if enabled, comes first.

The previous parts of the active branch as the model's own earlier answers - as many as fit into the context limit, newest first. Older parts that don't fit are left out (unless a summary covers them).
The user prompt with the instructions for the new part.
Show Prompt on any part shows exactly what was sent. See Book prompts for the templates.
Marginalia never makes you throw a version away. Every alternative you try is kept as a branch of the story, and you can go back to any of them.
Each part continues the part before it. When a part has more than one continuation, the story splits: each path from the first part to an end is a branch.
The active branch is the one the story editor shows and continues. Only its parts are sent to the model; the other branches don't influence the story.
There are three ways to get a new branch:

Swipe and Regenerate are in the menu of the last part only; Branch Story is in the menu of every part.

l: Trying another version of the last part
p: When you don't like the last part, choose Swipe in its menu. The model writes the part again from the same turn details, and the new version becomes the end of the active branch. The previous version is kept as its own branch; you can switch back to it in the Branch view.
To change what should happen before trying again, open Turn Details of the last part and edit the instructions.
Use Regenerate alone when you don't need the old version: it overwrites the part.

To take the story in a different direction from an earlier point, open the menu of that part and choose Branch Story. Marginalia copies the part to a new branch and makes it the end of the active branch, so the story editor now ends with that part. Continue with + as usual.
The parts that came after it are not lost: they stay on the old branch.
Summaries of the copied part are copied with it.
The Branch view tab shows the whole story tree. Each part is a card with its date, scene setting, characters present and instructions; hover over a card to see all its details.
The story tree
The parts of the active branch are highlighted, and its last part is marked.

Click the last part of another branch to make that branch active. The book switches to the Story tab and shows it. Only the ends of branches can be clicked; to continue from a part in the middle, use Branch Story.
Long stretches without any branching (more than 20 parts) are collapsed into a block showing the first ten and the last ten parts. Click the block to show all parts.

The box above the tree searches the text of all branches of the book, not only the active one. Type what you are looking for and press Enter or click Search; the box remembers your last searches, pick one from the list to repeat it. The x in the box clears the search.
A part matches when its text contains every word you typed, in any order: lighthouse key finds the parts that have both words. Put words in double quotes to look for a phrase: lighthouse key.
Use * for any characters: light* finds lighthouse and lightning. Other characters, including %, _ and \, are searched as they are.
Upper and lower case do not matter. For accented letters, a word typed in lower case also finds the same word in UPPER CASE or Capitalized (žluťoučký finds Žluťoučký and ŽLUŤOUČKÝ).
Only the text of the parts is searched, not the instructions, scene setting or the lorebook. Parts that you deleted are not searched.
The branch view with a search

Every part that matches is highlighted in orange and shows the text around the match; the line above the tree says how many parts were found. Long stretches that would be collapsed are opened when they contain a match. The search stays until you clear it or close the book window, and the highlighting is updated when you come back to the tab.
Click Show in story in a highlighted part to read it:
When the part is on the active branch, the book switches to the Story tab and scrolls to it.

When it is on another branch, that branch becomes the active branch first. It ends at the nearest end of a branch below the found part (the newer one when there are two), so the story editor shows the story up to the found part and what followed it. The book then switches to the Story tab and scrolls to the part, which flashes briefly.
Switching the branch is the same as clicking the end of a branch in the tree: nothing is lost, the previous branch stays as it was and you can go back to it from the tree.
Delete in the menu of a part removes just that part. The parts after it move up and continue from the part before it. To remove a whole branch, delete its parts from the end.
The word and token counts on the About tab show both the whole book (all branches) and the active branch.

The Prompts tab of a book holds the texts Marginalia builds the prompt from: two templates, the narrative settings and the summary and redraft prompts. They decide the voice of the book far more than the model settings do.
The Prompts tab

Every field is optional. An empty field is inherited: from the nearest folder above the book that sets it, else from the default in Settings → Templates (see Account & settings), and when that is empty too, the built-in default. The value it inherits is shown in grey in the empty field.
So set what all your books share in Settings, what a series shares in its folder, and only what is special to a book on its Prompts tab. Changes are saved as you type.
Under an empty field a line says where its value comes from, so it is clear why the book writes the way it does:
Inherited from the folder "Sci-fi" - a folder sets it (the nearest one above the book is named),
Inherited from your settings - the value of Settings → Templates,
Built-in default - nothing sets it.
The Prompts tab of a book in a folder

The same fields are in the settings of a folder, with the same lines. A blank text counts as not set. Because the lookup is done when the prompt is built, moving the book to another folder, or changing the folder, changes the next part you generate.

Each field has a hints popover with Insert Default Template, which copies the default into the field as a starting point for your own version. The template fields also list the Available Template Variables and the Available Macros.

p: The master template becomes the system message, the first message of the prompt. The built-in default has these blocks:
System role - the model is an author continuing the story.
World & lore context - the activated lorebook entries (backgroundLore).
Writing style & mechanics - point of view, tense, style, and general prose rules.
Summary of story so far - the summaries.
Author's notes on the story - only when you gave notes to the model.
If the inference provider has a jailbreak prompt enabled, it is put before the master template.

The user prompt is the last message of the prompt: the request for the part to write. It is filled from the New Turn Instructions (or the Turn Details for Regenerate and Swipe). The built-in default asks for the next section with the point of view character, location, characters present and the plot instructions, followed by rules: no new characters unless requested, follow the instructions, keep the continuity, and output only the story text.
Lorebook entries with the insertion mode Before User Prompt are put right before it; see Entries & activation.

The redraft of a part is one request made of two prompts: the Redraft System Prompt is the system message, the story before the part follows it as the earlier messages of the conversation (the parts as the answers of the model, like a generation sends them), and the Redraft Prompt is the last message from the user. The built-in default tells the model to apply your instructions, keep what you did not ask to change, stay consistent with the story before and after the part, keep the voice, and answer with the redrafted part only. Both prompts have the same variables; {{previousStory}} is only a note that the story follows as messages. Keep in the system prompt what stays the same from one redraft to the next and in the last prompt what changes (the lore, which is not the same for every part, the story after the part, the part, the instructions): a server that remembers the prompt it read can then reuse most of it. Your own version of the last prompt should keep the variables it needs: without {{text}} the model does not see the part. Each prompt follows the rule of all prompts: the book's field, else the one in Settings → Templates, else the built-in one.

When you redraft only a selected passage, the same prompt is used with {{selection}} filled: the built-in default then shows the part with the passage between [[PASSAGE TO REDRAFT]] and [[/PASSAGE TO REDRAFT]] and tells the model to answer with the text that replaces the passage only. A prompt of your own that does not know {{selection}} makes the model answer with the whole part, and the whole answer then replaces the selection; add a {#selection}...{{/selection}} block (and {{^selection}} for the other case) to handle it.

When a model annotates a part it gets the same kind of request as a redraft: the Annotate System Prompt as the system message, the story before the part as earlier messages and the Annotate Prompt as the last message. The built-in default makes the model an editor: it finds the passages that have a problem in the sense of your instructions, quotes each one letter for letter, and writes a short note for you, without praise or filler and without repeating the notes the part already has. The prompt has the variable {{outputFormat}} where the way of answering is described (JSON, text blocks or a free review, it depends on the answer format you choose); keep it in a prompt of your own, or the model is not told how to answer. Both annotate prompts follow the rule of all prompts: the book's field, else the one in Settings → Templates, else the built-in one.

When a model drafts the instructions of the next turn it gets one request, sent as the only message like the redraft. The built-in default asks the model to write what you would type into Instructions: a plot specification of the next part (what happens, who does what, where the part stops) that develops your guidance and follows the plan, continues the story from where it ended, is written like your own earlier instructions, and is not the prose itself. Without guidance it continues the story where it leads. Your guidance is where the prompt puts {{impersonateInstructions}}; keep it in a prompt of your own. The impersonate prompt follows the rule of all prompts: the book's field, else the Impersonate Prompt in Settings → Templates, else the built-in one.

l: How the prompt is put together
p: Earlier parts are sent as the model's own answers, so it continues them in the same voice. When the story is longer than the context limit, the oldest parts are left out first; summaries keep them in the story in condensed form.

Show Prompt in the menu of any part shows the exact prompt that part was written from. Compare Prompt puts it next to the prompt of an earlier part and shows where they first differ, which is where a server's prompt cache ends.

c:
system     jailbreak (if enabled) + master template
user       [ Generate story. ]
assistant  part #1
user       [ Generate more story. ]
assistant  part #2
...        (as many earlier parts as fit)
user       lore "Before User Prompt" + user prompt

p: Put rules that apply to every part (no new characters, length, formatting) into the user prompt: being the last message, it has the strongest effect.
Put lasting facts about the world and characters into the lorebook, not into Style.
Ask for a length in the instructions ("about 800 words") rather than relying on the response limit, which cuts the text off.
After changing a template, generate a part and check it with Show Prompt.

A model can only read a limited amount of text at once (its context). When a book grows beyond that, Marginalia leaves out the oldest parts, and the model forgets what happened in them. Summaries keep that history in the prompt in condensed form.
A summary belongs to one part and covers that part and all parts before it, back to the previous part with a summary:
Here S1 (on part #4) covers parts #1-#4 and S2 (on part #8) covers parts #5-#8.
When the next part is generated:
all summaries of the active branch go into the master template, oldest first, in the {{summaries}} block (Summary of story so far in the default template);
the parts covered by summaries are not sent any more;
the parts after the newest summary (#9 and #10 above) are sent in full, as many as fit.
Summaries are made only when you ask for them; Marginalia doesn't summarize on its own.
Pick the part that ends a stretch of the story you want to condense, for example the last part of a chapter.
In its menu (☰) choose Generate summary.
The summary dialog shows the summary as the model writes it (and its reasoning, for reasoning models). Stop interrupts it and discards the summary.
When it's done, close the dialog with Exit.
A summary being generated

The part menu now has View summary, which opens the summary again, and Delete summary, which removes it. To change a summary, edit it in the Summaries overview, or delete it and generate it again, possibly with a different summary prompt.

The summary is written by the book's model, with the book's protocol, and must fit into the context limit together with the text of the parts it covers. To summarize a long stretch with a small model, summarize in smaller steps.

Editing a summary changes what the model gets, nothing else: the summary stays valid. Only the text can be edited, not the reasoning.

l: Search and replace in the summaries
p: Search and Replace in the menu bar of the overview changes a name or a phrase in the summaries only, for instance when a character was renamed, and leaves the story as it is. It is the search and replace of the story with the same fields and options, except that there is no Search in summaries (the summaries are all it looks into). The table lists every summary with a match, and the matches in it.

It also looks into the summaries a meta summary stands in for and into the summary a meta summary replaced (they are shown under the meta summary and come back when it is unwound): a match in them is listed with the meta summary that holds them.

The text of the merged summaries is part of what makes a meta summary valid, so the replace works out the check value of those meta summaries again and they stay valid. Revalidate all summaries (on by default) does that for every summary of the book, also for those the replace did not touch and for those that were outdated before, see the story search. With it off, a meta summary on a branch that is not searched (Search in all branches off) would become outdated, and the window tells you how many and asks whether to go on.
The trash icon of a summary does the same as Delete summary in the part menu. For a meta summary it asks what to do, see Unwinding a meta summary.
Summaries stay in the prompt for good, so a long book fills the context with them. A meta summary condenses several summaries into one: it is a summary of summaries.
Here M merges S1, S2 and S3. It belongs to the part of the newest merged summary (#9 above, which had S3) and replaces that summary on the part. From then on:
only M goes into the {{summaries}} block, instead of S1, S2 and S3;
S1 and S2 stay on their parts, but are not sent. They are shown under M in the overview;
S3, the summary M replaced, is kept inside M, shown under it with a Replaced badge.
The parts covered by the merged summaries are still not sent in full; a meta summary doesn't change what the summaries cover, only how long the text for it is.
Open the Summaries overview.
Tick the Select box of the summaries to merge. At least two. You tick the summaries in use only (the ones on the top level of the grid).
Click Create meta summary.

Marginalia merges everything from the newest to the oldest ticked summary, including the summaries in between that were not ticked. The meta summary dialog works like the summary dialog: it shows the text as the model writes it, and Stop cancels it and changes nothing. When it ends, close the dialog with Exit and the overview shows the result.
Ticked summaries and the meta summary being generated
A meta summary can merge meta summaries too: tick them like any other summary. The merged ones are shown under the new one, with their own merged summaries under them.
The summaries to merge and the request for the model must fit into the context limit, so with a small model merge a few summaries at a time.
Deleting a meta summary (the trash icon in the overview, or Delete summary in the part menu) asks:
Button
Unwind

Removes the meta summary and puts back the summary it replaced on the part. Summaries that were merged into a meta summary made of meta summaries come back one level at a time, the way they were made.
Delete
Removes the meta summary and leaves the part without a summary. The summaries it merged are in use again (but the one it replaced is gone).
Cancel
Does nothing.
After unwinding, the summaries that were merged are in use again and the overview shows them on the top level.
Deleting a meta summary
The request for a meta summary is the Default Meta Summary Prompt of the book (on the Prompts tab, or the default from Settings → Templates). It gets two variables:
Variable
{{summaryBlocks}}
The summaries to merge, oldest first, separated by an empty line.
{{backgroundLore}}
The lorebook entries that were active when the part of the meta summary was written.

The built-in prompt asks for the events to be chained into shorter entries - roughly half the size - without losing names, items, agreements or unresolved plot threads, and without adding anything new.
A summary is only valid for the exact text it was made from. When you edit or delete a part covered by a summary, the summary no longer matches.

Marginalia checks this when it generates the next part. Outdated summaries are removed and you are asked Invalidated summaries for messages with IDs: [...]. Continue generation without those summaries? Answer Yes to generate without them, or No to stop and generate new summaries first. Either way the outdated summaries are gone; the parts they covered are sent in full again (as far as they fit) until you summarize them again.
A search and replace in the story keeps the summaries it covers valid and warns about the ones that become outdated. The search and replace of the summaries keeps the meta summaries valid.

A meta summary is outdated when a part it covers is edited or deleted, but also when a summary it merged is deleted. (That is why the merged summaries can't be edited one by one: the change would make the meta summary outdated. The search and replace works out the check value of the meta summary again.) Removing an outdated meta summary is the same as unwinding it: the summary it replaced comes back, and is checked as well. If it is outdated too, it is removed in the same way.
When you branch from a part with a summary, the new branch gets a copy of the summary. A copied meta summary keeps what it replaced, so it can be unwound in the new branch.
The request for a summary is the Default Summary Prompt of the book (on the Prompts tab, or the default from Settings → Templates). It gets two variables:
Variable
{{text}}
The text of the parts to summarize, oldest first.
{{backgroundLore}}
The lorebook entries that were active when the summarized part was written.

The built-in prompt asks for a detailed, chronological ledger of events - every beat, action and change of state - rather than a short retelling, because the summary is meant for the model, not for a reader. Replace it if you prefer shorter summaries or a different format.
Summarize at natural breaks: the end of a chapter or a scene.

When the summaries start to take too much of the context (the tooltip of the Summaries button shows how much), merge the oldest ones into a meta summary. Repeat it later with the meta summary and the summaries after it.

Summaries stay in the prompt for good. With many of them, the prompt can fill the context by itself, and generating stops with Contextual limit not sufficient. Then shorten them (a more concise summary prompt), merge them into meta summaries or raise the context limit.
Keep facts that must never be forgotten (names, relationships, rules of the world) in the lorebook rather than relying on summaries.
Check what the model got with Show Prompt on the next part.
