New agent opens the same window as Edit:

On (the default): the commands that have a model write something - the next turn, swipes, summaries, and the commands of extensions such as the Lore Generator and the Arc Outline - use the model above, whatever model your book has. Off: they use the model of your book (an extension command falls back to your default model from Settings when the book has none). That is how you mix models: a strong one that thinks and a cheaper or more fluent one that writes. A command can still name another model profile of the agent.
Optional limits of one run. The limit your administrator gave you applies in any case.
Required.
See below.
System prompt
The book the agent works on, required. Only books that have no agent are offered, and the book of an agent can't be changed later.

The language of everything the agent reads: the descriptions of its commands, their results and their errors. English is the default and the safest choice, because the commands and their parameters are in English whatever the language is (the descriptions in another language mix both), and models, small ones above all, use tools more reliably that way. The list holds the languages installed in the application (an extension can add one, like the Chinese localization). It has nothing to do with the language of the book: the agent is told to write the text of the book in the language of the book, which it can read with get-book-info. A run keeps the language it was started with, a change applies to the next run.
The model and the protocol the agent talks with. Both, or neither; an agent without them can't be started.
The model sees images
The models a sub-agent can run on, and whether it may run on the main one.
The prompts of the agent and the hints of the default template
The window of a new agent
Tick it when the model takes images (the API of the model does not say, so you do). The agent then has view_image and you can attach images to your messages; without it it never gets a picture.
What happens when the agent wants a command that changes or removes data: Run them, Ask first (a window asks you to approve it) or Refuse them.
What the agent is asked when you /compact it: to write the summary that replaces its earlier work. Empty follows the default, like the system prompt, with the same info icon.

What the agent is told to be. Leave it empty and the agent follows the default - yours from Settings, else your administrator's, else the built-in one - which is shown in grey. The info icon has Insert Default Template, which fills the default in so you can edit a copy of it; clear the field again to follow the default.

When the context of the model passes this share of its limit and the agent did not compact its work itself, the run does it: the agent writes the summary of its earlier work, which replaces it. Empty is 90, zero never (the run then stops when the context is full), otherwise 50 to 99.
Write the book with the model of the agent

Your instructions to the agent, added to its prompt in every run. The agent can read them, never change them. Empty follows your default from Settings, if you have one (it is shown in grey), else there are none. The info icon has Insert Default Template, which fills your default in so you can edit a copy of it. Under it a line says what the prompt, the instructions and the ticked commands weigh in every request, in tokens (an estimate, with the tools for files and for the run and the notes of the runner on top).

The agent is offered only the commands you tick. The table lists every command with its effect (Destructive changes or removes data, Non-destructive only reads or adds). The Selection box ticks many at once: All, None or All non-destructive (the default for a new agent), or a role; ticking a command yourself makes the selection Custom. The Search commands field above the table shows only the commands that have all the words you type (in any order, in the name or the description); the selection still applies to all commands, also the hidden ones. Commands that an extension brings stay allowed when the extension is not loaded, you just don't see them. The Batch column says whether the command is used Together with other calls in one answer or Alone (a command that makes a call to a model, such as next, swipe, regenerate, redraft-part, generate-annotation or the compaction, is alone; see Calls in one answer below). All the columns can be resized. The Tokens column is what the definition of the command (its name, description and parameters) adds to every request of the agent, and the line under the instructions adds up the ticked ones: the whole set is about 20 000 tokens, so a smaller selection (a role) leaves more room in the context for the work.
The allowed commands, with the roles of the Selection box
The roles are sets of commands for a job. All of them can read the book and the lorebooks (every command that only reads, those of extensions too), and none can remove data:
Role
Besides reading
Auditor
Nothing: continuity checks, name and term audits, reports.
Lore keeper
Creates and updates lorebook entries and lorebooks, their tags and sub-lorebooks.
Editor
Edits and appends to parts, sets their fields, keeps the summaries (also has the model write them again) and the book information and tags.
Drafter
Adds parts and branches, edits and appends, lets the model write the next turn (/next, /swipe), keeps the summaries, creates and updates lorebook entries of what it invents.
Every command ticked adds its definition to every request, so a role is also the cheapest way to a small prompt for a weak model.

The phone layout has an Agents tab in the drawer, for users who may use agents, with the count of the agents that need you beside its name. Each agent is a card with its name, its state and the buttons of the table (they wrap onto more lines). The windows - the console, the review, the agent's settings - fill the screen, and the review shows the table above the detail of the item. Everything works as on the desktop, only smaller. The console is laid out for a thumb:
The Agents tab on a phone
The console on a phone
Tabs are icons (run, runs, workspace, checkpoints, context, book copy, sub-agents, diagnostics); the title of the window names the one that is open.

Pause, Pause now, Resume, Finish and Stop are icon buttons at the bottom, and only the ones that can be used now are shown; Review changes keeps its words, it is what a finished run waits for. Refresh and Close are icons in the header.

The message box is one line with the Send and Attach image icons beside it. The command line (the terminal icon) is hidden until you open it, so the keyboard does not cover the transcript for nothing. The messages of the transcript use the whole width.

Tables are lists of cards: a run, a checkpoint, a command of the agent's settings, an item of the review each show their name and state with the details under it and their buttons below, in place of columns. The files of the workspace show their size under the name, and the toolbar of the workspace is icons. The context table keeps the number, name and tokens; the type and share of a part are under the text of the part you pick.

The top bar shows who waits for you. While the drawer is closed, a red number in the top bar (next to the title of the open part) counts the agents that need you, as the badge on the Agents tab does in the drawer; tap it to go to the Agents tab. It is hidden when nobody waits, while the drawer is open and in the Agents tab itself.

Swipe between the parts. A swipe sideways over the content goes to the next part of the drawer (swipe to the left) or the previous one (to the right). It does nothing with the drawer open or while the application locks the navigation, and a touch that starts in a text field, a table or anything that scrolls sideways is left to it.
For long work with the transcript or the review a larger screen is still more comfortable.

Clone asks for a name and a book that has no agent, and copies the definition of the agent and its files (not its runs) to a new agent of that book. You can have as many agents, clones included, as your administrator allows (five unless they set another number); at the limit New agent and Clone are off and say why.
Cloning an agent

While a run of an agent works or waits for you, its book is locked: you can read it, but nothing changes it, so the agent never works on text that moves under it. The book list does not open a locked book, it tells you which agent holds it, and generating, editing, search and replace, summaries and deleting the book are refused. Pause or Stop the run to edit the book again; a paused, stopped or finished run does not lock it.
A book an agent works on in the book list

The lorebooks of the book are locked with it: the lorebook the book uses and its sub-lorebooks. On the Lorebooks tab such a lorebook is shown the way it is on a phone, as plain text and without any editing, with a note that says which agent holds it; Refresh shows it for editing again after you paused or stopped the run. Other lorebooks are not affected.

A book in a folder that an agent works on keeps its place and its settings: moving or deleting a folder above it, and changing a setting such a folder passes down (language, templates, point of view, tense, style, prompts), is refused with the name of the book and the agent. Renaming a folder, or changing its description, is not refused. A paused, stopped or finished run lets go.
The lorebook of a book an agent works on

Deleted

Deleted objects stay in the trash until an administrator runs the cleanup, which removes them from the database for good. Whatever the cleanup has removed can no longer be restored (only a database backup made before still has it).

Deleting in Marginalia does not destroy anything right away: a deleted book, lorebook, story part or inference provider is only marked as deleted and hidden from your lists. The Trash tab lists these deleted objects and brings them back.

Opens the saved data of the object, see below.
Selects the object for restoring. The box in the header selects all objects.
The kind of object: book, lorebook, lorebook entry, message (a story part), summary, model (inference provider), protocol, tag, agent, agent run, resource...
The name of the object. Story parts and tag links have no name and show their id; use Extended Content to read a story part.
The table loads as you scroll. The most recently deleted objects are first.

Tick the objects you want back and click Restore Selected. Marginalia asks before it restores them. The objects are back in their lists, exactly as they were deleted, and the other tabs are refreshed.

l: Objects that belong to other objects
p: Deleting an object deletes what belongs to it, and restoring it brings that back: a book takes its story parts, their summaries and its tags with it, a lorebook its entries, a story part its summary and the parts below it, an inference provider its usage numbers. You don't need to tick them: restore the book, and its story comes with it. They show up in the table as separate rows (a book with a long story fills the table with its parts); restoring one of them alone only works when the object it belongs to is not deleted. Something you had deleted on its own earlier (an entry, a story part) comes back with its lorebook or book too, as Marginalia can't tell it from what was deleted together with it.
Some objects can't live without another object:
an entry needs its lorebook,
a story part and a summary need their book,
a book needs its model (inference provider), its protocol and its lorebook, as long as it uses them,
a tag link needs its tag.
An object whose lorebook, book... is deleted can only be restored together with it: tick both. If you tick only the entry, Marginalia restores nothing and tells you what is missing:
Nothing was restored. These objects need a deleted object that is not selected. Select it too, or leave them deleted. Lorebook Entry "Dragon" needs the deleted Lorebook "Bestiary" (lorebook)
Restore refused because the lorebook of the entry is deleted too
Tick the object it names and restore again. Objects that are not deleted any more (restored in the meantime, or an object you didn't delete) are not a problem.

A story part that was deleted from the middle of a story had its following parts moved to its parent. Restoring it brings the part back under its parent as a new branch, without the parts that followed it: they stay where they were moved to. Restore a whole book instead of single parts when you want the story as it was.

Waiting for the cleanup is not always what you want: a story part or a lorebook entry you know you never need again can be removed right away. Tick it and click Delete Permanently; Marginalia asks first, and this can't be undone.
Deleting a story part for good

Only story parts and lorebook entries can be deleted permanently (with their summaries and tags). The button is disabled while anything else is ticked: books, lorebooks and the rest wait for the administrator's cleanup, so you can't remove a whole book by accident.

Story parts that are below a removed part are not removed with it, whether they are deleted or not: they move to its parent, as when you delete a part in the editor. If the part was the position a book was open at, the book opens at the parent instead.
Marginalia deletes nothing when something can't be removed (for example an extension still needs the object) and tells you which one.

Marginalia keeps much of an object's data (the text of a story part, the settings of a lorebook entry, notes that extensions saved) as JSON next to it. Extended Content in a row shows it, so you can check what an object contains before you restore it, for example to find the right story part. Objects without such data (resources) have no link; an object that has none shows This object has no extended content.

Administrators see the deleted objects of all users and can restore any of them. The User filter above the table shows the objects of one user; the User column tells whose they are. Restored objects go back to their owner.
The same table is in Admin → Cleanup (Trash), so you can see what the next cleanup removes. Objects of a deleted user can't be restored: they depend on the user.
The phone layout can only select lorebooks, enable and disable them and their entries, and edit the content of an entry. Everything else on these pages needs the desktop layout.

A lorebook holds what the model must know about your world: characters, places, history, rules, terminology. Each piece of knowledge is an entry. Before every generated part, Marginalia decides which entries are relevant and puts them into the prompt - so the model knows who Captain Varro is when he walks into the scene, without every entry taking up space in every prompt.
The lorebook editor
A book uses one lorebook (on its Lorebook tab).

A lorebook can include other lorebooks as sub lorebooks. Their entries take part too, so you can keep shared material (a world used by several books, a cast of characters) in its own lorebook and include it where needed.
Each entry has the text that goes into the prompt, and conditions that decide when it is used.

c:
Book ──uses──▶ Lorebook "Saga" ──sub lorebooks──▶ "Characters", "Places", "Magic"
                   │                                   │
                 entries                             entries

p: For each generated part, an entry is activated when all of these are true:
the entry and its lorebook are enabled;
its tags fit the book's tags (if it has any);
its filter matches the instructions for the part (if it has one), or, when the entry looks into the story, the newest parts of the story as well.
Activated entries are inserted in their order - into the lore block of the system prompt, or right before the request for the part. See Entries & activation.
Entries without tags and without a filter are always active: use them for what the model must always know.
Lorebook entries can use templates and macros - SillyTavern world info keeps working.
SillyTavern world info can be imported.
Book backups contain the book's lorebook with its sub lorebooks.
The Lore Generator extension writes the content of an entry with the model, from the lore you already have.
The Lorebook VCS extension keeps a revision history of entries.
Creating lorebooks - the lorebook editor, sub lorebooks, using a lorebook in a book
Entries & activation - entry fields, tags, filters, order and insertion
Import & export - Marginalia lorebook files and SillyTavern world info

The toolbar has two rows, which wrap onto more lines in a narrow window: the first for the lorebooks (Lorebook to Tag lorebooks), the second for the entries of the selected lorebook (Add Entry to Refresh).

Under the settings, the estimate of the tokens of the enabled entries of the lorebook is shown. The link Count with subbooks next to it adds up the tokens of the enabled entries of the lorebook and of all its sub lorebooks, however deep, and shows the total next to it. As when a story is written, a disabled sub lorebook is left out together with the lorebooks under it, and a lorebook that is a sub lorebook in more than one place counts once. The total is a count of the moment you click: change an entry and it disappears, click again to count again.
When unchecked, the lorebook contributes nothing - neither its entries nor those of its sub lorebooks.

Mass edit opens a window with every entry of the selected lorebook and of its sub lorebooks (however deep) in one table, ordered by the Order of the entries (entries with the same order by lorebook, then by name). It is for tidying a big lorebook:

Change the enabled box, the Entry Name, the Order, the Tags, the Filtering Mode, the Filtering, the Insertion Mode, the Negative Tags and the Note of an entry in place, as in the editor. Every entry is one line; the table scrolls down (and to the side when the window is narrow). The row moves to its new place when you change the order. The text of an entry is shortened in the table; open the entry in the lorebook to read or edit all of it.
The Lorebook box of a row says in which lorebook the entry is. Pick another one (the lorebook itself or any of its sub lorebooks) to move the entry there.
To move many entries, tick them (the box in the header ticks all), pick Move to lorebook at the bottom and press Move checked.

A lorebook that an agent works on is locked: its entries are grayed out and can not be changed or moved, and nothing can be moved into it. This is checked for each lorebook, so a lorebook can be free while one of its sub lorebooks is locked (it is used by another book). Refresh reads the window again to see whether a lock is gone.
The lorebook in the editor is refreshed when the window is closed after a change.
Mass edit of a lorebook and its sub lorebooks

The two tags buttons of the toolbar open one window that puts a tag on many items, or takes it off them: Tag lorebooks lists your lorebooks, Tag entries the entries of the selected lorebook. Pick the Tag (or type a new one and press Enter); the list shows every item with its tags, and the items that have the picked tag come first with the tag highlighted. A row's + and - buttons apply or remove the tag for that item; tick several items (the box in the header ticks all) and use Apply the tag to the checked or Remove the tag from the checked at the bottom to do it for all of them. An item an agent works on (a lorebook of a book with a running agent, and so all its entries) is grayed out and can not be changed until the run is paused or stopped. The window also tags books. The tags it puts on entries are the ordinary ones, see Tags; negative tags are set on the entry itself.
Tagging the entries of a lorebook

l: Using a lorebook in a book
p: Open the book and its Lorebook tab, and pick the lorebook in the Lorebook field. The editor below shows the lorebook, so you can add and change entries while you write. Clear the field to write without a lorebook.
A book uses one lorebook. To use several, create a lorebook that includes them as sub lorebooks, and use that one.
The same lorebook can be used by any number of books. Changes to it affect all of them from the next generated part on; parts that were already written keep the lore they were written with.
Sub Lorebooks includes the entries of other lorebooks in this one. A typical setup:
Sub lorebooks can have sub lorebooks of their own; all levels are included.
A lorebook can be a sub lorebook of several lorebooks. When it is reached more than once, its entries are still used only once.
A lorebook can't include itself, directly or through other lorebooks: such a choice is refused with Cannot select sub lorebook: cycle detected.
A disabled sub lorebook is left out together with everything it includes.
A lorebook with two sub lorebooks: the tokens with and without them
The entries of all included lorebooks are put together and sorted by their order, regardless of which lorebook they come from.

c:
"Saga" (used by the books of the series)
 ├─ "World"       places, history, rules of magic
 ├─ "Characters"  the main cast
 └─ "Book 2 notes"

p: Uncheck Enabled to switch a lorebook off for a while, for example to see how a book reads without it. Books keep using it, and it works again when you check it.

Delete Lorebook removes the lorebook from your lists. Books that used it no longer get its entries, and lorebooks that included it as a sub lorebook skip it. The data stays in the database until an administrator runs Cleanup, and until then you can restore the lorebook from the Trash; copies in book backups and exported files are not affected.
Each row of the lorebook editor is one entry:

Add Entry in the toolbar adds an entry with order 100. Changes are saved as you type.

The box with the magnifier next to the buttons shows only the entries that have the text in their name, content, note or filter (the case does not matter); clear it to see all of them again. It looks only at the entries of the selected lorebook, not at the sub lorebooks. The phone layout has the box above the list.

The checkbox column at the left selects entries (the one in the header selects all that are shown, so a search and then the header box selects the matches). When something is selected, Delete selected appears in the toolbar with the number of the entries; it asks once and then moves them to the trash. The phone layout does not delete many entries at once.

Search and replace (right of Add Entry) changes a word, a name or a phrase in the name, the text and the comment of all the entries of the lorebook at once. It works like the search and replace of the story, without the options for summaries and branches: Search lists the entries with matches (the table shows their names) and the matches in them as they are and as they will be, Replace changes the entries. It has the options Search by regex (see Regular expressions) and Case sensitive (on by default; locked while the regex is on, which can use (?i) to ignore the case). Entries that are disabled are searched too. On the phone the button (an icon next to the Enabled check box) opens the same window in the phone layout.

The filter, see Filters. Empty means no filter.

When ticked, the words in this entry's content never bring other entries in, see Entries brought in by other entries. The phone layout shows it when it is ticked.
Where the filter is looked for: Instructions (the request for the part, the default) or Instructions and parts of the story, see Looking into the story.
With Instructions and parts of the story: how many of the newest parts of the story are searched together with the request, at least 1.

Your notes. Not sent to the model. Entries imported from SillyTavern list the settings that couldn't be imported here.
Before each generated part, Marginalia goes through the entries of the book's lorebook and its sub lorebooks. An entry is activated when:
the entry is enabled, and so is its lorebook;
none of its negative tags is a tag of the book;
it has no tags, or at least one of them is a tag of the book;
it has no filter, or the filter matches the instructions for the part (or, with Activation Context Instructions and parts of the story, the instructions and the newest parts of the story).
All conditions must hold. An entry without tags and filter is always active.
Tags connect entries with book tags (set on the book's About tab). Use them to share one lorebook between books that need different parts of it:
Entry tags
Negative tags
Active in a book tagged...

winter

book-1
anything but book-1

Tags must match exactly. A negative tag always wins over a tag.
Tags can also be given to a whole lorebook (the Tags field of the lorebook; lorebooks imported from files can carry them). They then count as tags of each of its entries.

A filter activates the entry only when the request for the part mentions it. It is matched against the user prompt of the part as it is sent - the Scene Setting, POV Character, Present Characters and Instructions you entered, inside the wording of the user prompt template.
An invalid regular expression never matches; the entry stays inactive.
Combine tags and a filter when an entry should only be used in some books, and there only when it's relevant.
For example, the regex \b(varro|captain)\b matches the whole word Varro or Captain, and varro.*(harbor|docks) matches only when Varro and the harbor or the docks are both mentioned, in that order.

Mode

The filter is a list of keywords separated by commas (Varro, Ostra); the request contains at least one of them, ignoring case. Spaces around a keyword are ignored.
The regular expression matches anywhere in the request, ignoring case, across lines.
The request also contains the text of the user prompt template itself. A filter for a word the template uses (the default one mentions characters, plot, tone...) is always active.
The same list, but the request must contain every keyword.
The text appears anywhere in the request, ignoring upper and lower case. varro matches Captain Varro.

Unless the entry looks into the story (see Looking into the story), a filter checks the instructions for the new part only, not the text of earlier parts. An entry about Varro is activated when Varro is mentioned in the scene, characters or instructions of the part you are writing - put him into Present Characters when he is in the scene.

By default the filter is looked for in the request for the part only, so an entry about the dragon is used when you mention the dragon. When the story should keep the entry in play - the dragon was in the last part, your new instruction only says "he flies away" - set Activation Context of the entry to Instructions and parts of the story and Parts to the number of the newest parts to search with the request (1 is the part before the one being written, 2 the two before it...).
The filter is looked for in the text of those parts and the request together, so keywords of Keywords (all) may be split between them. The request always counts.
Only the text of the parts is searched, not their summaries, and only the parts of the branch you are writing (a swipe or a regeneration does not search the part it replaces).
A story shorter than Parts is searched whole. Marginalia reads only as many parts as the entries that are switched on need, so a lorebook without such entries does not touch the story at all.
Entries brought in by other entries are not looked for in the story, only in the content of the entries that were used.

l: Entries brought in by other entries
p: Normally only the request for the part activates entries. With a scan depth (the field of the lorebook; 0, which is the default, switches this off) the content of the entries that were activated is searched for the filters of the entries that were not, as if it were part of the request. An entry whose filter is found there is activated too. That is pass 1; the content of the entries it activated is searched in pass 2, and so on, as many passes as the scan depth says (at most 5).

For example, with a scan depth of 1, an entry Captain Varro (filter varro) is activated by the request, and its content says "...serves the Duke of Ostra". An entry Ostra (filter ostra) is then activated too, although the request never mentions the city. With a scan depth of 2, the entry Ostra would in turn bring in an entry about the harbor it mentions.
Only filters count: an entry that is already used because it has no filter needs nothing, and an entry that is switched off, or excluded by its tags, is not brought in.
The content that is searched is the text of the entry as written, the templates in it are not run.
The setting of the lorebook the book uses counts; the scan depth of a sub lorebook is ignored.
An entry with Do not search its content for other entries ticked can be activated, but it brings nobody in.
The order in the prompt does not depend on how an entry was found, see Order and insertion.
Extensions that change which entries are used (see Extensions) are asked about the entries that are brought in too.

Preview activation (the button with the eye in the toolbar of the lorebook editor, and on the phone next to the search and replace button) answers "which entries would be used for this text?" without generating anything. Type the text of the request into Text of the turn (the scene, the characters and the instructions, as you would enter them) and the table lists every entry of the lorebook and of its sub lorebooks, in the order they are used:
a green check mark for the entries that would be used and a gray mark for the others;
the lorebook of the entry, its Order, the Pass (empty for the entries the text activated, 1, 2... for the entries brought in by other entries);

the Reason: no filter, filter found in the text, filter found in the content of another entry (with the filter and the entry), or why not: switched off, a negative tag of the book, the book lacks a tag of the entry, the filter was not found.

The tags decide too, so pick a book in Tags of the book to use its tags (without one, no tags count). That book also gives the parts of its story for the entries that look into the story (without one, they search the text only). Below the text, a line says how many entries would be used and about how many tokens of lore that is. The scan depth of the lorebook is used.
Preview activation of a lorebook
The preview applies the rules of Marginalia only: the text is the one you type (not the user prompt template around it), and what an extension changes while a part is generated is not part of it.

Activated entries are put into the prompt sorted by Order, lowest first. Entries with the same order keep the order in which they were created. Entries from all included lorebooks are sorted together.
Insertion Mode decides where an entry goes:
Mode
Where
In Lore Block
Into the {{backgroundLore}} block of the master template - World & lore context in the default template, in the system message. Use it for background knowledge.
Before User Prompt

Right before the request for the part, at the end of the prompt. The model pays most attention to it. Use it sparingly, for what must influence this very part (a character's current state, a rule for the scene).
Entries are separated by an empty line. Lore counts toward the context limit; with many long entries, less of the story fits into the prompt.
The content of an entry is a template like the book prompts. It can use:
Variable
{{sceneSetting}}, {{povCharacter}}, {{presentCharacters}}, {{instructions}}
The instructions for the part.
{{narrativePov}}, {{narrativeTense}}, {{style}}
The book's narrative settings.
and all macros. For example, an entry that adapts to the point of view character:
All activated entries of one part share their variables in activation order: an entry can setvar a value that entries later in the order (and the master template) read with getvar.
A syntax error in the content is shown under the field. The entry is still saved; until it is fixed, its content is used as plain text, without processing the template.

c: Varro {{#povCharacter}}is seen through the eyes of {{.}}: {{/povCharacter}}a stern, scarred officer.

p: Keep entries short and factual; the model doesn't need prose, it needs facts.
One entry per character, place or concept, so each can be activated on its own.
Use always-active entries for the core of the world, filters for the cast and places, and tags to share a lorebook between books.
Check what was activated with Show Prompt on a generated part, or try a text before you write with Preview activation.
Use the scan depth sparingly: one pass is enough for most books, and every pass can bring in more lore than you wanted.
Select the lorebook in the editor and click the export button (file icon, Export Lorebook). The browser downloads lorebook name.json with:
the lorebook and all its sub lorebooks (every level), with their names, enabled state and tags;
every entry with its content, note, order, filter, insertion mode, tags and negative tags.

Use it to keep a copy, to share a world with other users, or to move it to another installation. The data that extensions keep in a lorebook or an entry is in the file too, and is restored by the import. Entry revisions of the Lorebook VCS extension belong to the old entries and do not show on the entries the import creates; the extension has its own export for them.
A regular expression is written in the Java syntax. SillyTavern uses JavaScript, so simple expressions work, but something Java-only (possessive quantifiers, \p{...} classes) does not match there.

The export button opens a menu with two items: Export Lorebook (the file above) and Export to SillyTavern, which downloads the lorebook as a SillyTavern world info file that SillyTavern can import. It is the reverse of the import:
The first keyword is the primary key, the others are secondary keys with the logic AND ALL

The sub lorebooks are merged: the file has the entries of the lorebook first, then those of its sub lorebooks, as SillyTavern has no lorebooks inside lorebooks. What SillyTavern has no counterpart for is left out: the Note of an entry, negative tags together with tags, the data of extensions. SillyTavern matches the keys in the recent chat, see what works differently for the other direction.
Title / memo (comment)
Click the import button (file icon) and choose Import Marginalia Lorebook.
Upload a file exported from Marginalia.

The import always creates new lorebooks - the lorebook and its sub lorebooks, with the same structure - even when you already have lorebooks with the same names. The imported lorebook is selected in the editor. Tags are matched by name with your existing tags, or created.
Files from older Marginalia versions (a single lorebook without sub lorebooks) can be imported too.
Lorebooks also travel inside book backups. Restoring or cloning a backup can link to lorebooks you already have instead of creating copies; see Restoring a backup.

l: Importing an archive of text files
p: Click the import button and choose Import from archive.
Upload a .zip file with .md (Markdown) files.
Check the entry names in the table and change them if you want, then click Import.
The window to upload the archive
The names of the entries before the import

Marginalia creates a new lorebook named after the file (without .zip) with one entry for each .md file. The files are taken in the order of their names, numbers inside the names compared as numbers (2.md comes before 10.md), also in folders of the archive; the entries get the Order 1, 2, 3... in that sequence. The whole file is the Content. Other files, folders, hidden files (.name) and the __MACOSX folder of archives made on a Mac are skipped.
Entry names are filled in from, in this order:

a file names.txt in the root of the archive: one name on a line, the first line for the first .md file in the order above, and so on (an empty line leaves that file to the next rule; extra lines are ignored). Use it to name many files at once, for example from a script;
the first heading of the file (# Chapter 1 gives Chapter 1);
the file name without .md.
The table in the dialog shows the result, and you can type over any name.

The import then shows its progress. Stop ends it after the entry that is being stored: the lorebook keeps the entries that were already imported (the import is not undone), and a message tells how many of the files were imported.

The entries are imported disabled: they have no filter, so enabled they would be sent with every request, which for a whole book of chapters is hardly wanted. Turn on the ones you need, with a filter or tags - Mass edit is the quick way to do it for many entries.

Anything else - several keys, secondary keys (AND ANY, AND ALL, NOT ANY, NOT ALL), keys written as /regex/, case-sensitive or whole-word matching - becomes one Regex filter that does the same. For example, the keys dragon, wyrm with the secondary key fire (AND ANY) become:

You don't need to read these expressions; edit them only if you know regular expressions.

c: (?s)^(?=.*(?:\Qdragon\E|\Qwyrm\E))(?=.*(?:\Qfire\E))

p: SillyTavern settings without a Marginalia counterpart are listed in the entry's Note, for example Imported from SillyTavern, not supported: probability 50%, inclusion group "weather". These are:
probability, inclusion groups, sticky, cooldown and delay - the entry is simply active whenever it matches;
insertion at depth - the entry goes before the user prompt instead.

The biggest difference is what the keys are matched against. SillyTavern scans the recent chat. Marginalia matches the request for the part being written - its scene, characters and instructions - and an imported entry starts with exactly that (its Activation Context is Instructions), so an entry that SillyTavern activated because a name came up in the last messages is activated in Marginalia only when you mention the name in the turn. To get what SillyTavern does, set the Activation Context of the entry to Instructions and parts of the story and Parts to the number of the newest parts to look into, see Looking into the story. Recursive activation (entries activating other entries) is not set by the import either: switch it on with the scan depth of the lorebook, see Entries brought in by other entries.
After importing, look through the entries and decide which should be always active, which keep their filters, and which are better handled with tags.

Commands are small actions you run by typing them, instead of clicking through menus: look something up in the story or the lorebooks, search and replace, take a backup. Extensions add commands of their own, for example to generate a lore entry or to make up names. The same commands are what an agent works with, so a command does one clear thing and says what it does: you can read it while you type.
The command line is the field next to the menu below the story, in the story editor.

Click into the command line and type /. The list shows all the commands, each with its name and a short description. Typing more narrows the list: the filter looks at the name of the command, its title and its description.

Pick the command with the mouse, or with the arrow keys and Enter. A command that needs nothing runs at once; for one that takes arguments, /name is written into the field and you continue with the arguments. The list of commands, opened by typing a slash

Type the arguments and press Enter, or click the play button next to the field, to run it. The field is emptied as soon as the command starts; a text that is not a command stays, so you can correct it.
Text that does not start with / is not a command, and nothing is run. Clicking away from the field or pressing Esc never runs anything, so you cannot start a command by accident.
While you type, a small window opens above the field. It covers part of the story but moves nothing, and it closes when you leave the field or run the command. It shows:
what the command does,
the forms the command has (see Forms) that fit what you have typed so far, with the argument you are typing now highlighted and its description,
what the command returns,
a hint when you have typed more arguments than the command takes, or when no command has that name.
The help of /search-replace-lore-entries while its second argument is typed
While you are still typing the name, the list of commands is the help.
/search-parts say\ hi
/search-parts two words
/search-parts two\ words
\ (backslash, space) is a space
a backslash
A backslash in front of anything else stays as it is, so C:\books\story is passed unchanged. If you open a quote and never close it, everything to the end of the line belongs to that argument.
a double quote, with or without quotes around it: say \hi\ is say hi
an empty argument
Arguments are separated by spaces, and repeated spaces count as one. To put a space inside an argument, you have three ways:
Arguments are text. A command that wants a number, a yes/no or one of a few options converts the text itself; if the text does not fit, the command is not run and a notification says so.
double quotes keep everything inside together
one argument, say hi
one argument, two words
quotes can start in the middle of an argument
The command gets
The other special characters:
Why
You get
You type

One command can take different arguments: /list-parts with nothing, and /list-parts 2 with one argument are two forms of the same command. Marginalia picks the form by the number of arguments you typed and by what they look like. If no form fits, a notification says that the command does not take these arguments, and the help shows the forms it does have.

When a command returns something, it is shown in a window above the command line. Close it with the cross, with Esc, or just carry on: it disappears when you type something new or run another command. A command that returns nothing shows no window.
The result of /take-backup above the command line
If a command fails, or there is no such command, you get a notification with the reason.

Most commands answer at once. A command that needs time shows a window with an animated bar and a Stop button, and the story is locked until the command is done. Under the bar the command can say what it is doing now and, in smaller letters, the detail of the step. Stop cancels the command; it should return immediately. The commands that have the model write, like /next, are of this kind.
The window of a command that is running
Every command says what it does to the data that already exists, and the command bar shows it as a small label next to the command, in the list and in the help:
Destructive (red) - the command changes or removes data that exists, like the search and replace commands that rewrite the book. Point at the label to see the explanation.
Non-destructive (green) - the command only reads data or adds new data, like /take-backup, which adds a backup and changes nothing else.

The label is information for you; it does not stop the command when you run it. An agent goes by it: it is not given a destructive command, or has to ask you first, or runs it, as set for that agent. A command that asks for confirmation by itself is described below.

A command that changes a lot can ask before it does. The search and replace commands have no preview, so after the search they show how many matches they found in how many items and what would be replaced by what, and only Yes changes the book; No leaves everything as it was. The question stays until you answer it.

Search and replace in the story of the open book, like the Search and replace window of the story tab. The options are true/false, in this order, and each one you leave out has the default of that window (regex no, case sensitive yes, summaries yes, all branches no, revalidate yes); to set one, give those before it too. maxHits refuses a replace that finds more matches than that, and with dryRun true nothing is changed: the answer counts the matches and shows a few, which is how an agent looks before it replaces. There is no preview: after the search you are asked whether to replace the number of matches found, and only Yes changes the book. The replace cannot be stopped.

What it does

Which entries a generation would use for a text, or for a turn like the one that made a part, and why (no filter, filter found - in the text, or in the content of another entry when the lorebook has a scan depth - or not used because it is switched off, a tag of the book decides, or the filter is not in the text), with the lore text and its tokens. The text may be the handle of a part.

The commands above that read the book (/get-book-info to /get-template-variables) change nothing; they answer in JSON text, so an agent can use them as well. Every row of an answer has a handle: the identifier of the part (or lorebook, or entry), which does not change when parts are added, moved or deleted. A part is given by its handle, or by its position on a branch, the first part of the story being 1; a branch by the handle of any part of it, or by its number from /list-branches (the numbers follow the creation of the ends of the branches, so they change when a branch is added or deleted). Positions and numbers are easier to type, handles are what an agent should use, and the commands that change the story take handles only. Without a branch the commands work on the active branch. Lists are paged with offset and limit, long texts are cut into slices (offset, length) and the answer says the total length. As with the other commands the options are positional: to set one, give those before it too.

The commands that read the lorebooks (/list-lorebooks to /preview-lore-activation) work the same way and reach only the lorebooks of the open book: the root lorebook and its subbooks. A lorebook is its handle or its number from /list-lorebooks (the root is 1), an entry its handle or its number in the lorebook, in the order of the lorebook (the first entry is 1); the numbers change when entries or subbooks are added or removed. Without a lorebook the root lorebook is used.

These commands change the open book (or the working copy of an agent, which is where an agent's changes go). Templates combine two syntaxes:
Handlebars - variables like {{instructions}} and sections like {{#sceneSetting}}...{{/sceneSetting}} that are printed only when the value isn't empty. See Prompt templates.

For one generated part, the templates are processed in this order:
the user prompt;
the lorebook entries that were activated, in their order;
the master template.

All of them share one set of variables: a value set with {{setvar}} in the user prompt can be read in lorebook entries and the master template; a value set in a lorebook entry is visible to later entries and the master template, but not to the user prompt, which was already processed.
Lorebook filters see the processed user prompt, so a macro in the user prompt can produce text that activates entries.

A regular expression (regex) is a short pattern that describes text instead of spelling it out: "the word Harry, but not Harrys", "any two words in quotes", "three or more spaces in a row". Marginalia uses them in two places:
Search and replace of the story and of a lorebook, and the matching commands, when Search by regex is on. The pattern finds the text, the replacement can reuse pieces of it.
The Regex filter of a lorebook entry, which decides when the entry goes into the prompt.
The dialect is the one of Java. This page shows what you will use most; the complete reference is linked at the end.

You do not need regexes for plain words. With Search by regex off the text is searched exactly as typed, so a . or a ( in it is just a dot or a bracket. Turn the regex on only when a single fixed text is not enough.

Brackets make a group, and a vertical bar inside a group is "or": (Mr|Mrs) Dursley finds Mr Dursley and Mrs Dursley, and \b(Voldemort|You-Know-Who)\b finds either name. A ?, * or + after a group applies to all of it: (very )+good finds very good and very very good.

By default a regex ignores nothing: harry does not find Harry. Put (?i) at the start to ignore the case: (?i)harry finds Harry, HARRY and harry. l: Taking the match into the replacement
p: Everything a regex puts in round brackets is a group, numbered from the left by its opening bracket: the replacement $1 is the text of the first group, $2 of the second, $0 all of the match. In (\w+), (\w+) the first group is the word before the comma, the second the word after it, so $2 $1 swaps them: Potter, Harry becomes Harry Potter.
You can name a group, (?last\w+), (?first\w+), and use the name in the replacement: ${first} ${last}.
A $ or a \ that should stay as itself in the replacement has to be escaped: to put $5 into the text, write \$5. Without the regex the replacement is always taken exactly as typed.
If the pattern is wrong (a bracket that is never closed) or the replacement names a group the pattern does not have, a notification says so and nothing happens; a search never changes anything.
A lookahead (?=...) and a lookbehind (?=...) look at the text around the match without taking it, so only the part outside them is replaced:
Search
Finds
Harry(?= Potter)
Harry only when Potter follows (and leaves Potter alone)
(?=Professor )McGonagall
McGonagall only after Professor
Harry(?! Potter)
Harry not followed by Potter
* and + take as much as they can: in He said yes and no the pattern .* matches the whole yes and no. Add a ? (.*?), or say what is not allowed ([^]*), to stop at the first closing quote.
The search treats every line on its own: . does not cross a line break, and ^ and $ match at the start and the end of every line of a part, not only of the whole text. To match a line break write \n.

The filter of a lorebook entry set to Regex is matched against the request for the part, anywhere in it. It ignores the case, and . does match line breaks there, so varro.*harbor finds Varro and the harbor even on different lines. Typical filters:
\bvarro\b - Varro as a whole word.
\b(varro|captain)\b - Varro or the captain.
varro.*(harbor|docks) - Varro and then, later, the harbor or the docks.
dragons? - dragon or dragons.
(?!no )magic - magic, unless it stands right after no.
An invalid regex never activates the entry, and the reason is written to the log. See entries and activation for the rest of how an entry is chosen.

/search-replace-parts and /search-replace-lore-entries take the regex as the third argument (true), after the search and the replacement. The command line splits on spaces, so a pattern or a replacement with a space is put in double quotes. A backslash in front of a letter is passed on as it is (\b, \d), but \\ becomes a single backslash and \ a quote, so a literal backslash in the pattern is \\\\.

The commands show no list of matches: they ask you whether to replace the number of matches found. When you are not sure about a pattern, try it first in the Search and replace window, which shows every match as it is and as it will be.

c:
/search-replace-parts "\bHarry\b" Henry true
/search-replace-parts "(\w+), (\w+)" "$2 $1" true
/search-replace-parts "(?i)\bharry\b" Henry true

p: Try a pattern with Search first and open a few of the rows: the window shows each match with its surroundings, as it is and as it will be. Replace only when the result is what you wanted.
Start simple and add to the pattern step by step; a pattern that finds too much usually needs \b around a word, or ? to stop a *.
A backup before a big replace is cheap (/take-backup), and a replace cannot be stopped once it has started.
Changed summaries: when the replace touches the text that a summary was made from, the window warns that the summary would become outdated; see Search and replace.

This page covers the basics. Java's full syntax, with every construct, flag and character class, is in the documentation of java.util.regex.Pattern, and the replacement syntax ($1, ${name}, \$) in Matcher.appendReplacement.

Extensions are installed by an administrator for the whole Marginalia installation, in Admin → Extensions: they are JAR files, uploaded with Load Extension (.jar). See Managing extensions for the details.
Once installed, an extension is available to every user. An extension loaded while Marginalia runs shows up in windows opened afterwards: close and reopen a book (or reload the page) to see it.

Extensions hook into the user interface of one Marginalia version. An extension built for a different version may stop working or break parts of the application. Use the extensions that come with your version of Marginalia.
The eighteen extensions above are part of the Marginalia source code (marginalia/plugins) and are built separately; see the plugins README.

The phone layout has its own classes, so an extension has to support it. Arc Outline, Author's Note, Chapter Marker, Character Tracker, Instruction Exporter and Reviewer do; Side Query, Lore Generator and Lorebook VCS add nothing on a phone (see Using Marginalia on a phone). Name generator, Name provider, Place provider, Gemma 4 tools fix and Google Gemini have no screens of their own (Google Gemini only adds a provider to the model dialog, which a phone has as well), and Chinese localization is in the language selector of the phone menu. Extensions are installed from the Admin page, which a phone doesn't have.

Extensions with settings add a section to Settings → Extension Settings (the third tab of the Settings page). These settings belong to your account, like the rest of Settings, and are saved with its Save button.

Extensions keep their data together with the data it belongs to - reviews with the story part, conversations with the book, revisions with the lorebook - so it is included in database backups. Whether it is also part of book backups and exports is described on each extension's page.
Uninstalling an extension doesn't delete its data: installing it again brings it back.

A note to the model that is sent with every generation of the book: the tone you want right now, what the current chapter is about, a reminder the model keeps forgetting. Unlike the instructions of a turn, the note stays until you change it.
The left sidebar of the story editor gets an Author's Note tab next to Outline. Changes are saved to the book as you type and used by the next generation.
Field
Insert into prompt
Turns the note on or off without deleting it.
Insertion depth

Where the note goes, counted in messages from the end of the prompt: 0 - after the instructions of the turn (the very last message), 1 - right before them, 2 - before the last story part, and so on. A large depth puts the note right after the system prompt.
Role
Whether the note is sent as a System, User or Assistant message.
Author's Note
The text sent to the model. An empty note is not sent. Below it, an estimate of its size in tokens.
Author's Note (private)
Notes for yourself - plans, reminders. Never sent to the model.
The closer the note is to the end of the prompt, the stronger its effect. Depth 1 with role System is a good start. The note is not processed as a template: macros are sent as they are written.

A generation sends the system prompt first, then the story as a chat - each part as an answer of the model to Generate story - and the instructions of the turn last. With depth 1 the note is inserted right before the instructions:
system prompt (template, lore, summaries)
story parts…
the Author's Note
the instructions of the turn

The note's tokens are taken from the room for the story: a longer note means fewer story parts in the prompt. A note that doesn't leave room even for the rest of the prompt stops the generation with Contextual limit not sufficient.
The note is stored with the book, so it is part of book backups and copies.

l: Drafting the instructions for the current chapter
p: The pen with a feather next to Add new arc opens the window that lets the model draft the instructions of the next turn, with the data of the chapter the story is at as its Plan of the Story. The current chapter is the first chapter marked Current; when none is, the first one that is not Finished; an arc marked current that has no chapters yet stands alone. The model gets that arc and chapter with their descriptions and notes, and the title and description (not the note) of the chapter after it, with the warning that the story must not get there yet. The window starts with what you typed into Instructions of the new turn panel as the guidance; Use as Instructions puts the draft into that panel and opens it. Without a current chapter the button says so.
The same data is a source for the Side Query, see below.
Marking an arc Finished marks all its chapters Finished too. Changing an arc to another state leaves its chapters as they are.
The outline is saved with the book as soon as you change it, so it is included in its backups.

l: The outline as a source for other extensions
p: The outline is offered to other extensions as a source of data about the book: in Side Query check Arc outline in the plug popover to send the arcs, their states, descriptions and chapters with your questions. There are two versions: Arc outline is the terse one (descriptions only), Arc outline (with notes) adds the note of every arc and chapter under its description, which is where the details of generated arcs and chapters are. Your private notes are sent only when you check the second one. A third source, Arc outline: current chapter, sends only the arc and the chapter the story is at (see Drafting the instructions for the current chapter).

On the right you see the reasoning of the model as it is written and, as soon as the answer begins, the arc it proposes - a name, a terse description and a longer note - shown like an arc of the outline (the note under its description) and growing as the answer streams in. The description is what the outline shows, so the model is asked to keep it to a couple of sentences and to put the details into the note, which ends up in the Note of the saved arc. l: Importing an arc from the story
p: Import from story in the menu of the wand asks the model to read a part of your story and write it down as one arc with its chapters, so you can bring a book you have already written into the outline. The model always reads the active branch of the book, as it is when you open the dialog. The dialog is like the one for arcs, with these choices on the left:
From message, To message
The range of the story to send. The messages of the branch that have text are numbered from 1; at first the whole branch is chosen. Under each field you see the beginning of the message it points to.
Number of chapters (optional)
Choose a number to get exactly that many chapters (an answer with another number is rejected), leave it empty to let the model divide the story where it naturally divides.
State of the imported arc and its chapters
Finished at first, because the story is written; choose Current or Planned if you need it.
Token counter

How many messages the range has and their approximate tokens, and the approximate tokens of the whole prompt (instructions, lore, outline and story) next to what the model takes. It turns into a warning when the prompt does not fit, then choose fewer messages. It follows the range, the number of chapters, the prompt and the model.
Prompt
The instructions for the model, with the variables , , (the messages of the range) and. It starts as the Story import prompt of Settings → Extension Settings → Arc Outline.

There are no tools here, the names are in the story. On the right you see the reasoning, then the arc and its chapters as the model writes them. Save as arc adds the arc with its chapters at the end of the outline; every one of them keeps the reasoning and the answer of the model and has its own robot button. A long story is best imported in several steps, one arc for each range.
The wand button on an arc asks the model to divide that arc into chapters. The dialog is like the one for arcs, with these choices on the left:
What the model knows of the story

Whole story so far: the arcs up to this one, with all their chapters. Arc summaries only: the same arcs without chapters. Arc summaries and finished chapters: the same arcs with only the chapters you marked Finished. Arcs after this one are never sent.
What you want from the chapters in general
Pace, tone, what must happen. Can be empty.
Number of chapters

Write it in words ("about eight") or choose an exact number. A number adds a text area for each chapter where you can say what it should contain; all of them are optional. Using one of the two clears the other. With an exact number, an answer with a different number of chapters is rejected.

On the right you see the reasoning, then the arc with the chapters it already has, and the new chapters as the model writes them. Save as chapters adds them at the end of the arc, each with a terse description and the details in its note (like arcs). Every new chapter keeps the reasoning and the answer of the model, and has its own robot button.

The outline and its generators are also commands, for the command line and for agents. They work on the book that is open (an agent: on its working copy), and an open Arcs tab shows the change at once. Arcs and chapters are given by number, as the outline shows them: the first arc is 1, the first chapter of an arc is 1 (the numbers change when something before them is added, removed or moved). A command that changes an arc or a chapter takes only the fields you give it; an empty text clears a description or a note.

The three generating commands use the same prompts as the dialogs (your Extension Settings → Arc Outline, or the defaults), the model and protocol of the book (your default model when the book has none) and no tools: a caller that wants names gets them with the commands of the Name generator or the Name provider and writes them into the specification. Like the dialogs they save only when asked: with save false (the default) they return the arc or the chapters as JSON and store nothing, with save true they add them to the outline (an arc at the end, chapters at the end of the arc) and the answer has their numbers. A story that is too long for the model is refused by /import-arc-from-story: choose fewer messages. The generating commands take a while, and stop when the run is stopped.

The speech-bubble button opens a popover with In prompt, Depth and a role, like the Author's Note; the button is green while the characters are in the prompt. When In prompt is checked, every generation gets the characters as a message: a line with the name, the tagline in brackets and the note of each character, and a list of the relationships (Mara - Tomas: employs, - when it goes both ways). When you open an existing character, the dialog also lists its relationships: the ones the character points to (→), the ones that point to it (←) and the unidirectional ones (↔), each with a name and a tagline. The trash button deletes a relationship.

To add one, search for the other character, choose the Direction (this character → other, other → this character or both ways), enter a Name (e.g. employs, friends) and optionally a Tagline, and press Add relationship (the button is above these fields). Relationships are saved at once. A new character can get relationships after it has been saved.

If your characters are already in the lorebook, the wand menu creates them for you. Import lore entries as characters opens a dialog with the entries of the book's lorebook and of all its sub lorebooks, sorted by their order. Each shows its name and a checkbox, and an i icon that shows the content of the entry in a popover, for a quick look before you decide; the checkbox in the header of the list checks or clears all of them. Import creates a character with the name of every checked entry (the tagline, note, icon and color stay empty for you to fill in), Close leaves without importing.
Entries are not compared with the characters you already have: importing the same entry twice creates two characters.

Relationship map shows all relationships of the book as a graph. Every character that has a relationship is a circle with its icon (or a box without one) on its color, with its name and tagline; every relationship is an arrow between two characters with its name and tagline. An arrow points at the target; a unidirectional relationship has an arrow at both ends. Characters without relationships are not in the map.

The characters are arranged in rings around one character - at first the one with the most relationships: the characters it is related to are on the first ring, theirs on the second and so on. Double-click a character to arrange the map around it. You can also drag the characters, move the map and zoom with the mouse wheel.
