The tab is in the drawer of the story, next to the outline, like the Author's Note. The buttons for the POV and present characters are in the new turn form of the phone too.
Turns the Outline of the story editor into a table of contents.
Chapters in the outline
When the text of a part contains a Markdown heading - a line starting with # - the part's entry in the outline shows the heading instead of the usual #n (DB ID: m) label, highlighted:
shows in the outline as 5. Chapter 3: The Harbour - the number is the part's position in the branch, followed by the heading. Parts without a heading keep their normal label.
The heading can be on any line of the part; when there are several, the first one is used.
Any heading level works (#, ##, ###...).
The outline updates as soon as you save an edit: add a heading to start a chapter, remove it to merge the part back.

c:
# Chapter 3: The Harbour

Rain had been falling on Ostra since dawn...

p: There is nothing to configure. Either write the heading into the part yourself, or ask the model for it in the instructions, e.g. Start a new chapter titled "The Harbour" with a Markdown heading.
The default user prompt tells the model not to write titles or chapter headings. When you want the model to write them, say so explicitly in the instructions, or change that rule in the user prompt.
The headings are part of the story text, so they are also sent to the model and shown in the viewer and in backups.
The same rule finds the chapters in the table of contents of exported books.

Turn your story into a manga: the model adapts parts of the book into a script of pages and panels, and then writes image generation tags for every panel - ready for Stable Diffusion, Forge, Midjourney and the like. It is a port of the MangaGenerator extension of SillyTavern.
Choose Manga Generator in the settings menu (⚙) of the story editor. One large window opens; nothing is added to the story screen itself. You can drag the window and resize it.

A book can have several mangas, shown as tabs at the top of the window. The buttons next to the tabs add a manga (+), rename it, move it to the left or right and delete it. A manga is kept with the book, so it is in the book's backups and copies.
Additional rules
Below the tabs are the settings of the open manga:
Context before / after
Copies every script of the manga, then every tags text, to the clipboard.
Copy all
How long a script the model is asked for (`` in the prompt).
How many more parts before and after those a new section gives the model as the background.
How many parts of the story a new section adapts.
Model and protocol
Parts per section
Put in place of `` in the script prompt, for rules of your own (no sound effects, a style...).
Replace the built-in prompts of this manga. Reset to default brings the built-in text back.
Script prompt, Tags prompt
Setting
Token budget
What it does
What the requests go to. The book's own by default; the last choice is remembered.

Settings → Extension Settings → Manga Generator Settings holds what a new manga starts with: the token budget, parts per section, the context before and after, the script prompt, the tags prompt and the additional rules - and a text put before every request, for instructions that hold for all of your mangas. A prompt left empty, or unchanged, is the built-in one. A manga you made already keeps its own settings. The panel is saved with the Save button of the Settings page.
Add section adds a section for the parts of the story that follow the last section (the first one starts with part 1). Parts are numbered from 1 like in the outline. A section shows:
Adapt from part / to part - the parts the model turns into panels,

Context from part / to part - the parts the model reads; the ones outside the adapted range are only the background (earlier events, or what comes next), and the model is told not to adapt them. Change any of the four numbers whenever you want a different slice.
Each section has two views, Script and Tags:

Generate script streams the script into the section. A reasoning model's thinking is shown above it (Thought for 12.3 s). The script continues the page numbers of the section before it and does not repeat what that script already covers.
Switch to Tags and Generate tags: for each panel of the script, tags for the characters and the scene.
The Manga Generator window with the script of a section

Either text can be edited by hand (the pen), copied, and a generation can be stopped with Abort - what the model wrote so far is kept. Sections generate independently, so you can start several; while any model is writing, sections cannot be deleted and mangas cannot be changed.
The same section on the Tags view

Override gives one section its own script prompt, tags prompt or additional rules, or a Rules addendum that is added to the rules of the manga instead of replacing them. The eye shows the exact request the model would get, with its size.

l: The lore and the size of the context
p: The model gets the text of the section's parts, and with it the lore the text calls for: entries of the book's lorebook (and its sub lorebooks) whose filters appear in that text, found like in a generation, including the scan depth. Entries that are always on come too. So the characters and places of those parts reach the model with their descriptions, which the image tags need.

All of it has to fit the context size of the model - the context of the AI and the protocol, minus the room for the reply. When the entries do not fit, the later ones are left out (a notice tells how many; the eye shows it too) - make the section smaller, or the lore shorter. A request that does not fit even without the lore is still sent, with a warning.
A chat message is a part of the story; there are no names in front of messages, no persona and no character card - characters come from the lorebook.
The world info "trigger" of the extension is not needed: the lore is activated by the text itself.
The context size is taken from the AI and the protocol, there is no setting for it.
A new section takes 3 parts with 1 part of context on each side, as a part of a story is far longer than a chat message. Change this in the settings (below).
Tabs are moved with the arrow buttons, not by dragging.
Copies the instructions of the story, with the scene setting, POV character and present characters, to the clipboard.

The extension adds Export instructions to the settings menu (⚙) of the story editor. It goes over the parts of the active branch, from the first part to the current end of the story, collects the fields each part was generated from and copies them as one text. Every filled field is written as its name followed by a colon and its contents on the next line; the parts are separated by a blank line, in the order of the story:
Export instructions in the settings menu

Empty fields are left out, and so are parts with nothing filled in. Paste the text anywhere - to keep the plot outline of the book, to reuse the instructions in another book or to hand them to someone else.

c:
Scene Setting:
A harbour town at dawn
POV Character:
Mara
Present Characters:
Mara, the harbourmaster
Instructions:
Mara arrives and is questioned.

Scene Setting:
...

p: There is nothing to configure. Open a book and choose Export instructions in the settings menu; a notice confirms that the text is on the clipboard. When the branch has none of these fields filled in, nothing is copied and you are told so.
Only the active branch is exported - to export another one, switch to it first.
Browsers only allow a page to write to the clipboard when it is opened over https:// or on localhost. Over plain http:// on another address the item has no effect.
Makes function calling work with Gemma 4 models whose API expects another role for the results of the calls.

When the model calls a function, Marginalia sends the result back to it in a message with the role tool. Some servers that run Gemma 4 expect the role tool_responses instead, and answer an error or ignore the result otherwise.

The extension changes the role for such models: when the Model of an inference provider contains gemma4 or gemma-4 (in any letter case), the results of function calls to it are sent as tool_responses. Requests to other models are not touched. It is a port of the SillyTavern extension SillyTavern-Gemma4-Tools-Fix.
There is nothing to configure. Load the extension in Admin → Extensions; it applies to the next request.
Adds Google's Gemini models as an inference provider, over Google's own API instead of an OpenAI-compatible one.

Google also offers an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, which works with the normal OpenAI Compatible provider. This extension talks to the Gemini API directly (the Google Gen AI SDK), which gives the things the compatible endpoint doesn't: the summaries of the model's thinking shown as reasoning, the thinking level of Gemini 3 and the thinking budget of the earlier models, the safety filters, and the exact token counts Google reports.

Every request of an AI that uses this provider - the prompt with the story, the lorebook entries and the summaries, the answers of the model, the files and pictures an agent or a command sends - is sent to Google's servers (generativelanguage.googleapis.com, or the proxy you set). Google's terms and privacy policy for the Gemini API decide what happens to it there (retention, whether it is used to improve models; this depends on the plan of your API key). The other providers send to the server you chose, which may be your own. Do not use this provider for text you may not send to Google. On a server shared with other users, an administrator who shares an AI of this provider sends the story text of everybody who uses it to Google.

Load the extension in Admin → Extensions, as described in Managing extensions. The JAR is large (about 14 MB): it contains Google's SDK and the libraries only the SDK needs. Nothing else in Marginalia uses them.

Once it is loaded, the Type list of the inference provider dialog has a new entry, Extension, and the Provider list at the top of the Per Type Settings tab offers Google Gemini (it is chosen for you while it is the only one). Without a loaded extension that provides AIs, Extension is not offered.
Api Key
Field
Fill in the General Settings (context size, response size, reasoning) and the settings of the provider on the Per Type Settings tab, then click Test Connection.
Get an API key in Google AI Studio.
How long to wait for Google to answer, and for more text once it started writing. The default is 300.
How often a request is repeated when Google answers with a rate limit (429) or a server error (5xx), or cannot be reached. The default is 2, 0 turns retrying off.
Model
On the Inference Providers tab click Add Inference Provider, enter a Name, choose the type Extension and the provider Google Gemini.
Optional. Empty uses Google's API (generativelanguage.googleapis.com), set it to send the requests through a proxy.
Retries

Sends BLOCK_NONE for the adjustable safety categories (harassment, hate speech, sexually explicit, dangerous content). Fiction often runs into the filters. Google still blocks some content whatever is sent.
Test Connection lists the models and asks the chosen one for a few tokens, with the values in the dialog (before you save them).
The general settings of a provider of the type Extension
The Inference Providers list with a Google Gemini provider
The key of Google AI Studio. It is stored encrypted and not shown again; when you edit the provider, click Reset to enter another one.
The model to use, e.g. gemini-2.5-flash or gemini-3-pro-preview. Refresh lists the models your key can use for writing text; you can type a name that is not in the list.
The Per Type Settings of the Google Gemini provider
The provider is then on the list like any other, with the name of the provider in the Type column:
Timeout (seconds)
Turn off the safety filters
URL
The reasoning settings are those of the general settings of the provider, like for any provider:
With Enabled Reasoning off the model thinks as it does by default and its thinking is not shown.

With it on, the model sends the summaries of its thinking and they are shown as the reasoning of the story part. The Reasoning Effort sets how much it thinks: for Gemini 3 models it is the thinking level (low, medium, high), for the earlier models a budget of 1 024, 8 192 or 24 576 thinking tokens. None is the same as off.

Thinking tokens count as generated tokens, and they are taken from the response size you set: if the model uses it all for thinking, the story part comes back empty and the error says the response size was used up. Raise Max Response Tokens or lower the effort.

Everything a story needs works as with an OpenAI-compatible provider: streaming, stopping a generation, summaries, extensions that call the model, functions the model can call (the Name generator offers some), and images and files attached to a message. The tokens a user uses are counted in the Tokens sent and Tokens generated columns from the numbers Google reports, and the limits of a shared provider apply.

The token counts shown in the story (the size of a part, the prompt) are counted by Google (the countTokens request of the model), once for each text: the answers are remembered. When Google cannot be asked (no key, no network, an error), Marginalia estimates the count itself for a minute and then tries Google again; a text that is saved or edited while another save is going on is estimated too. The estimate differs a little from what Google bills.

l: When the extension is not loaded
p: The providers you created stay in the list when the extension is unloaded, with the type Extension: google-genai, and work again when the extension is loaded. While it is not loaded, a book that uses such a provider can't generate: the error tells you to load the extension or to choose another provider. The provider can still be opened and its general settings changed; the Gemini settings are only shown when the extension is loaded, and they are not touched.
Vertex AI (Google Cloud with a project and credentials). Only API keys of the Gemini API are supported.
Image generation and the other output types of Gemini: only text is written.
Adds Anthropic's Claude models as an inference provider, over Anthropic's own API instead of an OpenAI-compatible one.

Claude is also reachable through aggregators such as OpenRouter with the normal OpenAI Compatible provider. This extension talks to the Claude API directly (the Anthropic SDK), which gives the things a compatible endpoint doesn't: the summaries of the model's thinking shown as reasoning, the effort of Claude 4.6 and later models, and the exact token counts Anthropic reports and counts.

Every request of an AI that uses this provider - the prompt with the story, the lorebook entries and the summaries, the answers of the model, the files and pictures an agent or a command sends - is sent to Anthropic's servers (api.anthropic.com, or the proxy you set). Anthropic's terms and privacy policy for the API decide what happens to it there (retention, safeguards that can decline a request). The other providers send to the server you chose, which may be your own. Do not use this provider for text you may not send to Anthropic. On a server shared with other users, an administrator who shares an AI of this provider sends the story text of everybody who uses it to Anthropic.

Load the extension in Admin → Extensions, as described in Managing extensions. The JAR is large (about 36 MB): it contains Anthropic's SDK and the libraries only the SDK needs. Nothing else in Marginalia uses them.

Once it is loaded, the Type list of the inference provider dialog has a new entry, Extension, and the Provider list at the top of the Per Type Settings tab offers Anthropic Claude (it is chosen for you while it is the only one). Without a loaded extension that provides AIs, Extension is not offered.
Api Key
Field
Fill in the General Settings (context size, response size, reasoning) and the settings of the provider on the Per Type Settings tab, then click Test Connection.
Get an API key in the Claude Console.
How long to wait for Anthropic to answer, and for more text once it started writing. The default is 300.
How often a request is repeated when Anthropic answers with a rate limit (429) or a server error (5xx, also 529 overloaded), or cannot be reached. The default is 2, 0 turns retrying off.
Model
On the Inference Providers tab click Add Inference Provider, enter a Name, choose the type Extension and the provider Anthropic Claude.
Optional. Empty uses Anthropic's API (api.anthropic.com), set it to send the requests through a proxy.
Retries
Test Connection lists the models and asks the chosen one for a few tokens, with the values in the dialog (before you save them).
The Inference Providers list with a Claude provider
The key of the Claude Console. It is stored encrypted and not shown again; when you edit the provider, click Reset to enter another one.
The model to use, e.g. claude-opus-5-5 or claude-sonnet-5-5. Refresh lists the models your key can use; you can type a name that is not in the list.
The Per Type Settings of the Anthropic Claude provider
Timeout (seconds)
URL
The reasoning settings are those of the general settings of the provider, like for any provider:
With Enabled Reasoning off nothing about thinking is sent. The models that think by default (Opus 5.5 can't be told not to) do, and their thinking is not shown; the others do not think.

With it on, the model sends summaries of its thinking and they are shown as the reasoning of the story part. For Claude 4.6 and later the Reasoning Effort is the effort of the model (low, medium, high) with adaptive thinking: the model decides how much to think. For the earlier models (Claude 4.5 and before, Haiku 4.5 among them) it is a budget of 1 024, 8 192 or 24 576 thinking tokens. None is the same as off.

Thinking tokens count as generated tokens, and they are taken from the response size you set: if the model uses it all for thinking, the story part comes back empty and the error says the response size was used up. Raise Max Response Tokens or lower the effort. Claude needs a response size on every request: when neither the provider nor the protocol sets one, 16 000 is used.

Everything a story needs works as with an OpenAI-compatible provider: streaming, stopping a generation, summaries, extensions that call the model, functions the model can call (the Name generator offers some), and pictures (JPEG, PNG, GIF, WebP), PDF and text files attached to a message. The tokens a user uses are counted in the Tokens sent and Tokens generated columns from the numbers Anthropic reports (tokens read from the cache and written to it count as sent), and the limits of a shared provider apply.

The token counts shown in the story (the size of a part, the prompt) are counted by Anthropic (the count_tokens request of the model), once for each text: the answers are remembered. When Anthropic cannot be asked (no key, no network, an error), Marginalia estimates the count itself for a minute and then tries again; a text that is saved or edited while another save is going on is estimated too.
Two things differ from other providers:
Temperature, top p and the penalties of the protocol are not sent. The current Claude API refuses them; the model samples with its own settings. The response size of the protocol is used.

A conversation has to start and end with a message of the user, and Claude does not continue an answer. The prompt of a book always does; a request from an extension that does not is refused with a "bad request" error.

l: When the extension is not loaded
p: The providers you created stay in the list when the extension is unloaded, with the type Extension: anthropic, and work again when the extension is loaded. While it is not loaded, a book that uses such a provider can't generate: the error tells you to load the extension or to choose another provider. The provider can still be opened and its general settings changed; the Claude settings are only shown when the extension is loaded, and they are not touched.
Amazon Bedrock, Google Vertex AI and Microsoft Foundry. Only API keys of the Claude API are supported.
Prompt caching and the tools that run on Anthropic's servers (web search, code execution).

Revision history for lorebook entries: keep earlier versions of your lore and switch between them - for example the state of the world before and after a war, or a character at different points of the story.
Lorebook VCS is not available in the phone layout.

A revision is a snapshot of the whole entry: name, content, note, enabled, order, filter and filtering mode, insertion mode, Do not search its content for other entries, tags and negative tags. (Revisions made before that flag existed read as off.)
The revision bar of an entry
‹ / ›, or the list
A typical use:
Change revision 2 to the character after the events of chapter 10.
Control
Deletes the current revision and switches to the previous one. The last remaining revision can't be deleted.
n / total, Modified
Open the entry of a character and click + - revision 2 is a copy of revision 1.

Revisions work like slots. The entry always shows one of them - the current revision - and what you change in the entry belongs to that revision. Generation always uses the entry as it is, so the current revision is the one the model sees.
Saves the entry as it is now as a new revision and makes it current.
Switch to the previous / next / chosen revision. Your edits stay in the revision you leave; the other one is loaded into the entry.
The first time an entry's details are opened, its current state becomes revision 1.
Which revision is current, and when it was last changed.
With the extension installed, the details (⌄) of every lorebook entry start with a revision bar:
Write. When you go back to edit chapter 5, switch to revision 1 with ‹; switch back with › later.
The lorebook editor gets a Lorebook Revisions row with two buttons. They work on the lorebook selected in the editor:
Button
export
Downloads the history of all entries of the lorebook as lorebook_vcs_history.json.
import
Import Marginalia VCS JSON - a history exported by this extension; Import SillyTavern VCS Extension JSON - history from SillyTavern's lorebook version history extension.
An import replaces the history of the lorebook; when the lorebook already has a history, or the file was exported from a different lorebook, the import asks for confirmation first.

A Marginalia history is matched to the entries by the entries themselves first. Entries it doesn't find - for example when the history comes from another copy of the lorebook - are matched by the name and order of their current revision, or by the name alone when only one entry has it. Histories that match no entry are skipped; the confirmation says how many.

SillyTavern history is matched to the entries by their position in the lorebook, so import it into a lorebook imported from the same world info, before you add or delete entries. The trigger keys of its revisions become the entry's filter, the same way the world info import converts them.

The history is stored in the database with the lorebook, so database backups include it. The data an extension keeps in a lorebook is also written into lorebook exports and into the lorebooks of book backups, and into the copies of a book's lorebooks that agents work on. But importing a lorebook creates new entries, and the history belongs to the identity of the old ones, so it does not show on them. To move the history to an imported copy, export it from the original and import it into the copy - the entries are then matched by name and order (see Lorebook revisions).

Gives the model real places of the Earth to look up instead of inventing them: cities, countries, seas and bays, rivers, lakes, islands, mountains, deserts, ports and airports, with their coordinates and the countries they are in. It can also say what lies around a place and how far apart two places are, so a story set on the real map gets its distances and neighbours right.

The extension has no screen of its own and nothing to configure. The Lore Generator and the Arc Outline offer it to the model as the suite Place provider of their Tools button (Tools for the model), on or off; it is also commands for agents and the command line.

The data is Natural Earth (public domain), which is a map of the notable places: about 18 000, among them 4 900 cities, 250 countries, 4 500 provinces and states, 1 100 rivers, 500 lakes, 400 islands, 350 mountains and ranges, 1 000 ports and 900 airports. It is not a gazetteer: a small creek or a village is not there. Natural Earth also draws most inlets as bays, so asking for the inlets of Canada gives the four it has (Hamilton Inlet, Bathurst Inlet, Minto Inlet and Richard Collinson Inlet), not the hundreds of the coast of British Columbia.
All of them only read.
Command
What it does
/list-place-types
Lists the types of places (city, capital, bay, inlet, river, mountain range, island...) with how many there are.
/search-places query [type [country [limit]]]
Searches by name, type and country, the best match first. * as the query is any name: /search-places * inlets Canada lists the inlets of Canada.
/places-near place radius_km [type [limit]]
The places within the radius of a place or a point, the closest first, with the distance in kilometers and the direction.
/distance-between from to
The distance in a straight line over the Earth (not a road) in kilometers and miles, with the direction.

A place is a name (Ottawa; Paris, France when several have the name, the comma and the country or province pick one) or coordinates (45.42, -75.69). A type can be written in the plural or as people say it: inlets, mountains, towns, states. A country is a name or a code: Canada, Czechia, CA, CAN. Names are compared without case and accents. At most 100 places come back (25 without a limit), and the answer says how many fit in all.
A search for a type also finds the places of a similar water type that have the word in their name: inlet finds Hamilton Inlet, which Natural Earth calls a bay.

An agent that is allowed the commands (they are in the All non-destructive selection and the Auditor role) can call them as functions. They are made for a prompt like "set the first chapter in a fishing village on a fjord in Norway, two days by sea from the capital": the agent searches fjords of Norway, picks one and asks for the distance to Oslo.

Load the extension in Admin → Extensions. In the Lore Generator and the Arc Outline check Use this suite of the Place provider in Tools; its hint tells the model to look a real place up instead of guessing where it is or how far.

Lets the model write the content of a lorebook entry for you. It reads the lore you already have, so the new entry fits the world, and compacts the result into the short, dense form lore entries work best in.
Lore Generator is not available in the phone layout.

With the extension installed, every row of the lorebook editor gets a wand button (Generate lore entry). It opens the generator for that entry. If the entry already has content, the dialog says so at the top: copying the result to the entry replaces the content.

The generator starts with your Default Model and Default Protocol from Settings, see Account & settings. The Model and Protocols lists under the header of the dialog let you use another model or protocol for this generation (the choice is not saved); the protocol is optional. Without a model it only shows a warning.
The lore generator
The two choices at the top of the dialog decide which lore goes into the request:
Choice
Current Lorebook (default) / All Lore
Only the entries of the lorebook the entry is in, ignoring its sub lorebooks; or the entries of that lorebook together with all its sub lorebooks.
Only up to position (n) (default) / All entries

n is the order of the entry. Only the entries that come before it are shown (a lower order, or the same order and created earlier), so the model builds on what already exists and doesn't get lore that was written after the entry. All entries shows everything.

The entry you are generating is never included, with or without content. Whether other entries or lorebooks are enabled, their tags and filters and their insertion mode are ignored: what you pick here is what is sent, in the order the entries are inserted into a prompt. The templates of the entries are processed as usual.

The generation prompt is what you ask the model to write. The prompts are listed in the box next to the choices, in the same top row; the text of the selected one is in the text area on the left, and you can change it for a single generation without saving. The two halves of the dialog are separated by a splitter you can drag.
Button
Save
Saves the text under the selected name.
Save as
Asks for a name and saves the text as a new prompt (or replaces one of that name, after asking).
Delete
Deletes the selected prompt. When the last one is deleted, the built-in DEFAULT prompt comes back.

The built-in prompt has placeholders in brackets (the subject, the details to include, the length, the structure): fill them in before you run it. Prompts belong to your account, and the one you used last is selected again the next time the dialog opens.
The right side has two tabs.

Generation - Run Generation sends the lore followed by the generation prompt. The answer appears as it is written, with the model's reasoning (when it gives any) in a Thinking Process section above it. Stop (in place of Run Generation) ends it early; what was written so far is kept.

Compaction - available once there is a generation. Run Compaction sends the same lore followed by the compaction prompt, with the generated text in it, and the model condenses it into a compact entry. The compaction prompt is set in Settings → Extension Settings → Lore Generator; when it is empty, the built-in one is used (it strips the prose and keeps the facts). Running the generation again discards the compaction.
The compaction of a generated entry
While the model is working, all controls are frozen except Stop; you can't close the dialog either.

When you Copy to Lore Entry, the options of that generation are stored with the entry: the prompt text, which saved prompt it came from, the lore and entries choices and the checked name categories. Opening the generator for that entry again restores them, taking priority over the prompt you used last and your saved name categories. An entry that was never generated into opens with the usual defaults. The options belong to the entry, so they travel with backups and exports of the lorebook.

When a suite of tools for the model is installed (names from the Name generator or the Name provider, places from the Place provider), the top row has a Tools button. It opens the window where you choose which suites, and of the ones with categories which categories, the model may use; see Tools for the model for how it works. While something is checked the model can call the tools during the generation (not the compaction), and the hint of each suite it gets is added to the end of the generation prompt. The choice is saved with your account and with the entry.

Under the prompt you can add files for the model to look at: reference images, a map, a character sheet. Drop them on the upload area, choose them, or paste them into the prompt with Ctrl+V (a screenshot or a copied file becomes an attachment; pasted text is inserted as usual). Up to 20 MB each. They are listed with their name, type and size, and the trash button removes one. They are sent with the generation, not the compaction, and you can add and delete them only while no generation runs.

Whether the model can use them depends on the model and the inference provider: images are sent as images, audio only as WAV or MP3, other files as files. When the provider refuses an attachment, you get a message and nothing is generated.

Copy to Lore Entry is available when the compaction has a result. The compacted text becomes the content of the entry, and the generated text before the compaction goes into its note. Both are replaced. If the compaction is one code block (the built-in prompt asks for that, to make the text easy to copy), the code block around it is removed. The lorebook is refreshed, and the dialog stays open; Exit closes it.

The generator also works without the dialog, as three commands for the command line and for agents. They do the same two steps as the dialog and, like the dialog, they store nothing: they return the text, and putting it into an entry (what Copy to Lore Entry does) is up to the caller, so all three only read. The lorebook and the entry are given by number, as in /list-lorebooks and /list-lore-entries; the model is your default model and protocol.
Command
What it does
/list-lore-templates [template]
Lists your saved generation prompts (name, length, start of the text) and the one used last. With a name it returns the whole text of that prompt.
/generate-lore-entry [prompt [template [lorebook [entry [order [scope [limit [images [compact]]]]]]]]]

Generates a text with the lore of the lorebook, compacts it (like /compact-lore-entry) and returns the compacted text; with compact false it returns the generated text as it is. The text sent is a template followed by the prompt of the caller (see below). With images the model also looks at pictures, as with the attachments of the dialog.
/compact-lore-entry text [lorebook [entry [order [scope [limit]]]]]
Compacts the text with the same lore and returns the result, without the code block around it.

The entry the text is for decides which lore the model sees. Give its handle or its number as entry (and the lorebook it is in, by handle or number, when you give the number) and the lore is the same as in the dialog: with limit UP_TO_POSITION (the default) the entries before it, the entry itself never. An entry that does not exist yet has no number: give the order it will get instead (the order of /list-lore-entries, lower comes first) and the model sees the entries before that order; without either, the text is written for a new entry after all the others. scope is CURRENT_LOREBOOK (the default) or ALL_LORE, limit is UP_TO_POSITION or ALL_ENTRIES, as in the dialog.

A generation is only as good as its prompt, so the command always starts from one of your saved generation prompts (see Prompts): the one named in template, or the one used last when none is named. The prompt of the caller follows it under the heading Task for this entry and is where the subject, the facts, the length and the sections go, which is what the template asks for. template none sends the prompt alone, for a caller that has written the whole prompt itself, for example after getting the text of a template from /list-lore-templates and editing it. A command that is called with a template and no prompt sends just the template.

The images of /generate-lore-entry are the images the dialog would attach to the generation. An agent passes a list of paths of image files of its workspace (/refs/map.png; at most 8, PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP, scaled down when large), which you put there with Upload file in the Workspace tab. The command bar has no way to name an image, so images is for agents. It is your default model that looks at the pictures: if it does not take images the command fails and says so. Only the generation takes images, as in the dialog; the compaction works on the text alone.

The compact parameter of /generate-lore-entry is true by default: the command generates and compacts in one call, so an agent needs a single command and cannot forget the second step. Pass compact false to get the long generated text (for example to review or edit it), and run /compact-lore-entry on it later.

The model gets no tools here. A caller that wants names asks for them first, with /generate-names of the Name generator or /pick-real-names of the Name provider, and writes the ones it likes into the prompt. An agent can also take the text of a template from /list-lore-templates, change it and pass the result as the prompt.

The prompts and the compaction prompt are stored with your settings, so database backups include them. Nothing is stored with the lorebook; the generated text exists in the dialog only until you copy it.

Gives the model real names to pick from instead of inventing them: the most common forenames and surnames of many countries. Where the Name generator makes up new names that only sound like a category, this extension hands out names that exist, each with the original spelling next to the romanized one: Satō and 佐藤.

The extension has no screen of its own and nothing to configure. Other extensions offer its functions to the model: the Lore Generator and the Arc Outline, where you choose which lists the model may use. Its suite is Name provider in the tools window, next to the Name generator one, and you can check lists of both, of one of them or of none.
Function
What it does
list_real_name_lists
Lists the lists of names; with a filter only those that have its words in the name.
pick_real_names
Picks up to 100 different names of one list at random. Every name is a pair, the romanized name and the original one.

A list with fewer names than asked for returns all of them. The model is told (see the hint of the Name provider suite in the tools window) to pick a name from what it gets and to write it as it was returned, with the original next to it when that suits the setting; it may combine a forename with a surname of the same country.
The same names are available as commands, for the command line and for agents, which can use them in their own prompts (for example for /generate-lore-entry of the Lore Generator):
Command
What it does
/list-real-name-lists [filter]
Lists the lists as a JSON array; with a filter only those whose name has all its words (each at the start of a word, in any order, not case sensitive).
/pick-real-names list count
Picks up to 100 names of the list at random and returns them as a JSON array of pairs, the romanized name and the original one.
Both only read.

There are about 180 lists, named Country - Surnames and Country - Forenames: surnames of 75 countries and forenames of 106 (Japan - Surnames, Czechia - Forenames, Kosovo - Surnames). Forenames of both genders are in one list. A list has from 5 to about 150 names, the most common ones of the country. The names are not made new: a name you get is a name that people have.

A few dozen entries are groups of lists by language: Language - Forenames and Language - Surnames for Spanish (18 countries), Portuguese, French, German, English, Arabic, West, East and South Slavic, North Germanic, Nordic, Uralic, Baltic, Turkic, Persian, Chinese, South Asian, Southeast Asian, Caucasus, Albanian and Romanian (where there are such lists). They are listed like any list and are one item in the tools window. Every name of a group is picked from one of its lists chosen at random, each country with the same chance, so a request for 20 names gets names of several countries, never the same name twice. Countries where several languages are spoken (Belgium, Luxembourg, Malta, Andorra) are in no group. A group is a line in name-groups.json, see the plugin README.

The data is the popular names by country dataset (CC0), which takes them from Wikipedia's lists of the most common surnames and the most popular given names. The names written in non-Latin scripts (Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Arabic, Cyrillic...) have a romanization, either one from the source or one made by machine translation, so check the spelling when it matters.

Load the extension in Admin → Extensions. It applies to the next generation, also when it is installed after the extensions that use it or unloaded and installed again. Without it and the other suites there is no Tools button.

Gives the model a way to ask for names instead of inventing them. The names come from lists of real names - given names and surnames of many countries, places, deities, monsters, drugs, companies, foods, and more - and are made new by a Markov chain, so they sound like the category without being copies of it.

The extension has no screen of its own and nothing to configure. Other extensions offer its functions to the model; at the moment that are the Lore Generator and the Arc Outline, where you choose which categories the model may use (see Tools for the model); its suite is Name generator, next to the Name provider of the Name provider, which hands out real names instead of made up ones.
Choosing the categories of names in the Tools window of the Lore Generator
Function
What it does
list_name_categories
Lists the categories of names; with a filter only those that have its words in the name.
generate_names
Makes up to 100 new names of one category. Optionally with a shortest and longest length.

Without a length, the names are as long as the names of that category usually are (a category of long company names gives long names, one of short forenames short ones). The model can ask for other lengths between 2 and 30 letters. A small category may return fewer names than asked for, because the chain runs out of different ones. The model is free to pick one of the names, change it or combine two of them; see the hint of the Name generator suite in the tools window.
The same names are available as commands, for the command line and for agents, which can use them in their own prompts (for example for /generate-lore-entry of the Lore Generator):
Command
What it does
/list-name-categories [filter]

Lists the categories as a JSON array; with a filter only those whose name has all its words (each at the start of a word, in any order, not case sensitive: chad male finds Africa - Central Africa - Chad - Male but not …Female).
/generate-names category count [min_length [max_length]]
Makes up to 100 names of the category and returns them as a JSON array. Different names each time.
Both only read.
There are about 1270 categories. Their names say what they are:
Given names and surnames of the world, from Kate Monk's Onomastikon: Europe Western - France - Surnames, Ancient World - Egypt - Male, India - Hindu Gods - Goddesses. Several hundred of them.

Surnames of 75 countries, the romanized surnames of the popular names by country dataset (CC0): Armenia - Surnames, Japan - Surnames, Kosovo - Surnames. They are small lists (6 to about 150 names), so the chains stay short and the new names are close to the real ones; for the real ones themselves use the Name provider.

Lists from other collections: gods, angels, demons, ancient cities and states, emperors, planets (fantasygen), Corpora (animals, tarot, Tolkien names, Game of Thrones houses, drugs, hospitals, fabrics, gemstones, programming languages...) and markov-namegen-lib (Pokemon, dragons, cocktails, banks, Roman place names...).

About 170 entries are groups of categories. They put the many small lists of a language together, so you ask for German - Male instead of picking among Germany - Germanic - Male, Germany - Biblical - Male, Austria - First names - Male and the rest. They are listed like any category, and a group is one item in the tools window. The groups:

By language, each as - Male, - Female and - Surnames where there are such lists: German, French, Spanish (the surnames include Latin America), Italian, Portuguese, Dutch, Scandinavian, Finnic, Baltic, Irish, Scottish, Welsh, Celtic (all of them), West, East and South Slavic, Greek, Hungarian, Romanian, Albanian, Caucasian, Turkic, Persian, Arabic, Jewish, Hindu (the four alphabetical lists of male names as one), South Asian, Southeast Asian, Malay-Indonesian, Polynesian and the African regions (West, East, Southern, North, Central). Chinese, Japanese, Korean and Vietnamese have - Surnames.

Any gender: Language - Forenames (German - Forenames, Spanish - Forenames, Celtic - Forenames...) takes the male and the female lists of the language and its lists of names for both genders, so a call returns men's and women's names mixed (the shares follow the sizes of the lists, mostly between half and three quarters men). Chinese, Japanese, Korean and Vietnamese have it too. Languages where the mix would be lopsided (Turkic, South Asian, West and Southern African, Malay-Indonesian) have only the male and female groups.
Of the past: Anglo-Saxon, Medieval Germanic, Medieval English, Ancient Near East.

Native American: Native American - Male, - Female and - Surnames (the northern American categories of the Onomastikon: Apache, Sioux, Iroquois, Cherokee, Inuit...) and the same for Central and South America (Aztec, Maya, Inca, Amazonian).
Other: English - Surnames (patronymics, trades, places...), Saints, Deities, Fantasy Creatures, Game of Thrones Houses.

For every name the extension first picks one of the categories of the group at random, and then makes the name with the chain of that category (with its usual lengths). A name sounds like one people and language instead of a blend of all of them, and one call returns names of several. The lists of the countries, which are split by origin or by letter, are chosen by their size (a list of 600 names is chosen more often than one of 10); in the groups of whole languages and countries (Turkic, Caucasian, Baltic, Polynesian, the African regions, Native American...) every member has the same chance. The sources of some groups are short and partly English translations (Calf-Woman), so the names are rough. A group is a line in name-groups.json (the members and how they are chosen), see the plugin README.

Each category has a chain of the length that suited it best (short lists get short chains, which repeat the originals less) and the lengths its names usually have. The lists themselves are not part of Marginalia: only the probabilities are, so the original names can't be read out of the extension. Some of the sources have licences of their own, see the plugin README.

Load the extension in Admin → Extensions. It applies to the next generation; extensions that use it find it when it is loaded, also if it is installed after them or unloaded and installed again - there is no need to restart the Lore Generator. Without it and the other suites, the Lore Generator has no Tools button.

Lets the model review what you've written: reader reactions, an editor's critique, a continuity check - whatever you prompt it for. Reviews are kept with the part, next to the story, and never become part of the book.
A review of a story part
The menu (☰) of every part in the story editor gets a Review submenu:
Item
View / Generate Review
Opens the review dialog. When the part has no review yet, one is generated right away.
Advanced Options
Opens the advanced options, then generates a review with them.
Delete Review
Removes all reviews of the part.
In the review dialog:
‹ / › page through the reviews of the part; › on the last review generates a new one;
Stop generating interrupts the review being written;
click the text of a review to edit it; it is saved when you click outside the field;
Thinking Process shows the reasoning of reasoning models;
Close closes the dialog.

By default the review uses the same prompt the part was written from (Use standard prompt info): the system prompt with the lore and summaries, the earlier parts, then the part itself, and finally the review prompt. The model reviews the part with the full context of the story.
The pre-prompt of the profile, if set, comes first as a system message.
Option
Prompt Override
A different review prompt for this review. Starts with the prompt of the profile.
Use standard prompt info
On: the prompt the part was written from, as above. Off: only the story parts, with the options below.
Include Lorebook
(off only) Adds the lore that was active when the part was written.
Token Limit
(off only) How many tokens of story to send: the parts up to and including the reviewed one, newest first, as many as fit. Starts with the room for the prompt of the model.
With Use standard prompt info off, the dialog shows the size of the request (Total tokens). Generate opens the review dialog with these options; further reviews generated in that dialog use them too.
Advanced review options
A system message sent first, e.g. You are a demanding fiction editor.
As a line editor, point out clichés, repetitions and weak verbs in the last part, with suggestions.
Click Save at the top of the Settings page to keep the changes.
Create a profile for each kind of review and select the one you want before reviewing. A cheaper model for reviews saves cost: set it as the profile's Reviewer Model.
Describe how a first-time reader would feel at the end of this part, and what they expect next.
Field
List continuity errors in the last part compared to the earlier story. Quote the passages.
Manage profiles. The _Default profile can't be renamed or deleted.
New, Rename, Delete
Profile
Review Post-Prompt (User)
Review Pre-Prompt (System)
Reviewer Model
Reviewer Protocol
Reviewer settings are in Settings → Extension Settings → Reviewer Settings. They are organized in profiles:
The default post-prompt simulates a discussion on a story forum: a made-up thread with thirty replies from different readers, positive and negative. Other ideas:
The inference provider that writes reviews. Empty: the book's model.
The profile to edit - and the one used for all reviews.
The protocol. Empty: the book's protocol.
The request for the review, sent last.
The Reviewer settings
Reviews are stored with the story part, so they are part of book backups and copies. Branch Story doesn't copy them. Profiles are stored in your user settings.

Some extensions give the model tools: functions it can call while it writes, to get names, to look up real places, and so on, instead of inventing them. The tools of one extension are a suite; the suites there are:
Suite
Extension
What the model can do with it
Name generator
Get names made up to sound like a category (places, deities, surnames of a country...).
Name provider
Get real names with their original spelling.
Place provider
Look up real places, what is around them and how far apart they are.

A dialog that runs the model with tools has a Tools button: the generators of the Lore Generator and of the Arc Outline (not its story import, whose names are in the story already). The button is shown only while at least one suite is installed, and when you have chosen something it says how many things are on: Tools (3).

Tools opens a window with one section for each suite, under the name of the suite, with the number of things checked in it. A section with something checked starts open. What is in a section depends on the suite:

A suite with items (the Name generator and the Name provider have one for each category or list of names) shows a table with a checkbox each and a filter field of its own above it: type a part of a name to show only the matching items. The items that are checked always stay in the table, whatever the filter says. Check shown checks all the items the table shows at that moment, Uncheck shown unchecks them, and a line below says how many are checked. The model gets only the checked items: it can list them and ask for names of them, and no others.
A suite without items (the Place provider) is on or off: Use this suite.
The Tools window with the categories of the Name generator filtered by Japan

Every section also has a Hint for the model. It is a short text added to the end of the prompt when the model gets the suite, telling it when and how to use the tools (for the names: call the tools instead of inventing names, pick from what you get, keep a real name as it was returned). The built-in text is shown in grey in the field; write your own to replace it, leave the field empty to use the built-in one.
A suite that is on, with its hint for the model open; the other two sections closed with the number of items checked

The model gets the suites that have something checked: nothing checked in any of them, no tools. The choice is saved with your account, so it is the same the next time; the Lore Generator also saves the choice with each entry it generated, and opens that entry with it. A suite that was unloaded is skipped, and a checked item that the extension no longer has is ignored. Extensions can be loaded and unloaded while Marginalia runs; the button follows.
If two suites had a function of the same name the generation would not start and say which; the suites that come with Marginalia do not.

The suites are also commands of the command bar and of agents (/pick-real-names, /generate-names, /search-places...), so what the model gets here and what an agent can call are the same suite under the same name.

The Name tools button became Tools. The categories you had checked are checked in the suites of the Name generator and the Name provider, and the hints you wrote in Settings → Extension Settings (Name generator hint, Name provider hint) are now the hints of those two suites in this window; the fields in the settings are gone.
This extension was called SillyTavern Converter before 1.6.0. Only the name changed; its files, the data stored with your books and the saved layouts are the same.

Rewrite a SillyTavern roleplay chat as a story, turn by turn: load the chat into a book, let the model split it into turn details using the chat and the lore of the book, and put each turn into the new turn form of the story with one click.

The source does not have to be a chat: the converter can also take the parts of another book of yours (from a backup file or the book itself) and give you their instructions one by one, to redraft a book.

To make a book out of a chat directly (every message, or every user and assistant pair, a part), see Importing from SillyTavern. The converter is for the other way: you keep the chat next to you and write the story again, with the model, from instructions made of the chat.
The Converter is not available in the phone layout.

The left sidebar of the story editor gets a Converter tab (small text, and the tab scrolls when the sidebar is low). Above its two lists is the section Convert to turn details, closed until you open it so that the lists get the room. It holds:
Model and Protocol
What the wand runs with. They start with the model and protocol of the book; the choice is kept with the book.
From, To
The range of messages the wand works on. Type the numbers, click in the chat, or use All.
Token count
How many tokens the request takes: the messages of the range plus the prompt and the lore (counted once). Use it to keep the range within the context of the model.
Convert range
The wand: asks the model for the turn details of the range. It becomes Stop while the model works.
Pen button
Edits the prompt of the wand (variables , , , , ``), with a Default button.
Align to turns
Moves the range to the boundaries of the turns, see below. Kept with the book.
Auto mode
Shows the controls that convert the whole range in batches, see below.

A turn of the story is the messages of the user (the instructions) followed by the message of the character. With Align to turns ticked, every range you choose (by clicking, typing the numbers or All) is moved to the boundaries of the turns: the start goes back to the first message of its turn, and the end goes back to the last message of the character before it, so the range never ends on a message of the user that belongs to the turn after it. The end of the chat stays where it is. A range that lies wholly in the messages of the user before a reply is extended forward to that reply.

Auto mode shows a line with Messages per batch, the button Convert in batches and how many requests that makes, with the tokens they take in all. The button splits the current range into batches of that many messages and sends them to the model one after another (after asking), the same as the wand does for one range. With Align to turns every batch ends at the end of a turn (the last message of the character within the size, or the end of the turn when it is longer than the size), so no turn is cut in two; without it the batches are cut exactly by the number, and a turn on the border can be split in two.

While it runs the chat shows the batch it is at, the status line tells which batch of how many, and the button becomes Stop. The turn details of each batch are stored as soon as it is done, as with the wand (the turns that touch the range and that you have not ticked are replaced). When all batches are done the range is as you had it and the Turn details tab opens. A batch whose answer can't be used (empty, or not matching what was asked for) is sent again, up to three times in all. When you stop, or a batch still fails, the notification says why and the range is what is left, so you can go on from there.

The prompt tells the model the details of the last turn that ends before the range (its scene setting, POV character, present characters and instructions, in ``), so the turns of the range keep the same point of view and scene until the chat changes them. This is how a batch of the auto mode continues from the one before it: the turn details of a batch are stored before the next one is sent. When there is no turn before the range the part of the prompt is left out.

Upload the .jsonl file of a chat (in SillyTavern it is in data/user/chats/character/, or export it from the chat). The chat must have no branches: of every message the swipe that was shown is read, and hidden system messages and empty ones are left out. If your chat has branches, import the one you want to rewrite first (see Importing from SillyTavern for joining branches into a tree).
The Chat tab is a table of the messages: a checkbox, the number and the message, with the name of who said it in bold above the text (the messages of the user are marked with »).

Tick the checkbox of a message you have gone through, so you can see what is left. The button with the double arrow above the table scrolls to the next unchecked message (after the one you ticked or clicked last, starting again from the top at the end).
Click a message to make it the range, Shift+click another to extend the range up to it. The range is highlighted and the token count follows.
The button with the cross above the table removes the chat and the turn details from the book (after asking).
The Converter tab with a chat and the range chosen

Use the wand and the Turn details tab opens with what the model prepared, in the order of the chat. A row is a turn: the messages it is made from and, in one element, the scene setting, the POV character, the characters who are present and the instructions, each under a bold line with its name. The model is told to cover every message of the range exactly once; numbers outside of the range are cut to it.
Click a row to open the new turn form of the story and copy all four fields of the turn into it. Change what you want and generate. (A row's checkbox and delete button do not open the form.)
Tick the checkbox of a turn you have used; the double arrow goes to the next unchecked turn.
Running the wand again for a range replaces the earlier turns that touch the range, except the ticked ones.
The turn details the model prepared
To write a book again, part by part, load the old one as the source. The tab shows Upload a chat, Load a backup and Pick a book while it has no source:
Pick a book opens a list of your books (not the one you are in). The parts of the branch the book is on are loaded, from the first part to the one the book is at now.

Load a backup takes a backup file of a book: the JSON, the .zip with the images, or a file you downloaded from the backups of a book. The backup is only read, nothing is restored. The branch is the one the book was on when the backup was made.

Of every part the converter keeps the instructions, the scene setting, the POV character, the present characters and the text of the part, and nothing else (no summaries, lorebook, reasoning, images, other branches or settings), so a long book stays small. A book that has no parts loads nothing, and a backup whose parts do not lead back to the first part is refused as damaged.
The tab then has two lists, as with a chat but without the wand (the book already has its instructions, so the Convert to turn details section is not there):
Parts is the text of each part, with the same checkbox and the arrow to the next unchecked part. Read the old text next to the story you write.

Turn details has one row per part with its scene setting, POV character, present characters and instructions. Click a row to put them into the new turn form of the story, as with a chat, and generate the new part. Tick the turns you have done.
Only one source is kept with a book. To load another, remove the current one with the cross (after asking); this also forgets the ticks made on it.

The uploaded file is stored as a resource of yours (a chat of SillyTavern can be megabytes, with all that SillyTavern adds to the messages), linked to the book. The parts of a book are stored the same way as a small JSON file (book name.redraft.json) with the instructions and the text; the book keeps only the ticks. The ticks, the turn details, the model and the prompt are stored in the attributes of the book, so they are in book backups and copies.

The file of the chat is not in book backups, and a copy of a book points to the same file. After a restore the ticks and turn details are there, but the converter asks for the chat again (upload the same file; this replaces the turn details and the ticks). The same goes for the parts of a book: load the book or the backup again and tick again. Removing the source with the cross deletes the resource.
A chat with the model next to your story: ask about the plot, check continuity, brainstorm names or the next chapter - without adding anything to the book.
Side Query is not available in the phone layout.
Side Query next to the story
The left sidebar of the story editor gets a Side Query tab next to Outline. Drag the divider to give it more room.

The tab holds conversations, each in its own tab: + opens a new one (Tab 2, Tab 3...), the pen renames a tab, × closes it (the last tab can't be closed). With Enable AI Tab Naming in the profile, the model names a tab after its first answer, unless you renamed the tab yourself. Conversations belong to the book and are kept until you close their tab.
Type a question into the box at the bottom and click SEND. The answer appears as it is written; STOP (in place of SEND) interrupts it.
Button
SEND
Sends the question.
UNDO
Removes the last message. If it was your question, it goes back into the box to be edited.
REGENERATE
Removes the last answer and asks again.

Every message has buttons to move it up or down, edit it, copy it to the clipboard, and exclude it from the context (or include it again). Excluded messages stay in the conversation but are not sent to the model - useful to drop a wrong answer without deleting it.
The options above the conversation choose what is sent with your questions:
Option
Lorebook
The lore of the book (see below).
Chat Logs from … to
The story parts of the active branch in that range, numbered from 1 as in the outline: 1 to 6 are the parts #1 to #6.
Plug button
Opens a list of the data other extensions offer, with a checkbox for each (see below).
Tokens
The approximate size of the request.

Lorebook collects the lore like a generation does: the book's lorebook and its sub lorebooks (disabled lorebooks are skipped), the enabled entries whose tags match the book's tags, with macros processed. Keyword filters are not applied - there is no story prompt to match, so every applicable entry is sent. Variables set by the entries are not stored.
The plug button opens a popover with the additional sources that other extensions offer, for example the Arc Outline offers your outline. Every source has a checkbox; the list has up to two parts:
About the book: a checked source is added to the request after the lorebook, under its name.
About story parts: a checked source is asked for every story part in the Chat Logs range and what it returns is added after the text of that part. It has an effect only while Chat Logs is on.

The choice is kept with the tab. If an extension is not installed (or stopped) its sources are not in the list and not sent, and they come back when the extension does. With none offered the popover says so.
The request is built like this:

one system message: the profile's Initial System Query, the lorebook entries (Lorebook Context), the checked sources about the book and the story parts (Chat History Context, labelled with their outline numbers Message #1, #2..., each followed by the checked sources about story parts);
the messages of the conversation that are included, as a chat. The profile's Instructions Before User Input are put at the start of your last question, before its text.
The model and protocol come from the profile (see below), by default those of the book. A cheap, fast model is usually enough for questions about the story.
Questions you ask often can be saved:
Save prompt (disk icon) saves the text in the box under the name selected in the list, or asks for a name;
Save prompt as... saves it under a new name;
pick a name in the list to put the saved text into the box;
the trash button deletes the selected saved query.
Saved queries belong to your account and are available in every book.
Some useful ones:
List every named character that appeared so far, with one line about each.
Which threads of the plot are still open?
Suggest five names for a harbor town in this world.
Side Query settings are in Settings → Extension Settings → SideQuery Settings, organized in profiles like the Reviewer ones. The selected profile is the one used:
The SideQuery settings
Field
Profile, New, Rename, Delete
Choose and manage profiles. _Default can't be renamed or deleted.
SideQuery Model, SideQuery Protocol
The inference provider and protocol to use. Empty: the book's.
Initial System Query
The start of the system message, e.g. the role of the assistant.
Instructions Before User Input
Text put right before your last question - rules for the answers, e.g. Answer briefly. Quote the story when you can.
Enable AI Tab Naming
After the first answer in a tab, the model is asked for a short name of the conversation (one extra request). Tabs you renamed keep their name.

A sub-permission: the box can be ticked only while Notifications is granted (it is greyed out otherwise, and taking the permission away clears it). Without it only addresses on the internet are called: not localhost, not a private network (10.x.x.x, 172.16-31.x.x, 192.168.x.x), not a link-local or shared address (169.254.x.x, which is where cloud hosts keep their metadata service, 100.64-127.x.x), not the unique local addresses of IPv6. A database backup is a complete copy of the Marginalia database: all users with all their books, lorebooks, settings and extension data. Use it to protect the installation against mistakes and failures, and to move it to another computer. To back up a single book, users have book backups.
The Database Backups tab

Click Create Backup on the Database Backups tab. The copy is made while Marginalia runs, consistent even when people are writing. It appears in the list with its Name, Created date, Type (Manual or Scheduled) and Size. The toolbar shows the current size of the database.
Each backup has:
Button
Download
Downloads the backup file (.sqlite) - keep a copy outside the server.
Restore on restart
Restores the backup, see below.
trash
Deletes the backup.

Upload Backup adds a backup file (.sqlite or .db) to the list, for example one downloaded from another installation. The file is checked first and refused with The database can't be restored: ... and the reason when it is not a SQLite database, is damaged, is not a Marginalia database (another application's database), or comes from a newer Marginalia version than the one running.

A database backup contains everything, including the password hashes of all users and their API keys. The API keys are encrypted with the secret.key file in the data folder, which is not part of the backup - but anyone with both the backup and secret.key can read them. Keep downloaded backups as safe as the server itself.

The files are stored in the db-backups folder of the data folder. Copies Marginalia makes itself - pre-restore-... before a restore and pre-migration-... before an upgrade - are in the list too, shown as Manual, so they are never deleted by the rotation of scheduled backups. Book backups and extension JARs are separate files and are not part of a database backup.

Uploaded files (the pictures of the parts) are not part of a database backup either. The database only knows them as entries of the Resources tab; the files are in the data/login/images folder of the data folder. That is fine: after a restore the entries are the ones from the time of the backup and the pictures they use are still in the folder. Files of pictures that were added after the backup are just left over (nothing refers to them) and take disk space. To keep the pictures safe, include the whole data folder in your own backups, or pack them into a book backup.

When you restore a backup on another installation, copy secret.key from the original installation as well (with Marginalia stopped), otherwise the saved API keys can't be decrypted and every user has to enter them again.

How many scheduled backups to keep; older ones are deleted. 0 keeps all. Manual and uploaded backups are never deleted.
Click Save Schedule to apply it. The status line shows when the last scheduled backup was made and when the next one is due.
When Marginalia wasn't running at a scheduled time - typical for the desktop app, which runs only while you write - it makes the missed backup about 30 seconds after the next start.
The schedule is a cron expression with five fields, minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week:
Expression
Runs
every day at 3:00

Mondays at 2:30 (day of week: 0 or 7 is Sunday, 1 Monday...)

Times are in the time zone of the server (in Docker, set it with the TZ environment variable).

To turn scheduled backups off, uncheck Create backups automatically and click Save Schedule. The expression is kept, so you can turn the backups on again later. It is still checked - an invalid expression is never saved - but while the backups are off, the field may also be empty.
A database can't be replaced while Marginalia uses it, so a restore happens on the next start:
Click Restore on restart next to the backup and confirm. The tab shows Database restore is scheduled. Restart the application to apply it. - Cancel Restore undoes it.
Restart Marginalia: quit and start the desktop app, or docker compose restart on the server.

On the start, the current database is moved to db-backups/pre-restore-time-marginalia.sqlite - it appears in the list, so a restore can be undone by restoring that file - and the backup takes its place. A backup from an older Marginalia version is upgraded automatically.

The backup is checked again before it is swapped in (the same checks as for Upload Backup, also Restore on restart refuses a backup that fails them). If it fails the check, or upgrading it fails, Marginalia keeps (or puts back) the current database and starts normally; the refused file is moved to db-backups/rejected-restore-time-marginalia.sqlite and the log says why.
Everything after the backup is lost: books, parts and settings created since. Users who are logged in have to log in again if their account changed.

When a new version of Marginalia is going to change the structure of an existing database, it first saves a copy as db-backups/pre-migration-time-Vversion-marginalia.sqlite, where the version is the one the database was at. The copy is in the list of backups, so an upgrade can be undone by installing the old version of Marginalia and restoring that copy. The last three copies are kept. A new installation has nothing to copy, and if the copy can't be made (for example the disk is full), the log says so and the upgrade goes on.
A migration that fails halfway is rolled back by itself and Marginalia does not start; the copy is for an upgrade that went through but did something you don't want.
Create a backup and Download it.
Install Marginalia on the new computer, create a temporary administrator on the first start.
Upload Backup, Restore on restart, restart.
Log in with the accounts from the backup.
Copy the data folder (book backups and the pictures of the parts) and extensions folder from the old data folder as well. Or simply stop Marginalia and copy the whole .marginalia folder.

The files of resources (the pictures users attach to story parts, uploaded files) are stored in the data folder of each user, in data/login/images and data/login/resources. Deleting a resource, or replacing its content, only changes the database: the file stays on the disk, and neither the cleanup nor anything else removes it. Resource Files finds the files that nothing uses any more, lets you download them and deletes them from the disk to get the space back.
Open the Resource Files tab of the admin page and click Scan files. A progress bar shows the folders being read. Nothing is changed.

The table lists the files no resource points to: the path (user folder/images/file), the size and the date they were last modified. All of them are ticked. Untick what you want to keep, Select all and Select none change all of them, and the arrow in the header of the first column does the same. A line above the table tells how many of the files are unused, their size, and how many are ticked.
Optionally click Download as ZIP to get the ticked files in one archive (the entries are named by their path), or the arrow in a row for a single file. That is the backup to keep before deleting.
Delete selected removes the ticked files from the disk after you confirm. Close empties the table without deleting anything.
The Resource Files tab after a scan
Deleted files can't be brought back. Download them as a ZIP first when in doubt.

A file is used when any resource of any user points to it, a deleted one included: a resource in the Trash can be restored, and its picture must work again. So the files of resources that are deleted are listed only after the cleanup has removed the resources from the database, together with the files of content that was replaced (the old file stays behind) and files left by failed uploads.

The files are compared by name (a random identifier), in the folders of all users, also the login-deleted folders of deleted users: their files stay used until the cleanup purges the user and their resources.
Only the images and resources folders of the folders in the data folder are read, nothing else (database backups, agent workspaces and so on are not touched).
A file that a user uploads after the scan is not deleted: Delete selected reads the database again and keeps the files that resources point to by then (the message says how many files were kept).
The scan reads the data folder, which can take a while with many files; Stop on the progress bar cancels it.

When users delete something in Marginalia - a book, a story part, a lorebook, an inference provider - it disappears from their lists, but stays in the database. That makes deleting safe and keeps references working (a book still knows the provider that wrote its parts). Until then users can restore their deleted objects from the Trash tab. Cleanup removes such deleted data for good, to keep the database small.
The Cleanup tab
Cleanup can't be undone, what it removes is gone from the Trash too. Create a database backup first.
Open the Cleanup tab of the admin page and click Analyze. Nothing is changed yet.
Check the result (see below).
Click Run Cleanup and confirm n objects will be permanently removed.
Cleanup covers the data of all users.

Cleanup deletes entries from the database, and only the files of agents: the workspace of a purged agent and the folder of a purged run. The files of deleted resources (pictures of the parts) stay in the data folder of their owner until you remove them in the Resource Files tab.

Trash below the tables lists the deleted objects of all users, one row per object (open it to load the table), so you can see what a cleanup would remove and restore what somebody asked you to bring back. It is the same table as the Trash tab, including the filters by user and type and the Extended Content link.

Meaning
