The Extensions tab of the admin page installs and removes extensions for the whole installation.
The Extensions tab
Actions
Active when it is running; Stopped when you stopped it (see Stopping and starting); Installed or Resolved when it failed to start (see When an extension fails).

Click Load Extension (.jar) (or drop the file on it) and choose the extension's JAR file. It is copied to the extensions folder of the data folder and started right away; Extension loaded successfully. confirms it. The extension appears in the list:
Column
Extension Name

Extensions change parts of the user interface of one Marginalia version. Use the extensions built from the same source as the application (see the plugins README). An incompatible extension may fail to load or break parts of the application. The extension API is not frozen in 1.0, so expect to update extensions together with Marginalia.
ID
Its name.
Its version. The # button next to it shows the SHA-256 hash of the extension's JAR when you hover it; click it to copy the hash, e.g. to compare it with the one published by the author.

JAR files can also be copied into the extensions folder directly, for example on a server without access to the UI; they are loaded on the next start. This is also how the Docker setup can be prepared: put the JARs into ./data/extensions. The JARs can be built in Docker too, see Plugins in the server guide.
State
Stop / Start, Log and Unload.
The internal number of the extension in this run.
Users see the extension in windows they open from then on - a book that was already open has to be closed and opened again, or the page reloaded.
Valid or Invalid; click it to read the report of the check Marginalia made before starting the extension.
Verification
Version

Stop unloads the extension immediately without removing it: it disappears from the screens it added to, but its JAR and data stay, and it is listed with the state Stopped. The button then reads Start, which loads it again (it is checked first, like at the start of the application; if the check fails, it stays stopped and the report is shown). A stopped extension stays stopped after Marginalia restarts. Uploading a new version of a stopped extension starts it.

The stop is remembered by an empty file named like the JAR with .STOPPED added (sidequery.jar.STOPPED) in the extensions folder. On a server without access to the UI, create it to keep an extension from starting, or delete it to let the extension start on the next start.

Log opens the log of the extension: what the extension itself wrote with the logger Marginalia gives to extensions (Logging). It shows the last part of the file, Refresh reads it again and Clear deletes it. The file is extensions/name.jar.log (for example sidequery.jar.log); when it grows over 2 MB it is moved to .log.old and a new one is started. It is deleted when the extension is unloaded. Extensions that don't log anything have an empty log. What the extension logs also goes to the application log (named extension.name, at the level of the line), so it is in the log of the server too; problems of Marginalia itself are only there.
The log of an extension

Unload asks for confirmation, then stops the extension immediately and deletes its JAR (and its log) from the extensions folder. Its data stays (see Where extension data is kept); loading it again brings the data back.

To install a newer version of an extension, Load Extension (.jar) with the new file - the file name doesn't matter. The installed version is unloaded, its JAR deleted and the new version started in its place. If the new version fails to load, the upload shows the error and the old version keeps running.
If an uploaded extension can't be loaded, the upload shows Failed to load extension: ... and its JAR is not kept.

Marginalia checks an extension against the version it is running in before it starts it. An extension that does not fit - typically one built for another version of Marginalia - is not loaded. An upload shows the report of the check and is not kept; an extension in the extensions folder stays in the list, not started, with Invalid in the Verification column, and the report is in the log. The check is repeated after Marginalia is updated, so an extension that worked before can be refused afterwards: get the version of the extension that was built for the new version of Marginalia and load it. While an extension is invalid, a red bar at the top of the workspace tells everybody: an administrator sees which extensions on hover, other users are asked to tell the administrator (an extension you stopped yourself is not counted). Next to each extension's JAR you'll find a small .valid or .invalid file with the report; it is removed with the extension and can be left alone.
The red bar over the workspace when an extension is invalid
The verification report of an extension that does not fit, and a stopped extension (Start button)

An extension in the extensions folder that fails to start (for example one built for another version) doesn't stop the others from loading. It is listed with the state Installed or Resolved instead of Active and can be removed with Unload. A file that isn't an extension at all is skipped and not listed - delete it from the extensions folder. The log (docker compose logs, or desktop/logs/marginalia.log for the desktop app) has the details of the error.

The help assistant is a chat that answers questions about Marginalia from its manual. An administrator chooses which model it uses and gives the permission Help assistant to the users who can ask it, in their permissions (administrators always can); they need no model of their own. Users that existed when the permissions were introduced got it if the assistant was on at the time; new users have none.

Once a user can use it, they see a round robot button in the bottom right corner of the window. It opens the chat; the panel says which model answers and warns when the user's limit applies (see Who pays). The model looks the answers up in the manual (it can search it and read its pages), names the pages it used as links to the published manual (they open in a new tab), and explains: it changes nothing and does not see the user's books unless the user allows it (see Your books). It can also look at what went wrong when something fails (see When something goes wrong) and take the user somewhere, if you allow it (see Showing the way). The conversation is kept until the user logs out (closing the panel or reloading the page keeps it), the broom button clears it.
The help assistant answering a question

The button appears when a user opens Marginalia, and the model and the limit warning are read each time the panel is opened; if you take the permission away or remove the model, users who already have the page open lose the button when they reload it (or when they open the panel).
Allow navigating the interface

An administrator who has no such permission is answered with both off.

Lets the assistant open a section, select a tab or open the dialog to add something when a user asks it to show them where something is, see Showing the way.

Lets the assistant read the state of the extensions and their logs, the database backups and the other data of the Admin page for an administrator who asks it, see Administration data. Off by default.
Model
One of your own models, shared with the users or not. Models that other administrators share are not in the list.

The Help assistant tab
The instructions the model gets with every question; see Prompts.

The settings are saved with Save. The assistant asks the model without a protocol, so the settings of the model itself apply. It stops working by itself when the model is deleted, or when its owner is no longer an administrator, so a model that belongs to an ordinary user is never handed to everybody.
Two settings depend on the user and are in their Help assistant permission (open it with the key button in Admin → Users; both are off by default):

l: What the assistant sees of the screen
p: The model can look at what the user is doing right now (it is told to when a question is about "here" or "this"): which section, tab or dialog is open, as a short description for each part of the screen - for example the title of the open book and its open tab, or the title of an open dialog. The tabs that are not open are only listed, and it reads them only when the question needs it. For a form that is open it also gets what is wrong with it right now: the fields that the form marks as invalid with the message it shows, the required fields that are empty, and what the form checks across fields (for a model: the response must be smaller than the context). Only the names of the fields, never what is typed in them. It never gets the text of a story, a lorebook entry, an API key or a password.
The assistant explaining why the form of a new model can not be saved yet

The panel of the assistant has the check box Let the assistant look at my books, off by default and set by each user for themselves (it is kept in their settings). A notice under it says what it means: the assistant reads folder names, titles, descriptions and the writing settings of the books and searches their text, never reads the text of a story, and what it reads is sent to the AI that answers - which is the model you chose above, so say so to the users if it is a service outside your control.
The assistant panel with the check box for the books
When it is on, the model gets three functions, all read-only and only for the books of the user who asks:
Function
list_folder
The subfolders of a folder, with the number of books beneath each, and its books with title and description. A path like Sci-fi/Expanse names the folder, none is the top level.
search_books

Finds books by the words of the title or description, or by the text of the story, optionally within a folder ("where is my book about true lovers?"). It says where a match was and in which folder; the text found is not returned.
get_book_settings

The language, point of view, tense and style of a book and where each comes from (the book, a folder, the user settings or the built-in default). The prompts are only told as a custom text or the built-in text, with where they come from.
It can not change, move or create anything. The lists are cut (a hundred entries, twenty matches) and the descriptions shortened.

When a user says that something failed ("I get an error", "it does not save", "the model does not answer"), the assistant can read what Marginalia showed them: the last errors, the failed requests to the model provider (wrong key, no such model, limit reached, timeout...), the warnings and the messages of forms that could not be saved, newest first and with how long ago each happened. It explains what the message means and what to fix, and for a form that is open it says which fields to change.
What is written down, and where:
everything a user is shown as an error or a warning in a notification, and the message of a failed validation, is kept for the session (the last 20);

unexpected failures (the ones with a stack trace dialog) and failed requests to a provider are also kept by the browser tab (the last three, in its session storage), so they are still there after the page is reloaded or the session expired.

The assistant gets the text the user saw and, for a failure, the names and messages of the exceptions, without the stack trace. Each text is cut at 400 characters and what looks like a key, a token or a password is removed, but the text of a message can still contain a part of what a provider or the system said, for example the answer of a provider to a request. The model that answers is the one you chose, which may be an external provider: keep that in mind when you choose it.

With Allow navigating the interface on in the permission of the user, the assistant can do a few things in the window itself when a user asks it ("show me where the lorebooks are", "take me to the backups", "how do I add a model?"): open a section (Books, Lorebooks, Settings, ...), the Admin page (only administrators have it), select a tab of the Settings, of the Admin page or of the story editor, or press the button that opens the dialog to add a book, a model or a protocol (the dialog only opens, nothing is created until the user fills it in and confirms; it is not offered while another dialog is open). It tells the user what it did. It can do nothing else: it does not press other buttons, type, save, delete, generate, close a dialog or log out, and a user who cannot open something cannot have the assistant open it for them. It does not move on its own initiative, only when asked. Where the navigation is locked (the open section has unsaved changes, a book is being generated) it can not move.
The assistant opened the Database Backups tab on request
Allowing it also tells the model the names of the elements on the screen and what they offer; that is the same kind of information as in What the assistant sees of the screen.

It is read only: the assistant cannot start, stop or remove anything there. Keep in mind that all of it is sent to the model that answers, which may be an external provider, and that the log of an extension can contain text the extension wrote (a log line is cut at 400 characters and keys, tokens and passwords are removed, but nothing more is done to it). That is why the setting is off until you turn it on.

What it reads

With Allow reading administration data on, the assistant can read the data of the Admin page for an administrator who asks it ("why does Side Query not work?", "when was the last backup?"), and for nobody else; an ordinary user never gets it, whatever the setting says, and it is checked again every time it is read.

There are two prompts: one for administrators (who may ask about the Admin page) and one for everybody else (who are told that administration is for administrators). Both are filled in with the defaults; change the text and save, Reset to default puts the default back. A prompt that is empty or equal to the default is stored as "the default", so it improves with a new version of Marginalia, one you changed is yours to keep up to date.

`` in a prompt is replaced by the list of the manual's pages (path, title and what the page is about), which is how the model knows what it can read. Leave it out and the model only finds pages by searching. Keep the instructions to look things up in the manual and to say so when it does not cover a question, otherwise the answers get less reliable. The rules for the tools that read errors, move through the interface and read the administration data are added to the prompt by Marginalia (you do not have to keep them in it), and only for the tools that are allowed.
The users never see the model or its API key; their questions go through the application.
Model
Apply limits (permission of the user)
What happens
Shared
on

A question is a request like any other to the shared model: the limit you set for the user is checked and the tokens are added to the user's usage. A user whose limit is reached (or who may not use the model) gets no answer.
off
The model's owner pays. The user's limit is ignored and nothing is counted for the user.
Not shared
(no effect)
The model's owner pays: no limit, nothing counted for the user. The model is only used by the assistant.
Your own questions count in the same way, for you the model is just another model.

Installation
Log
Desktop app
~/.marginalia/desktop/logs/marginalia.log (%USERPROFILE%\.marginalia\desktop\logs on Windows); the previous run is in marginalia.log.1

Error dialogs in the application (Internal Server Error) show the error as well; the log has the full details.
When you report a problem, include the version text in the bottom left corner of the page (for example Marginalia 1.5.0 (93ec118): the version and the Git commit of the build).
macOS says the app "is damaged" or "can't be opened". The app isn't signed yet. Right-click it and choose Open, or run xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/Marginalia.app. See Desktop app.
Windows SmartScreen blocks the app. Click More info → Run anyway.
The browser opens a different port than 8765. Port 8765 was taken, so the desktop app picked a free one. Use Open Marginalia in the tray menu, or start it with --port to fix the port.
"Marginalia did not start in time". The desktop app couldn't start its server. The log says why - often another program holding the files, or a broken extension (see below).
Docker: port 8080 is already in use. Change the left side of the port mapping in docker-compose.yml, e.g. 8081:8080, and open port 8081.
Marginalia is slow or stops with "OutOfMemoryError". Raise the memory: -Xmx2g (or more) in JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS in docker-compose.yml.
"Save login" doesn't keep me logged in. Saved logins need HTTPS on a server. Put Marginalia behind a reverse proxy with HTTPS, see Server (Docker).

I forgot my password. An administrator can set a new one, or clear it so you can log in with an empty password and set a new one yourself, in Admin → Users (see Resetting a forgotten password). There is no password reset by e-mail.
Nobody can log in as an administrator any more. Without an administrator, the password can only be reset in the database:
Stop Marginalia and copy marginalia.sqlite from the data folder as a backup.
Remove the password of the administrator with the sqlite3 tool:
(use the right user name).
Start Marginalia, log in with that user name and an empty password, and immediately set a new password with Change Password.

"Server connection lost" or the page keeps reloading. Behind a reverse proxy, the proxy must forward WebSockets and allow long requests - see the nginx example in Server (Docker). With the desktop app, the app was probably quit; start it again.

The workspace freezes the browser when it opens. Marginalia opens again what you had open when you left, so a very long book (for example one imported from an archive) can freeze the page before you can change anything. Open /reset on your Marginalia address (for example https://marginalia.example.com/reset) and log in: the saved state of the workspace (open books, selected tabs, filters) is forgotten and you land in an empty workspace. Then set Parts loaded at once in the story in your account before you open the book again.
c: sqlite3 marginalia.sqlite "UPDATE users SET passwordHash = NULL WHERE login = 'admin';"

p: "Failed to download model list". Check that the URL ends with /v1, the API key is right and the model server is running. Some services don't list their models - type the model ID instead. See Inference providers.

Docker: a model server on the same machine can't be reached. Inside the container, localhost is the container. Use http://host.docker.internal:port/v1 and make the model server listen on all addresses, see Models on the same machine.
"Book is missing model." / "Book is missing protocol." Select them on the book's About tab. Set Default Model and Default Protocol in Settings so new books get them.

"Contextual limit not sufficient." The prompt without any story is already bigger than the room the context leaves after the response. Raise Max Context Size of the provider (or Max Context Tokens of the protocol), lower Max Response Tokens, or shorten the templates, lorebook entries and summaries. See Limits.

The model reports that the context is too long. Marginalia's token count is a little off for some models. Lower Max Context Size by a few hundred tokens. A warning before the request names the estimated sizes when the prompt already looks too big.

"The provider did not answer in time", "The provider is limiting requests", "The provider rejected the API key"... Marginalia explains failures of the model API in plain words, see Error messages. Test Connection in the provider dialog checks URL, key and model without a book. Timeout and retries are set per provider.

The text stops in the middle of a sentence. The response limit was reached. Raise Max Response Tokens (or the protocol's Max Reply Tokens) - reasoning models need much more, because the reasoning counts too.
Requests fail when reasoning is enabled. The API doesn't support reasoning_effort. Turn off Enable Reasoning on the provider.

"Invalidated summaries for messages with IDs ... Continue generation without those summaries?" A part covered by a summary was edited or deleted. Answer Yes to continue without the outdated summaries, then generate new ones. See When summaries become outdated.

The prompt contains the word "Error". A template uses a variable or macro that doesn't exist, often a typo like instruction instead of instructions. The template field lists such names under it. See Typos.
An entry isn't used. Go through the conditions in Activation:
Is the entry enabled? Is its lorebook enabled - and every sub lorebook on the way to it?
Does it have tags? Then the book needs one of them (book tags are on the About tab). Negative tags exclude it.
Does the lorebook itself have Tags? They apply to all its entries.
Does it have a filter? Filters only see the instructions of the part being written, not the earlier story - mention the character in Present Characters or the instructions.
Is the filter a regular expression? An invalid one never matches.
Show Prompt on a generated part shows which lore was sent.
I can't switch to another tab. The Settings tab has unsaved changes. Click Save or Discard Changes.

My summary prompt isn't used. A book's own summary prompt (Prompts tab) wins over the Default Summary Prompt in Settings; clear the book's field to use the default. Meta summaries have their own prompt, the Default Meta Summary Prompt.
Macros in Style, Point of View or Tense don't work. These fields are plain text; only templates process macros. Put the macro into the master template or user prompt.
I restored a database backup, but nothing changed. A restore is applied on the next start. Restart Marginalia. See Restoring.
Book backups are missing after moving to another computer. Book backups are files, not part of the database. Copy the data folder too, see The data folder.
An installed extension doesn't show up. Close and reopen the book, or reload the page.
An extension fails to load and isn't listed in Admin → Extensions. Stop Marginalia, delete its JAR from the extensions folder, start again. See When an extension fails.

An extension was refused or stopped working after Marginalia was updated. Extensions are built for one version of Marginalia and are checked when they are loaded. Open the report (Admin → Extensions → Verification) and load the version of the extension that matches your Marginalia. See When an extension fails.
After updating an extension, the old version still runs. Unload the old version first, then load the new one - or restart Marginalia.

Is my writing sent anywhere? Only to the inference providers you configure: the prompt for each part (and token counting requests) goes to that provider's API. With a model running on your own computer, nothing leaves it. Marginalia has no telemetry.

Which model should I use? Any model that writes good fiction and has a large enough context; a context of 32 000 tokens or more is comfortable for long books. Try a few with the same book - switching the provider is one click on the About tab.
Can several people work on one book? No. Every book belongs to one user. Other users can read it when it's published.
Can I use Marginalia offline? Yes, with a model running locally (llama.cpp, LM Studio, Ollama...). Marginalia itself needs no internet connection.

How do I get my book out of Marginalia? Export the story as text, HTML, Word, PDF or EPUB from the settings menu (⚙) of the Story tab. To keep everything including all branches, export a book backup (JSON). You can also read it in the viewer.

Does it work on a phone? The viewer is made for phones, and Marginalia can be added to the home screen like an app (Install app / Add to Home Screen in the browser menu). The editor has a phone layout when the browser window is narrower than 768 pixels. It has no Admin page, a reduced lorebook editor and not all extensions, so it works best for writing and reading; set-up and administration are easier on a larger screen.

Is there a light theme or another language? Yes to both: the button with the sun / moon next to the language selector switches the theme (dark by default), and the language selector offers Japanese and the languages that extensions bring (see Account).

This part of the manual is for people who want to change Marginalia itself, write an extension for it, or just understand how it works inside. If you only want to install and use Marginalia, see the User guide.

Marginalia is a single Java web application. The browser UI is written in Java with Vaadin Flow, the services are plain Spring beans wired in XML, the data lives in one SQLite file accessed through Hibernate, and extensions are OSGi bundles that hook into the UI at runtime. The same WAR runs on a server (Docker, Jetty) and inside the desktop app.

p: Vaadin runs either in development mode (frontend served from a development bundle that Vaadin builds into src/main/bundles/, ignored by Git; Vaadin's dev tools available, more checks) or in production mode (optimized frontend bundle, no dev tools). The mode is decided by META-INF/VAADIN/config/flow-build-info.json, the build info that vaadin-maven-plugin writes:
prepare-frontend (every build, also mvn compile and mvn jetty:run) writes a development build info with the absolute paths of your checkout into target/classes;
build-frontend (in prepare-package, so only mvn package / install) builds the optimized bundle, writes a production build info into the WAR and removes the development one from target/classes.

By default Vaadin scans the bytecode of the app and puts only the components it finds referenced into the production bundle. Extensions are loaded at runtime and may use any Vaadin component, so the plugin is configured with optimizeBundlefalse/optimizeBundle (-Dvaadin.devmode.optimizeBundle=false on the command line): the bundle contains every component on the classpath, at the price of a bigger bundle and a slower frontend build.

So mvn package always produces a production WAR - the one the Dockerfile, the desktop profile and CI use, and the one to deploy. Nothing has to be copied around. A build info in src/main/resources is never packaged into the WAR (maven-war-plugin excludes META-INF/VAADIN/config/flow-build-info.json*).

Development mode is for running from the IDE (see IntelliJ IDEA) or mvn jetty:run. Without a build info Vaadin also starts in development mode and finds the project by the vaadin.project.basedir system property, the classpath or the working directory.
To check a WAR:

c: unzip -p target/marginalia-1.5.0.war WEB-INF/classes/META-INF/VAADIN/config/flow-build-info.json   # "productionMode" : true

p: Marginalia relies on compile-time AspectJ weaving with the spring-aspects library: Vaadin components are created with new, not by Spring, so classes annotated @Configurable (all routes, the workspace, dialogs, parts...) get their @Autowired fields injected by the woven AnnotationBeanConfigurerAspect.
Transactions are not woven: @CommonTx, @CommonTxReadOnly and @NoTx are applied by Spring's class-based proxies around the service beans (see Services).

If the classes are compiled by plain javac, nothing fails at build time, but at runtime every @Autowired field of a UI class is null and the first screen fails with a NullPointerException. Maven always uses ajc; in your IDE, make sure the AspectJ compiler is used too (see IntelliJ IDEA).

The compiler also keeps parameter names (-parameters) and all local variables (preserveAllLocals): extensions read method arguments and local variables of @Extendable methods by name, so don't remove these options.
Marginalia is a plain WAR without an embedded server, so you run it in a servlet container: from the IDE, with mvn jetty:run, in a local Jetty, or in Docker.

Marginalia keeps everything in ~/.marginalia (System.getProperty(user.home) + .marginalia), the same folder the desktop app uses. To keep test data away from your real books, start the container with another home folder:

p: The schema is created and upgraded by Flyway from src/main/resources/migration/Vn__name.sql; Hibernate only validates it (hibernate.hbm2ddl.auto=validate), so an entity change without a migration makes the application fail on start.

com.github.enerccio.tools.GenerateFlywayDiff (in src/main/java/com/github/enerccio/tools/) helps write the migration: it compares the entities listed in persistence.xml with an existing database and prints the SQL Hibernate would run to update it. Run it from the repository root (it reads marginalia/src/main/webapp/config/persistence.xml) with the same -Duser.home as your development instance - it uses the database in user.home/.marginalia. Review the output before using it: Hibernate's SQLite updates are a starting point, not a finished migration. Database & migrations explains the rules for migrations.

Marginalia is one Java web application running in one JVM. There is no separate frontend project, no REST API and no external database: the browser shows Vaadin components that live on the server, the components call Spring services, and the services store everything in a single SQLite file. Story generation runs on background threads that talk to an OpenAI-compatible HTTP API and push the text to the browser as it arrives. Extensions are OSGi bundles loaded into the same JVM; they change the UI by hooking into methods of instrumented classes.

Server-side UI. Vaadin Flow keeps the component tree on the server; the browser renders it and sends events back. UI code is ordinary Java that calls services directly - there is no API layer to keep in sync.

Spring without Spring Boot. The application context is built from XML files; services and repositories are explicit beans. Vaadin components are created with new and get their dependencies through AspectJ-woven @Configurable.
One file of data. SQLite in WAL mode, schema managed by Flyway, mapped by Hibernate. Backing up an installation means copying one folder.
Multi-user, single process. Every entity belongs to a user; services filter by the user of the current HTTP session. All users share one JVM and one database.
Pipeline generation. A story part is generated by a fixed sequence of steps with events between them, so extensions can inspect or change the prompt, the lore and the result.
Runtime extensions. OSGi bundles can be loaded and unloaded without a restart. The UI classes they extend are instrumented at startup so that any of their methods can be decorated.

Configuration resolves the data folder (user.home/.marginalia) and creates its subfolders. When the data source asks for the database URL (configuration.resolveDb(...)), a staged database restore (marginalia.sqlite.restore) is swapped in first - a restore can't replace a database that is open. Then a copy of an existing database that is behind the bundled migrations is saved in db-backups (pre-migration-*, see Startup).
Flyway migrates the schema (classpath:migration), then Hibernate builds the EntityManagerFactory with hbm2ddl.auto=validate. A mismatch between entities and schema stops the startup here.
RuntimeInstrumentationInitializer installs the ByteBuddy agent and registers a transformer for all classes annotated @Extendable (see Extensions). Classes already loaded are retransformed.

When the root context is refreshed, OsgiServiceImpl starts Apache Felix with ~/.marginalia/extensions as its storage, installs and starts every JAR in that folder and calls onExtensionLoad on each registered MarginaliaExtension. A JAR that fails is logged and skipped. When the root context closes, the extensions are unloaded and the framework is stopped.

p: Main shows the login (or the create administrator dialog on an empty installation), restores a saved login from cookies, and after login replaces its content with the DesktopWorkspace (the implementation of the Workspace interface), then restores the autosaved state of the workspace (the tab, the open book...) with restoreAutosaved(); see Remembering where the user was. It also adds the HelpAssistantWidget (the round robot button with the chat panel, hidden while the help assistant is off). The classes of the UI describe themselves to the assistant's model through LLMInteract, see Letting the help assistant see the UI.
DesktopWorkspace holds the left-hand tabs. Each tab is a WorkspaceComponent (create, refresh, onTabSwitched, onTabClosed) and is Restorable (it stores and restores its own state).

Opening a book opens ManuscriptDialog, whose tabs are ManuscriptDialogParts. The story editor (ManuscriptStoryPart) is the largest UI class: the parts sidebar, the text, the instruction panel, generation.
Viewer is a separate route for reading published books without the workspace.

Most of these classes are @Extendable, which is what makes them extension points. See User interface for details.
All data entities extend ExtendableEntity. User extends BaseEntity directly and Resource and Usage are OwnedEntitys.
Every entity has a numeric id (database key) and a uuid (stable identity used in URLs, backups and exports).
Deleting is soft by default (deleted = true); the admin Cleanup page purges deleted rows that nothing references any more, following the @CleanupReference annotations.

OwnedEntity.owner ties data to a user. ExtendableEntity.attributes is a JSON object, stored serialized in extendedContent by ExtendableEntityListener, where extensions keep their own data (and where @ExtendedAttribute fields of the entity are stored) - so that data travels with backups and exports without schema changes. The same listener fills _fulltext with the text of the @Fulltextable fields, for searching.
The story is a tree of ChatMessages (parts): regenerate, swipe and branch create siblings; the book remembers the active leaf.

The database is SQLite in WAL mode (busy_timeout=10000), through commons-dbcp pools (read-write transactions begin with the write lock, see Database & migrations) and a TransactionAwareDataSourceProxy. Vaadin UI state may only be changed while holding the session lock. Code on other threads - generation, backups, summaries - updates the UI with ui.access(...), and the change reaches the browser through server push (@Push on AppShellConfig, WebSocket with long-polling fallback). Two helpers make this safe:
UIPushGuard.push(ui) pushes explicitly but never re-entrantly from the same thread.
ThreadAccessDialog (and ProgressBarDialog) run a task on a worker thread and route its UI updates through ui.access.

Background threads have no HTTP request, so session-scoped beans (the current user) would not resolve. generateNextTurn therefore captures the request attributes in a ThreadCopyRequestAttributes and the engine wraps its work in ThreadCopyRequestAttributes.InRequestScope, which makes the session of the user who started the generation current on the worker thread.

An agent run is not started by a request at all: AgentRunner works it in a background worker of its own (a thread pool, one round of the model at a time) and sets up the request context from the run, not from a browser: AgentRequestAttributes make the user bean resolve to the owner of the agent and the session point an AgenticSessionPoint (the working copy is the open book, the language is the one of the run). What a run keeps of its session is the AgentSession record (the uuid of the owner and the language), made up again at every start and resume. Anything that shows on the screen of the owner goes through ui.access like any other background work, see the request context of a run.
bound/SessionManager (bean sessionManager, defined in container-config.xml) knows every HTTP session of the application and which user is logged into it.

Tracking. SessionTrackingListener is an HttpSessionListener registered in WebappApplicationInitializer; it looks the bean up in the root context and calls onSessionCreate / onSessionDestroy. Each session gets a SessionInformation. After a successful login Main and Viewer call userLoggedIn(user, VaadinSession), which fills it in once: the Vaadin session, the user, the current UI as the main UI and a ThreadCopyRequestAttributes copy of the request. Note that login calls VaadinService.reinitializeSession - the old session is destroyed and a new one created, so the bound session is the new one.

Running code in other sessions. runForUsers(test, runnable, uiBound) runs a RunInSession for every session whose user matches the predicate, with that session's request attributes in scope (so the session-scoped user resolves to that user). With uiBound the runnable is queued with VaadinSession.access on a live UI of the session (the main UI, or any other open one if it was closed) - it runs asynchronously, once the session lock is free, and changes are pushed when the lock is released. The sessions are processed on a separate thread (ThreadUtils.executeInThread), so the caller's Vaadin and request thread locals don't leak into them; the call waits for the dispatch, not for the queued access tasks. The skipCurrent overload leaves out the caller's own Vaadin session. UserServiceImpl.changePassword / clearPassword use it to invalidate the other sessions of the user whose password changed - a user changing their own password stays logged in in the current session. reloadUser(user) reloads the page of every UI of the sessions of a user the same way (runForUsers with the main UI's Page.reload()): the permissions dialog uses it after it changed the permissions of another user.

The help chat. SessionPoint (the session-scoped bean with the language and the workspace of the page) also keeps the conversation with the help assistant (getHelpChat(), a synchronized list of messages) and the problems the user was shown (getProblems(), see What went wrong); Main attaches that log to the Vaadin session after login so that code on threads without a request can write to it. Logout invalidates the session, which ends both.

Open UIs. After login Main and Viewer register their UI in ApplicationPoint (bean applicationPoint) with the workspace (Main only) and a copy of the user. SessionInformation.getUI(workspaceClass, applicationPoint) / getWorkspace(...) find the session's UI showing a given workspace type.

Dead UI detection. SessionManager is also a daemon thread (Inactive session watcher), started by afterPropertiesSet and stopped on context shutdown. Every DEAD_SESSION_CHECK_TIMEOUT / 10 seconds (see Constants) it tryLocks each logged-in session - a locked session is in use and skipped - and closes UIs whose last heartbeat is older than the timeout. Threads queued on the session lock count as activity. The timeout is never shorter than three Vaadin heartbeat intervals (5 minutes by default), otherwise an open but idle tab would be closed between two heartbeats. When every UI of the session is closing, the HTTP session is invalidated.

Close notifications. addSessionCloseListener registers a SessionCloseListener on the current session. When another session is destroyed, every listener of every remaining session is called inside its own session's access and request scope with the SessionInformation of the closed session.
getActiveUsers(), getOpenedSessions(user), getSessionInformation(id) and getActiveSessionIds() expose the registry, e.g. for admin views.

Loading. Extensions are OSGi bundles run by an embedded Apache Felix framework (OsgiServiceImpl). Boot delegation is open for all packages (org.osgi.framework.bootdelegation=*, parent = the framework's class loader, which is the web application's), so bundles see the application's classes and libraries directly without importing them. A bundle registers a MarginaliaExtension service; Marginalia calls onExtensionLoad / onExtensionUnload and passes the ExtensionService. Before an extension is started, ExtensionService.verifyExtension checks the classes, methods, arguments, locals and fields its decorators use against the running application (the result is kept in name.valid / name.invalid next to the JAR); an extension that doesn't fit is not started.

Instrumentation. At startup a ByteBuddy agent rewrites every non-static, non-constructor method of each class annotated @Extendable: ExtendableMethodVisitor adds a call to ExtensionService.onExtendableMethodEnter at the start, records each local variable as it is stored, and calls onExtendableMethodLeave on every return and throw (at the return of a value the original value is registered first and the one the decorators leave is returned). This happens on every call, with or without decorators, so @Extendable belongs on UI classes, not on hot code.

Decorators. ExtensionService.registerDecorator(decorator, className, methodName) attaches code before and after a method. Through the ExtendableMethodContext it can read the method's arguments, read local variables by name (for example the menu the method just built, to add an item to it) and access fields and methods reflectively. On enter it can replace arguments, on leave it can replace the return value (chained through the decorators); it can't skip the method.

Data. Extensions keep their data in the attributes of existing entities, so no schema changes are needed and the data is part of backups. They can also listen to generation events and take part in cleanup (CleanupService.registerContributor).

UI lifetime. An extension registers the components it adds with OsgiService.bindAttachableComponent together with a callback that removes them; the callbacks of components still attached run when the extension is unloaded, each inside ui.access(...) of the component's UI.

Languages. An extension that implements ExtensionHasLocalization adds languages to the UI: OsgiServiceImpl registers its LocalizationBundles in Localization after the extension loads and removes them on unload (Localization).

Other extensions. Extensions don't import each other. ToolService lets them offer suites of tools (functions and commands) that a dialog with a Tools button gives the model, and IPCService lets them register providers of text about a book or a story part under their bundle's symbolic name (removed when the extension is unloaded) and ask for it; to use one particular extension (the name generator) the others find it among OsgiService.getLoadedExtensions() and call it by reflection (Sharing data between extensions).

Styles. An extension that implements ExtensionHasCss gets its CSS put into every open page: CssRegistry (owned by Main and Viewer) reads the loaded extensions when its page is attached and listens to the loaded/unloaded events of OsgiService afterwards (Styles of a plugin).
Because hooks are attached by class and method name and read local variables by name, extensions are tied to one version of the application. See Plugin development.

All UI texts are looked up through the Localization bean by an L key (loc.getValue(L.LABEL_SAVE)). The bean (LocalizationImpl) holds one LocalizationBundle per Language: the texts of every key, the Locale and the date formats of that language, and the name shown in the language selector. The application ships LocalizationBundleEN (the default language, which has to be complete - the application doesn't start otherwise) and LocalizationBundleJP; they are listed in the localization bean in container-config.xml. Texts of template variables and macros (the hints shown next to prompt fields) are localized the same way.

Which language. getValue and the formats use the language in the session's SessionPoint. Without a request (startup, scheduled backups) or with a language that has no bundle (any more) the default language is used, and a text a bundle doesn't have is taken from the default language, so a bundle that lags behind the keys keeps working. Worker threads get the session through ThreadCopyRequestAttributes like the user bean.

Choosing. The language of a user is UserSetting.language (a language code, null for the default). Main.proceedWithLogin sets SessionPoint.language from it before the workspace is created, so the login page itself is always in the default language. The LanguageSelector at the bottom of the workspace (desktop sidebar, phone drawer) offers Localization.getAvailableLanguages(); a change saves the setting, sets the session and reloads every UI of every session of the user (SessionManager.runForUsers), where the workspace opens again with the new language. Viewer doesn't choose anything, it uses what is in its SessionPoint.

Extensions. An extension that implements ExtensionHasLocalization returns bundles of its own; OsgiServiceImpl registers them after onExtensionLoad and removes them when the extension is unloaded (see Example plugin). A language that already has a bundle is refused, so an extension can't replace English.

Adding a language to the application. Copy LocalizationBundleEN, translate, add the class as a bean to the bundles list of localization. BundleCompletenessTest checks that a bundle has every key and the same %s/%d placeholders as the English text.

Every entity except User has an owner, so each user has a separate set of books, lorebooks, providers, protocols and settings. The relationships between them never cross users: a book can only use the owner's provider, protocol and lorebook.

A book has thousands of messages, so the messages and summaries are soft deleted with one bulk UPDATE per kind (softDeleteByManuscript, softDeleteByIds; deleted = true, modification = now): the rows are not loaded, no entity listener or event runs and extendedContent stays as it is. The rest goes through the services' delete. Objects that only reference the deleted one (a book using a deleted provider or lorebook, a lorebook that includes the deleted one as a subbook) are not deleted. A hard delete does not cascade. Code that adds an entity owned by another one has to add it to the cascade, or the owned rows stay live while their owner is in the trash.

A soft delete takes the dependent rows with it. The services whose entities own other rows override delete and, when it is not a hard delete, soft delete those rows first (the OWNED_BY / OWNS rows of the cleanup references), so the trash and the cleanup see the whole group deleted:

Most of an entity's data is not in table columns but in one JSON document stored in the extendedContent blob. Two kinds of fields end up there:
fields annotated @ExtendedAttribute (they are also @Transient, so Hibernate ignores them), and
attributes, a free-form JsonObject for extensions. Its keys are stored with the prefix attributes_ next to the other fields.
ExtendableEntityListener converts between the fields and the document:

Load (@PostLoad): the JSON is parsed and the fields are set. Supported field types are String, numbers, Boolean, Date (ISO-8601 instant in UTC, e.g. 2026-10-09T08:15:30.123Z; values in the old yyyy.MM.dd'Z'HH:mm:ss.SSS format, written in the server's time zone, are still read), enums (by name) and any type for inject = true: a JsonObject has its keys stored flat as injectPrefix_key, any other type is converted with Gson (object-shaped results are flattened the same way, lists and scalars are stored under the plain injectPrefix key).

Types: the values are written with toString(), so a field can't be a collection. A list is kept as a JSON string in a String field with typed accessors, like ChatMessage.imageAttachments (getImages() / setImages(...), a JSON array of ImageAttachment(resource uuid, caption)).
Save: JpaExtendableRepository.save serializes the fields into extendedContent before the entity is written.

Compression. The document is mostly text, and an entity keeps it next to the fields made from it, so ExtendableEntity stores it gzipped when it is 256 bytes or more: setExtendedContent compresses and getExtendedContent gives the plain JSON, so only the field of the column is compressed and the code that works with the bytes doesn't change. A row stored plain (before app version 6) still reads - a gzip stream starts with 1f 8b, which no JSON or text does - and is compressed when it is saved again; ExtendedContentMigration does it for all of them once. What reads the column without the entity (SELECT e.extendedContent, the trash viewer) must call ExtendableEntity.plain(bytes).

Because the fields are @Transient, Hibernate's dirty checking doesn't see them. A change to an extended attribute is only stored by calling the service's save. Changing it on a managed entity and letting the transaction commit does nothing.

saveWithoutEvent writes extendedContent as it is, without serializing the fields first. It is used when extendedContent was set directly - copying the JSON of a backup into a restored entity - and must not be overwritten by the (empty) fields. The repository then reads the fields back from the JSON and rebuilds _fulltext from them.

Every ExtendableEntity table has a _fulltext text column (clob, @Lob String) next to extendedContent: the text of the entity that a search should find, in one place, even when the text is spread over columns and JSON. Fields annotated @Fulltextable (a column such as LorebookEntry.name or an @ExtendedAttribute) are collected by ExtendableEntityListener:

serialize (called by every save) writes _fulltext right after extendedContent: the string value of each marked field (toString(), dates as ISO-8601), empty ones skipped, joined by a newline in declaration order. An entity without marked fields, or with all of them empty, has NULL.
updateFulltext rebuilds only _fulltext, from the fields as they are. saveWithoutEvent uses it after reading the fields from the restored JSON, and FulltextMigration uses it to fill existing rows.

The searches over _fulltext are ChatMessageService.searchFulltext(manuscript, query), used by the search of the story tree. FulltextQuery.parse splits the query into words (double quotes make a phrase); a part matches when its text contains every word. In SQL (ChatMessageRepository.findFulltexts) each word is a _fulltext LIKE :pattern ESCAPE '\', built like the name filter of the book list (LikePatterns.fromWildcards): * becomes %, and \, _ and % are escaped so they are searched as typed. Only the id and _fulltext of the messages are read, never the whole entity. SQLite's LIKE ignores case only for A-Z, so every word is also tried in lower case, upper case and capitalized (FulltextQuery.likePatterns), which covers accented letters in the usual spellings; a word written in mixed case in the text (ŽlutÝ) is not found by a differently cased query. The snippet shown with a hit is cut from the text by FulltextQuery.snippet. The service checks that the book belongs to the current user. The advanced search of the book list uses the same LIKEs over all the candidate books at once (ChatMessageRepository.findFulltextHits, ids only) and, unless it searches all branches, keeps the books whose hit lies on the branch of the active part (findActiveBranchIds, a walk up the parent links).

Like extendedContent, the column is invisible to dirty checking of the fields, so it is only current after a service save. Marking a field of an entity that already has rows (or changing which fields are marked) leaves old rows out of date: add an app migration that calls updateFulltext for the entity, as FulltextMigration does (see Database & migrations).

The summaries of a branch are walked from the newest part to the root (SummaryService.collectBlocks; the generation, the invalidation check and the overview all use it):
A part with a summary starts a block: the part and the parts after it (older), up to the next block.

After a meta summary the summaries are skipped (they belong to its block) until the one whose uuid is its nextSummaryUuid, which starts the next block. The meta summary block's hash includes the text of the skipped summaries.

The hash of a block is SHA-512 over, part by part: the text of the part, and the text of the summary of the part if it has one - except for the head of the block, whose own summary is what the hash checks (it didn't exist yet when the hash was made). A normal block has no other summaries in it, so its hash is that of the texts only.

Deleting a meta summary (SummaryService.removeSummary(part, unwind)) with unwind restores the summary from replacedSummary: it is deserialized into a new Summary. Because that summary can be a meta summary with its own replacedSummary, unwinding nests. A meta summary takes over the uuid of the summary it replaces (attachMetaSummary), and the restored summary gets it back, so the nextSummaryUuid of other meta summaries stays valid. Restoring a backup creates all summaries with new uuids, so ManuscriptServiceImpl.restoreMessages rewrites the nextSummaryUuid of the restored meta summaries (also inside replacedSummary) to the new ones.

utils.QuoteFinder finds a quote in a text: letter for letter (several places: the context around it and the hint decide), then ignoring case and white space, then the passage with the most words of the quote in order (70 %). The same finder serves the AI annotate, the commands and the selection of the browser.

utils.TextAlignment aligns an old and a new text token by token (TextTokens: white space, words, single characters; longest common subsequence after the common start and end are cut off, 4 million cells at most, an insertion or deletion block is slid to the latest place it can sit, so "hours. Then" to "hours. Very much. Then" keeps the full stop with the old sentence) and refines the gaps by letters (a typo in a word is the same word). mapStart / mapEnd move a range like the markers of a word processor: an edit before moves it, inside grows or shrinks it, text typed exactly at the start or the end is outside; isPartlyRetained is false when no letter of the range survived (it is gone), isApproximate when the texts were too different to align (then a range that is not inside a retained stretch is handled by the quote).

l: Limits of the users of a shared AI
p: AI.limits is an @ExtendedAttribute string holding a JSON object: the AILimit of each user under the user's uuid (strategy LimitStrategy UNLIMITED / TOKEN_LIMIT / NOT_AVAILABLE, resetStrategy ResetStrategy DAILY / WEEKLY / MONTHLY, and prefillTokens, generatedTokens, totalTokens, each null for unlimited). AILimits reads and writes it; a user without an entry is not limited. These are only the settings and they are set by the owner (an administrator). What a user used is not in this JSON on purpose: it changes with every request, from the thread of any user, and AIService.save is for the owner and would lose parallel updates, so it is in the two period* columns of the user's Usage, added up in SQL like the other counters.

The reset is lazy. ResetStrategy.periodStart(now) is the start of the calendar day / week (from Monday) / month in the server's time zone. UsageService.add (under record) of a user with a TOKEN_LIMIT first runs UsageRepository.resetPeriod (zeroes the period counters when lastUsed is before the period start) and then adds; for a user without one it zeroes them. AILimitService.getStatus does not write: it reports 0 used when lastUsed is before the period start. LimitStatus.block(promptTokens) is the first reached of the sent, generated and total limits, or NOT_AVAILABLE. The prompt is known before the request, so a request is refused when the sent (or total) counter is at its limit or the estimated prompt (approximatePromptTokens, our count) would take it over; the generated counter is only compared with its limit, so the last response can go over - unless AILimit.hardGeneratedLimit is set: then the generated counter plus the response the request reserves (TokenLimits.responseTokens(ai, protocol), the max_completion_tokens it sends; 0 when there is none) has to fit into the generated limit. The hard flag does not apply to the total limit. AILimit.validate() rejects negative numbers and, when all three are set, sent plus generated below the total (the total could never be reached).

Policy

Soft-deleted rows are purged by CleanupService (Admin → Cleanup, administrators only: every method calls AdminGuard.requireAdmin()). Before purging, it builds a graph of all references between rows and decides what may go. Each reference has a policy (@CleanupReference, in domain/traits/):
STRONG (default)
The reference doesn't block the purge; it is cleared when the referenced row goes.
The referenced row belongs to the referencing one and is purged with it, unless referenced elsewhere.
The referenced row can't be purged while the reference exists.
The referencing row belongs to the referenced one and is purged with it.
Used for
WEAK

The same reference model drives the trash (TrashService, implemented by CleanupServiceImpl; Trash tab and Admin → Cleanup). It lists the soft-deleted rows of every root entity that is an OwnedEntity (Protocol stands for its subclasses) with narrow projections - the extendedContent blob is only read by getExtendedContent, which pretty-prints it - and restores them with a bulk UPDATE ... SET deleted = false, modification = now, so no entity listener runs and extended attributes stay untouched. Before it restores, it looks up the parents of the selected rows:
Reference
Parent
STRONG, OWNED_BY held by the row
the referenced row (Manuscript.ai, ChatMessage.parentScript, LorebookEntry.lorebook, owner...)
OWNS held by another row
that row (the ChatMessage whose summary it is)
WEAK
none, purge clears it anyway

When a parent is deleted and not part of the same selection, nothing is restored and the result lists the blockers. A deleted owner counts as a parent, so the objects of a deleted user can't be restored.

The restore is the reverse of the soft delete cascade: the selection is first extended with the deleted rows it owns (OWNED_BY rows pointing at a selected row, rows a selected row OWNS, repeatedly), so restoring a book brings back its parts, summaries and tags, and RestoreResult.getRestored() counts them too. It can't tell a row that was deleted together with its owner from one deleted on its own earlier, so the latter comes back as well. A restored ChatMessage deleted by deleteNodeAndMigrateChildren does not get its children back: they were moved to its parent when it was deleted.

TrashService.deletePermanently removes deleted rows for good, for the Delete Permanently button of TrashGrid. It is limited to getPermanentlyDeletableTypes() (ChatMessage, LorebookEntry; anything else raises IllegalArgumentException) so a user can't purge a whole book, and checks ownership like restore. It runs the purge of the cleanup (executePurge) on the selection: the rows that go with it are only Summary and TagRelation rows, a summary something else uses stays, and a block by a CleanupContributor (or any other row that would have to go) makes the whole call return DeleteResult.getBlocked() and roll back. Before that, moveChildrenOfMessages moves the children of the selected messages - deleted ones too, which the editor's deleteNodeAndMigrateChildren never sees - and the activeLeaf of books to the nearest ancestor that is not selected, with bulk updates, so removing a chain of parts keeps the parts below it connected.

So a deleted provider that a book still uses shows up as blocked on the Cleanup page until the book is switched to another provider, while a deleted book takes its parts, their summaries and its tag relations with it.

Because the soft delete deletes the owned rows too, they are purge roots of their own. A root whose owner (OWNED_BY, directly or through other rows) is blocked is held back: it stays, is not listed as blocked itself and is not counted as purgeable, so a blocked lorebook that is still restorable keeps its entries.

Book backups (BackupService) serialize a book as JSON: its columns, its extendedContent as is, its tags, all parts (with extendedContent and summaries) and references to its provider, protocol and lorebook by uuid and name. The backup also names the folders the book was in (the optional key folder, written by takeBackup, read by BackupFolders; see Folders). Restoring or cloning creates new rows (new ids and uuids for the parts) and copies extendedContent unchanged, so extended attributes and extension data come back exactly as they were. Linked entities are resolved among the current user's own entities, first by uuid, then by name.

Lorebooks list their fields one by one (name, payload, comment, filtering...) in LorebookService.marshalLorebooks, which the lorebook export (exportLorebook), the lorebooks inside a book backup and the copy of the lorebooks for an agent share. Since 1.4.0 it adds the attributes of lorebooks and entries under attributes (when there are any), and the import (unmarshalContent, importLorebooks) sets them on the new lorebooks and entries, so extension data such as the Lorebook VCS history travels too. A field that is a real column, or an @ExtendedAttribute field that is not listed there, does not (add it to the marshalling). Imported entries have new uuids (the format has none), so data that refers to an entry by its uuid does not find it.

Keep this in mind when adding data: for books and parts anything in extendedContent is backed up automatically, while a new column has to be added to the backup and restore code (BackupServiceImpl, ManuscriptServiceImpl.restoreBackup / restoreMessages); a new column or @ExtendedAttribute field of a lorebook or entry has to be added to marshalLorebooks and unmarshalContent, data in the attributes goes along by itself.

l: Adding a field or an entity
p: A field on an existing entity:
Decide where it lives. Prefer an extended attribute (@ExtendedAttribute @Transient) - no migration, backed up automatically. Use a column only when you need to query, sort or join on it.
For a column: add a Flyway migration (see Database & migrations); Hibernate validates the schema on start. Extend the backup / restore code if the value should survive a backup.

For a reference to another entity: think about its cleanup policy and annotate it if STRONG isn't right. Soft references (ids) must be annotated with target or targetClassField, otherwise cleanup may purge the referenced row.
Save it through the service's save (not saveWithoutEvent).
If its text should be found by a search, annotate it @Fulltextable (see Full-text column) and add an app migration that refills _fulltext of the existing rows.
A new entity:
Extend ExtendableEntity (or OwnedEntity if it never needs extended data) and annotate the references.
List the class in src/main/webapp/config/persistence.xml - unlisted classes are ignored.
Write a Flyway migration creating the table, its table_SEQ table and indexes.
Add a repository (JpaExtendableRepository subclass) and a service (ExtendableServiceImpl subclass), and define both beans in services-config.xml.
Add a CRUD test based on ExtendableCrudContract (see Testing).
Decide whether it belongs in book backups or lorebook exports.

Folders put books into a tree and let the books in a tree inherit settings. This page follows the feature through the layers: the entity, how a setting is resolved, the services, the lists and windows, and the places that had to learn about folders (backups, agents, the help assistant, cleanup). The user's view is in Folders.

Manuscript.folder is a nullable ManyToOne column folder_id (null is the top level), annotated @CleanupReference(WEAK): a purge of the folder unlinks the books that are still alive instead of deleting them. The migration is V21__folders.sql (table, sequence, manuscripts.folder_id and the indexes (parent_id, is_deleted), (userId, is_deleted) and (folder_id, is_deleted)). persistence.xml lists the entity, services-config.xml the repository and the service.

The settings are extended attributes and not columns because nothing queries them in SQL; the price is the usual one, they are persisted only by FolderService.save/update. The name is a column because the lists sort and filter on it.

Two more extended attributes of UserSetting serve the feature: favoriteBooks (the uuids of the favorite books) and helpAssistantBooks (the opt-in of the help assistant). UserSetting.defaultStoryLayout is not about folders but arrived with the same work (see the story layout).
A book's setting is the first non-blank of: the book, the folders above it (nearest first), the UserSetting, the built-in default (Defaults). The code is in three places:

PromptField (domain/service) is an enum of the twelve text settings (MASTER_TEMPLATE, POV, TENSE, STYLE and the eight prompts). It holds the getters of each level (ofBook, ofFolder, ofUser), the setters (setOfBook, setOfFolder, which store a blank as null) and the built-in fallback(). A new inheritable setting is a new constant here plus the field on Manuscript and Folder, and nothing else in the resolver.

EffectiveSettingT(value, origin, folder) is what the resolver returns: the value, where it is set (Origin is BOOK, FOLDER, USER or DEFAULT) and the folder when it is FOLDER. isCustom() is true for the book and the folders.

ManuscriptService.resolve(book, field) and resolveLanguage(book) do the lookup; resolveInherited(folder, field) and resolveInheritedLanguage(folder) start from a folder (what an empty field would inherit, for the placeholders of the dialogs). The old getters (getPov, getStyle, getTemplate...) keep their signatures and return resolve(...).value(); they were twelve copies of the same lookup before. getLanguage(book) is the resolved language, Manuscript.getLanguage() is still the book's own or English, and Manuscript.getOwnLanguage() is null when the book sets none.

FolderService.findChain(folder) reads the folder and its ancestors by id (folder first, stopping at a deleted one), with no current user, so a generation can resolve from a worker thread. The lookups are done when needed and nothing is copied into the book, so moving a book or editing a folder changes the next generation. A resolve of all twelve settings and the language costs about 1 ms with no folder and 3 ms through ten folders (measured on the test database), a generation does a handful of them before an LLM call, so there is no cache; add one per generation only if the chain gets much longer or the lookups end up in a loop over many books.

Everything that used the book's fields directly now goes through the resolver: the generation steps, the summaries, redraft, annotate and impersonate, the story export (language), the reader, the assistant commands (get-book-info and the book settings commands report the effective values) and the help assistant.

Lists. search takes the same ManuscriptFilterValues as the book search (inFolder, the name, the tags), sorters on name, creation, modification. resolveScope turns "the folder, or everything below it" into the ids the repositories filter by (FolderScope adds the clause to the books' query and to the folders').

Copy and move of books and folders, see below.

Errors: IllegalArgumentException for what can never be right (a blank name, a folder that is not the user's), IllegalStateException for what is wrong now (the name is taken, a folder into itself), ManuscriptLockedException / FolderBookLockedException for the agent lock. ManuscriptService.moveToFolder(books, folder) moves books, save checks that the folder of a book is its owner's, and findRegularInFolder, getFavorites and setFavorite serve the lists.

transfer takes a Transfer(books, folders, target, copy, onlyCurrentBranch, choices) and checks everything first: the target and every item belong to the user, a folder does not go into itself or below itself, every clash has a Choice (RENAME, SKIP or MERGE, keyed by the id of the folder; findClashes tells which need one), and no book (also in a moved or copied folder) is locked by an agent. Then:
a move is one transaction;

a copy has none. It can take long and the database has one writer, so each folder made and each book cloned (BackupService.cloneManuscript(..., folder)) is a step of its own, and the step callback is called after each (the progress bar of OrganiseDialog). A failure leaves the copies already made, each complete. This is the pattern of the other long tasks: transactions per step, never around the lot.
The result is an Outcome(books, folders, skipped).

Folder.modification follows the books below it. JpaManuscriptRepository.changed(book) (the hook of JpaBaseRepository.write, which the repositories override to tell the owner of an entity; JpaChatMessageRepository.touchBook does it for the parts) calls FolderModification.touch, which walks the parent chain and sets the time with one UPDATE ... WHERE id IN. It skips agentic working copies. saveWithoutModification, opening a book and moving a book change nothing; the active-leaf change (swipeAndSwitch, branchAndSwitch) saves the book as it did, so it counts.

The dialogs keep entities for as long as they are open, and a generation held its book from start to finish, so saving such a copy wrote old values over a setting changed in the meantime (or undid a move to a folder). The writers that change one thing now call ManuscriptService.update(book, BookChange), which loads the stored book and applies the change to it. Use it instead of save for a change that is yours alone.

p: Backups. BackupServiceImpl.takeBackup writes the optional key folder (the folder's uuid and the path from the top, each with name, uuid, description, language and text settings) from findChain; BackupFolders.resolve finds the folder by uuid, else by the name path (creating the missing levels with the saved settings), else returns null (the top level, also on any failure). createBackup, which the agents' snapshots and cloneManuscript share, is unchanged and writes no folder. exportBackup(backup, withImages, includeInherited, progress) rewrites the stored file on its way out through BackupInheritance: it drops folder and, with the option, writes the values the book inherits (from the backup's own folder path, then the user settings, never the built-in defaults) as the book's own. The old three-argument overload exports with the option on.

Agents. The working copy (agentic = true) used to have no folder and so ignored the folders' settings. It is put in the folder of the original: createAgenticCopy, replaceWorkingCopy (restore of a checkpoint) and AgentMergeServiceImpl.sync call ManuscriptService.setAgenticCopyFolder. A merge is a diff of JSON without a folder, so it never moves the book. The lock is AgentRunService.checkNotLocked, applied by the folder service to every book below a folder that would change (FolderServiceImpl.checkNoLockedBook); a paused or stopped run does not lock.

Marginalia keeps all its data in one SQLite file. The schema is created and upgraded by Flyway migrations, and Hibernate maps the entities onto it but never changes it. This page explains the setup, the conventions of the schema and how to write a migration. What the tables contain is described in Domain model.
commons-dbcp BasicDataSource, 10-20 connections, validated with SELECT 1; a second one (writeDataSource, 2-20) for read-write transactions
Driver
File
flyway migrates the database when the context starts; emf depends on it, so Hibernate only sees a migrated schema.
Foreign keys
Hibernate and jdbcTemplate use the data source through TransactionAwareDataSourceProxy, so plain JDBC code joins the current JPA transaction.

jdbc:sqlite:file?busy_timeout=10000journal_mode=WAL (built by Configuration.resolveDb); the pool of read-write transactions adds transaction_mode=IMMEDIATE (Configuration.resolveWriteDb)

Not enforced (PRAGMA foreign_keys is off), see Conventions

Pool

Read-write transactions take the write lock when they begin. A deferred transaction reads, takes its snapshot and needs the lock at its first write; when another connection has committed in between, the write fails at once with SQLITE_BUSY or SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT and busy_timeout does not help. So routingDataSource (ReadWriteRoutingDataSource) gives a read-write transaction a connection of writeDataSource (transaction_mode=IMMEDIATE, writers queue for the busy timeout) and a read-only one (@CommonTxReadOnly) a plain connection of dataSource (never waits for a writer). The transaction manager asks for the connection before it publishes the read-only flag, so the jpaDialect bean (ReadWriteRoutingDataSource.Dialect) notes it while the transaction begins. Flyway and code outside a transaction use dataSource. ConcurrentTransactionsTest covers both sides.

There is also a second, Java-level version check: ApplicationInitializer compares AppSettings.dbVersion / appVersion with the versions set in container-config.xml and runs registered Migration beans for data changes that are easier in Java than in SQL. The columns of BaseEntity / OwnedEntity / ExtendableEntity are always the same: id, creation, is_deleted, modification, uuid, userId (owner), extendedContent and _fulltext. Then list the class in persistence.xml. For joined inheritance (a subtype of AI or Protocol), the subtype table has only id plus its own columns.

SQLite can rename a column (ALTER TABLE ... RENAME COLUMN) and, since 3.35, drop a simple one (ALTER TABLE ... DROP COLUMN), but it can't change a column's type, nullability, default or constraints. For those, rebuild the table - V3 and V5 show the pattern:
Recreate every index of the old table. Removing an entity field without removing the column is harmless - validation only checks that mapped columns exist.

db/FlywayMigrationTest checks, without the rest of the application:
an empty database migrates through all versions and the schema validates against persistence.xml,

Names. Tables are plural (manuscripts, messages, entries), set by @Table(name = ...). Columns use the Java field name (maxTokens, lastOpened); relations end in _id (lorebook_id, parentScript_id), except the owner, which is userId, and the soft delete flag, is_deleted. Indexes exist only in the migrations, see Indexes.

No foreign key constraints. The tables have no REFERENCES clauses (V2's summary_id declares one, but SQLite doesn't enforce it because PRAGMA foreign_keys is off). Integrity is kept by the application: rows are soft deleted, so references stay valid, and the admin Cleanup follows the cleanup references to decide what may be purged. Code that hard deletes must clear or move references itself (see ChatMessageService.deleteNodeAndMigrateChildren).

Enums. AI.aiType and Protocol.protocolType are stored as ordinals (tinyint), all other enums by name. SaneSQLiteDialect turns off the CHECK constraints that Hibernate would otherwise generate for enum columns, so a new enum value doesn't need a table rebuild.

Large values. Text that can be long (name, uri, apiKey...) is @Lob → clob; extendedContent is a blob with JSON (gzipped when big, see ExtendableEntity). SQLite doesn't enforce lengths, so varchar(255) is only documentation.
Encrypted columns. Secrets are stored encrypted, see Encrypted columns.

Hibernate's temporary tables. V1__initial.sql contains HT_* and HTE_* tables. Hibernate uses them for bulk updates and deletes on entities with joined inheritance (AI, Protocol) and for inserts into such hierarchies. They are part of the schema - don't drop them.

A single-column index on is_deleted alone helps only the Cleanup (few rows are deleted); don't add new ones. Check a query with EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN in SQLite - SCAN table means a full table scan, SEARCH ... USING INDEX means the index is used.
