Never hard-code user-visible text. Add a key to loc/L.java and the text to LocalizationBundleEN (and LocalizationBundleJP), and use loc.getValue(L.KEY) (Localization is injected into every UI class). Date formats come from the same bean (loc.getDateFormat()...). The name of a kind of entity (book, lorebook...) is loc.localizeDomainObject(entityClass); it falls back to the closest known superclass, then to the simple class name, so a new entity type needs a mapping in LocalizationImpl.loadMaps(). The texts are in the language of the user's session, so never keep a text in a field that outlives the page or the request - look it up when you show it (Localization).

Wrap event handlers in try/catch and report unexpected exceptions with UIUtils.internalServerError(loc, e) - it logs the exception and opens an ErrorDialog with the stack trace. Expected problems (validation, missing configuration) are shown with Notification.error(...) or a message next to the field; UIUtils.showValidationErrors(loc, e) formats a binder's ValidationException. Failures of a request to the model API (InferenceException: wrong key, wrong URL, timeout...) go through UIUtils.inferenceError(loc, e), which shows the localized cause (InferenceErrors) as a notification and falls back to internalServerError for anything else. AIDialog has, for the type Extension (offered while an extension provides AIs), a Provider selector and the settings form of the chosen ExtensionAIFactory (see Inference providers from a plugin); the type of an existing AI is read-only. It has the Test Connection button (InferenceService.testConnection() with the values of the form) and, for administrators only, the Shared with all users checkbox. The API key stays editable when its tab is not the one shown (the tab sheet disables the hidden tabs, so the dialog keeps its own apiKeyEditable flag), and Refresh of the model list keeps the model that was selected. AIPart / PhoneAIPart (the type column shows the name of the extension's provider, AITypes.label) list the user's AIs and the shared ones with the user's own Usage (tokens sent / generated); the edit and delete buttons are only shown for AIs the user owns (AIService.isOwnedByCurrentUser) and the add button only when AIService.canCreate(). The service refuses the same things itself. Rows of shared AIs have an info button (AILimitInfoDialog), and the owning administrator a Limits button (AILimitsDialog, AILimitService). AIPart also has a Usage per user button, visible to administrators only, that opens UsageDialog (UsageService.findAllUsages(): user, model, tokens sent / generated, requests, last used); the service checks the administrator itself.

Most forms save automatically: value change listeners call an autosave() method of the part (guarded so that loading values into the fields doesn't trigger a save). The story editor saves an edited part when the edit is closed (autosaveAndSwapToMarkdown) and before a generation starts (autosaveAndSwapAllToMarkdown). Entities held by the UI are detached copies - reload them through the service before changing them, and keep the object returned by save.
Vaadin component state may only be touched on a thread holding the session lock. The rules:
Long work (generation, summaries, backups, imports) runs on another thread; the UI thread returns immediately.
Updates from that thread go through ui.access(() - ...), with the UI captured on the UI thread (UI.getCurrent() is null elsewhere). UIPushGuard.push(ui) sends them right away.
Service calls on that thread need the user's request scope - capture ThreadCopyRequestAttributes.create() on the UI thread and wrap the work in InRequestScope (see The current user).

ThreadAccessDialog packages all of this for dialogs: run() starts runInThread() on a new thread in the request scope, and vaadinLocked(...) / vaadinLockedSync(...) run UI updates with ui.access / ui.accessSynchronously and push. ProgressBarDialog builds on it.

The story editor is the main example: startGeneration freezes the book window, calls StoryGenerationService.generateNextTurn with a GenerationListener, and every callback (onNodeCreated, onResponseChunk, onComplete...) updates the cards inside ui.access(...) and pushes.

Prefer Java components. When the browser has to do something (scroll positions, element sizes), the script is a static method of ui.JavascriptLibrary - UI classes don't call executeJs themselves. The element is passed explicitly ($0, not this), and a script that returns a value returns the PendingJavaScriptResult, read with .then(...); see UIUtils.getPositionAndSizeOfElement, JavascriptLibrary.watchEdge (fires edge-top / edge-bottom when a scroll element gets close to that edge, with the distance of the opposite edge in detail.far; it remembers the part the user sees first, and restoreAnchor puts it back after the server added or dropped parts, which keeps the position while the lazy loading of the story and the viewer works; the story and the reader panels set overflow-anchor: none so the browser does not correct it a second time), JavascriptLibrary.rememberReaderPosition / readReaderPosition (the viewer keeps the id of the first visible part per book uuid in the localStorage of the browser, key marginalia.reader.position.uuid; the server only reads it once when the book opens, it is never stored in the database) and JavascriptLibrary.scrollTextAreaToBottom (the extension log is shown scrolled to its newest line). Extensions keep their own scripts.

There are three JavaScript modules, all documented in Custom components. src/main/frontend/chart-connector.js is loaded by ChartJs (@JsModule, with the npm package chart.js); it registers Chart.js and draws the configuration it gets from JavascriptLibrary.renderChart, taking the text and grid colors from the Lumo variables of the page.

src/main/frontend/treant-connector.js is loaded by TreantTree (@JsModule) together with the npm packages treant-js and raphael (@NpmPackage) and treant's CSS (@CssImport). It draws the story tree; TreantTree sends the tree as JSON and receives clicks back: node-click (a card was clicked, with the data-node-id of the card) and node-goto (an element with data-goto-id inside a card was clicked; the card itself is not clicked then). src/main/frontend/graph-connector.js is loaded by GraphView (npm package cytoscape).
Only the desktop layout has them (ManuscriptStoryPart; its phone twin has none). The code lives in ui.shortcuts:

KeyCombo is the canonical text of a key combination (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+Meta+key, the key as the browser's event.key: lower-case characters, Space, Enter, F5; Shift is dropped for a character that is not a letter or digit). The browser script produces it (window.marginaliaKeyCombo in JavascriptLibrary) and KeyCombo.normalize must give the same text; keep the two in step. It also knows the keys the browser keeps (isBrowserReserved).

ShortcutRegistry (static) lists the ShortcutActions (id, label from the Localization, default key, handler); the application registers its story actions (ShortcutActions) in its static initializer, an extension registers its own and unregisters them in onExtensionUnload. The application's actions have no handler: ManuscriptStoryPart.handleShortcut does them, for other ids it calls the handler with the component of the story tab. Besides the writing loop they are the command bar (/), the search of the branch, annotate selection and the next / previous tab (TabDock.selectRelative).

KeyBindings resolves the key of every action from UserSetting.keyBindings (an injected JsonObject, id to key, only what differs from the default, empty text = no key) and builds what is stored (toStored keeps the bindings of actions that are not registered now, e.g. of an extension that is not loaded).
KeyBindingsEditor (a CustomField, so the settings part tracks it like any field) is the table of the tab Keyboard shortcuts of UserPart.

In the browser JavascriptLibrary.fireShortcutEvents puts a keydown listener (capture) on the document for the story tab and fires marginalia-shortcut (detail = action id) on the tab's element, which the story part listens to. The keys are the page-wide window.marginaliaKeys (setShortcutKeys replaces them, UserPart.save and the story's onTabEnter do), so a change of the settings reaches open stories. The script ignores the key when the element is not visible (not the open tab), when a dialog is open above the one that holds the story (the book window is a modal dialog itself), and for a key without Ctrl/Alt/Meta when an input, textarea or editable element has the focus (the focused element is found through shadow roots). Before it fires the event the script sends the change of a focused text field to the server (a Vaadin field syncs its value on change, i.e. on blur), so the action sees what was just typed. On a Mac a combination with Meta that no action has is tried again with Ctrl in its place. recordKeyCombo records the next combination for the table.

The three menus that act on the story are not written item by item in the story tabs, they are built from the StoryMenuRegistry (ui.menu, a Spring bean that fills itself in afterPropertiesSet): the settings menu (MenuKind.TOOLS, the cogs of the story), the menu of a part (CARD, the hamburger button of a card) and the right click menu of its text (TEXT).

StoryMenuItem defines an item: its key (StoryMenuKeys has the ones of the application, a plugin prefixes its own), the label, an optional icon, the callback (ConsumerStoryEditor for the tools menu, BiConsumerStoryEditor, StoryCard for the other two), an optional default key (null = none), the phone flag (default true, false for the items only the desktop shows), visibleWhen / enabledWhen / checkedWhen predicates and contextLabel (text that depends on the part: Edit / Save) that are asked each time the menu opens, and a parent key that makes the item an item of the sub menu of another one (the parent has no callback, so a sub menu can have items that come and go). StoryEditor and StoryCard are the interfaces both the desktop (ManuscriptStoryPart) and the phone (PhoneManuscriptStoryPart) tab and their cards implement, so one definition serves both.

Every item with a callback is also a ShortcutAction of the key bindings (id menu.key, or actionId(..) for the ones the user already has a key stored for, such as story.swipe; Annotate selection is only an item of the text menu, story.annotateSelection: opening the menu of a part takes the selection away), registered with its default key, also none. So a new item is listed in Settings → Keyboard shortcuts the moment it is registered.

StoryMenuRegistry.definition(kind, phone, bindings) returns a MenuDefinition: the items of the kind in the order they were registered, and the keys (the ones the user changed, else the defaults; null bindings = the phone, which shows no keys). MenuDefinition.build(menu, loc, editor, card) adds the items to a ContextMenu or the sub menu of a menu bar item and wires them; the BuiltMenu it returns finds an item by key (get(key)) and refresh(definition) works out text, visibility, enabled and ticked state and the key hint of every item again. The story tab refreshes a menu when it opens (the part menus are LazyContextMenus, filled the first time) and the tools menu after an item ran and when the story tab is entered (the user may have changed the keys).

A key of a CARD or TEXT item acts on the part that is edited, else the part that holds the text selection (JavascriptLibrary.selectionOwner), else the last part, and on the last part when the item does not apply to the chosen one (ManuscriptStoryPart.runMenuItem).

The hooks stay for extensions that decorate them (how to register an item and the details: UI extensions): createCogsMenuItem (local cogs) and the card's createMenuItems (field hamburgerMenu) run after the registry has filled the menu, and what they add directly is no registry item (no shortcut row, no key hint). Registering the item is the way to go for new code. An extension unregisters its items in onExtensionUnload; a bundle that is unloaded loses the rest by its symbolic name (OsgiServiceImpl).
The marks, the notes and the list share a few classes in ui.dialogs.story; the desktop and the phone card use them the same way.

utils.TextMarkup puts all layers into the text in one go: the generated text of the diff view (GeneratedTextHighlighter.ranges), the matches of the search (StoryBranchSearch.marks) and the annotations (StoryAnnotations.marks) are ranges of the raw source text, and TextMarkup.apply cuts the text where a range starts or ends and wraps each piece in the mark elements of the ranges that cover it (the first range outermost), line by line and outside of the white space and the markdown that opens a line. The layers can not be chained (the HTML of one would shift the offsets of the next). renderResponse() of the card collects the ranges and sets the content of the Markdown. The sanitizer of the component (DOMPurify) keeps class and data-*, which the marks use: data-annotation is the uuid of the annotation.

StoryAnnotations keeps the annotations of the book (one query, dropped by invalidate() when the story is drawn again or a text changed), gives the marks and the counts, and makes the changes (create, update, setStatus, reattach, remove: they go through AnnotationService, invalidate, redraw the card of the part through the StoryLazyLoader and tell the listeners, the list). A mark is drawn only when the card is not generating (a regeneration streams into the card, the passages are not in the text yet).

CardAnnotations is what a card does with its part's annotations: the badge (the number of open and orphaned ones), the popover (Popover whose target is a small absolutely placed anchor in the card; JavascriptLibrary.fireAnnotationClickEvent moves it onto the mark that was clicked, in the browser, before it tells the server which annotations cover the point, innermost first), Annotate part, Annotate selection and Attach to selection. The selection is the offsets of the editor when the part is edited (getTextAreaSelection, the edit is saved first), otherwise the text the browser shows with some text around it (getSelectionContext), found in the source with QuoteFinder (StoryAnnotations.locate).

AnnotationView is one annotation with its actions, AnnotationDialog asks for a new note, AnnotationsPanel is the tab of the book (ManuscriptStoryPart.ANNOTATIONS_TAB, in the default layout of the dock; the phone has it in the drawer), AnnotateDialog runs AnnotateService and lists the proposals. Opened on a part (open) it annotates that part; opened without one (openRange, from the Annotate a range of parts with AI item of the tools menu, StoryEditor.openAnnotateRangeDialog, which shows the story again afterwards) it needs a range of the parts of the branch (both From part and To part, annotateNext): the parts are annotated one after another, the next one is started from the callback of the one before (inside ui.access, in the request scope copied when the run started), the proposals are Entry records that remember their part, and accepting calls AnnotateService.accept once per part. The service itself still annotates one part per call. Automatic annotation. The Automatic annotation item of the tools menu (StoryMenuKeys.AUTO_ANNOTATE, StoryEditor.openAutoAnnotateDialog / isAutoAnnotate, the item is ticked while it is on) opens AutoAnnotateDialog, which stores the settings in the extended attributes autoAnnotate* of Manuscript (the AI and the protocol as uuids). StoryGenerationListener.onComplete calls the new Callbacks.partCompleted(message) (a default method) after the story was drawn again, and both story tabs answer it with new AutoAnnotate(manuscript, reload).run(message): when the book has it on and the part has a text, AnnotateDialog.openAuto opens the annotation window on the reloaded part with an AnnotateDialog.Auto (instructions, AI, protocol, accept) and starts the run at once. At the end of a run that was not stopped (endRun(true)) and with accept, the dialog calls accept() itself (a closed dialog, isOpened() false, does nothing: a late answer of a model the author stopped by closing the window must not add notes) or, when the model found nothing and there is no note about a part that could not be read, says so and closes. accept() calls onAdded, which only then moves on: it shows the story again and, with autoAnnotateRedraft (and accept), calls RedraftDialog.openAuto(book, part, autoAnnotateAcceptRedraft, ...), which starts the redraft at once with the open annotations; with apply the dialog applies the text itself when the model finished (completed, not when it was stopped, and not when the dialog was closed). A closed window never calls its callback, so closing ends the run; nothing is redrafted when no note was added. The automatic redraft dialog never offers the summaries' revalidation box.

Notes in the margin (desktop): the cogs menu item Annotations in the margin (an item of the StoryMenuRegistry; ManuscriptStoryPart.setAnnotationsInMargin) stores the preference in UserSetting.annotationsInMargin and tells every card (ChatMessageCard.applyAnnotationMargin). The card puts CardAnnotations.getMargin() (a column of AnnotationViews of the notes that need a look, in the order of the passages; data-annotation-id is the uuid) before the text; with the mode on the card content has the class annotations-in-margin, a two column grid (the margin left, the text and the editor right, the rest spans both), and a click on a mark finds the note in the column (flashMarginNote) instead of opening the popover. JavascriptLibrary.linkMarginNotes lights the note and its marks together (annotation-lit). The notes are drawn again with the card (CardAnnotations.refresh). The phone has no margin. Not done: aligning each note with the line of its passage.
The styles are annotation-* in shared-styles.css (wavy underline in the colour of the source, nested marks lower).

ManuscriptTreePart has a search bar above the tree: an editable ComboBox (the last 15 searches; typed text is a custom value that the part sets as the value) and a button. A search calls ChatMessageService.searchFulltext and keeps the result as lastQuery and hitSnippets (part id → text around the match); renderTree then adds the CSS class search-hit (shared-styles.css) to the cards of the found parts and, in them, the snippet and a "Show in story" link (data-goto-id). Stretches of more than 20 parts that would be collapsed stay open when they contain a hit. The search is kept while the tab is open and repeated on every onTabEnter; load (opening the book) clears it.

The link fires NodeGotoEvent. onNodeGoto resolves the id among the messages of the book only, asks ChatMessageService.findLeafFor for the end of the branch to show, makes it the book's active leaf when it is not (ManuscriptDialog.save) and calls ManuscriptDialog.showMessage(id). That tells ManuscriptStoryPart which part to scroll to (scrollToMessageOnNextRender) and selects the story tab; entering the tab renders the story, which scrolls to the part (and flashes it) instead of scrolling to the bottom; the window of parts is moved around it (StoryLazyLoader).

Global styles are in src/main/frontend/styles/shared-styles.css (imported by AppShellConfig): spacing helpers, the loading indicator, the story text (.chat-message), the story tree (.Treant) and the utility classes (.text-secondary, .hint-text, .min-width-0...). The book style of the reader and editor (.manuscript-styles .chat-message-markdown) is in reading-mode-styles.css, imported separately by AppShellConfig. Components are styled by adding these classes (addClassName(CssStyles.TEXT_SECONDARY)), not with getStyle().set(...); keep that only for values computed at runtime (the combo box overlay width). A new class goes into the stylesheet and into CssStyles together. All vaadin-markdown elements wrap long lines (and break long words of paragraphs, code, headings, lists, quotes, tables and links) through the rules there, so a Markdown needs no extra call. Class names used from Java are constants in CssStyles; column widths and offsets in UIConstants. Use Lumo's CSS custom properties (--lumo-space-m, --lumo-contrast-10pct...) instead of fixed colors, so the dark theme stays consistent.

Styles of plugins are not in the stylesheet. Main and Viewer (the ApplicationEntryPoints) own a CssRegistry that injects the CSS returned by loaded extensions (ExtensionHasCss.getCss) as style elements and removes it when the extension is unloaded (Styles of a plugin).

l: Letting the help assistant see the UI
p: The help assistant's model has a function, get_ui_state(path, deep), that returns what the user currently sees. The UI describes itself through LLMInteract (ui), which every UI class that matters implements: Workspace, WorkspaceComponent (so all parts of both layouts), ManuscriptDialogPart and PhoneManuscriptDialogPart, every class that extends Dialog, Main, the admin panels, and LorebookView, PhoneLorebookView, LorebookPreview, TagsView, TrashGrid. An element has a name (getLLMName, the simple class name), a state (getLLMState, Markdown: free text suits the very different things to say, and it is what a model reads best) and children (getLLMChildren(deep)). takeLLMSnapshot() builds the tree, LLMSnapshot (a record path, state, children, interactions, problems, element) holds it: the path of a node is the names from the root (UI/Main/DesktopWorkspace/ManuscriptPart), siblings with one name are numbered (Panel[1], Panel[2]), a node that throws is listed with a note, depth is capped. read(path, maxChars) renders a subtree as Markdown (a heading with the path per node) and cuts it with the outline of the rest; an unknown path throws with the outline of the paths there are.

Only the active branch. takeLLMSnapshot() expands what is shown: invisible components, dialogs that are not open and the content of tabs that are not selected are left out. Where the UI has alternatives the element reports them with LLMInteract.options(all, active, deep) (the others become inactive stubs: the name and "Not open", no children), or LLMInteract.parts(partsWithComponents, active, deep) for parts that created a component each. With deep = true (takeLLMSnapshot(true), the function's deep parameter, for something that is not on the screen) the alternatives are expanded and hidden elements are included and marked *Hidden*.

Defaults. A component finds its children as the nearest visible descendants that are LLMInteract; a dialog describes itself by its title. Something that is not a component (a workspace part, a dialog part) has no children unless it says so: LLMInteract.within(part, component) adds the elements of the component the part created. A bare Text node has no visibility (isVisible() throws) and counts as shown; it is never an element, the search goes on below it.

What to put in a state. What the user sees and would say himself: the title of the open book, the open tab, a filter. Never a secret, an id, the text of a story or a lorebook (the state goes to the AI of the help assistant, which may be a provider outside the installation), and nothing long: the model reads all of it.

Problems with a form. getLLMProblems() lists what is wrong with the form an element shows now, one line each, and the snapshot renders it under the state (Problems with the form:, also without the interactions flag). The default, LLMFormProblems.scan(component), walks the visible, enabled fields inside the component (not the ones inside another LLMInteract, which reports its own, and not what is hidden or a dialog that is not open): a field marked invalid (HasValidation.isInvalid()) with the message it shows, and a required (setRequired / required indicator) field that is empty, named by its label, aria label or placeholder. Never a value. A form that checks across fields in its save method overrides it and adds those rules (AIDialog: the numbers positive, the response smaller than the context, the additional parameters a JSON object); within(part, component) scans the component of a part that is not a component itself. At most 15 lines.
Called on the UI thread under the session lock (the widget reads through ui.access); quick, read only.

In the extendable classes (Main, both workspaces, AdminPart, both manuscript dialogs) the overrides carry @PublicAPI like any method; DesktopWorkspace / PhoneWorkspace describe the sections through WorkspaceLLMSupport.

Extensions implement LLMInteract on their own components (a tab, a panel) and are found like any other: they appear under the nearest element above them, so a tab an extension adds to the story editor shows up when it is the open one.

The widget builds the root with LLMSnapshot.ofComponentTree(UI, ..., ui, deep), so the dialogs open on top of the page appear next to Main; Main reports the workspace of its UI (from ApplicationPoint) as its only child. The function is HelpTools.getUiState, bound with the manual tools by HelpAssistantService.ask(history, uiState, callback); UiStateSource is how the widget answers it.

PermissionsDialog (ui.dialogs.permissions, opened by AdminPart.openPermissionsDialog from the key button of the user list) edits the Permissions of a user: a modal dialog (ModalityMode.STRICT, no close on Esc or outside click) with a grid of the permissions (name from Localization.getPermissionType, a Granted checkbox, a delete button), a combo box of the types the user has none of with Add permission, and Exit / Save in the footer. The columns have fixed widths (name takes the rest, Granted and the delete button TOOL_COLUMN_SIZE_LARGE: an icon button does not fit the narrower TOOL_COLUMN_SIZE; the rows are kept in the order of PermissionType); the settings component of a permission is the detail row of the grid, folded by the arrow button in front of the name (expanded, a set of types that survives re-reading the rows; a row without settings has the fold-spacer class in its place, a new permission is unfolded). It edits a copy in memory: Save is on only when something differs (isDirty: a new permission, a changed granted, an edited settings component or a deleted permission), Exit asks with MSG_UNSAVED_CHANGES_EXIT when it is, and a delete is a hard delete (PermissionService.delete(permission, true)) done by Save, before the saves. After the save the rows are read again and, unless the user is the current one, SessionManager.reloadUser reloads their pages (Page.reload in each live session, the caller's own session is skipped).

A permission type with settings of its own has a PermissionUIComponent that PermissionUIFactory.createComponent(type) returns (null for a type without; the implementation is PermissionUIFactoryImpl, a switch on the type): getComponent() is shown in the detail row of the grid, model2component / component2model copy the settings between the component and the Permission (they are extended attributes of Permission, helperApplyLimits / helperInteractions; HelperPermissionComponent for HELPER), onChange tells the dialog the user edited it (not fired by model2component), and the default method onGrantedChanged(granted) (called when the component is made and when the Granted box changes) lets a setting that makes sense only while the permission is given (a sub-permission, NotificationsPermissionComponent for NOTIFICATIONS) follow it. To add a type: a constant in PermissionType, ENUM_PERMISSION_* in L and the bundles and the map of LocalizationImpl, and, if it has settings, an @ExtendedAttribute field in Permission and a component.

When the permission HELPER of the user allows it (Allow navigating the interface in their permissions, Permission.helperInteractions, off by default) the model can also move through the UI for the user, with a second function, interact_with_ui(path, interactions) (InteractiveHelpTools, bound instead of HelpTools only when the permission setting is on and the question comes from a page). An element offers interactions by overriding getInteraction(): a map from a key to an LLMInteraction (description for the model, action a Runnable). The map is what is possible now: the section that is open is not offered again, nothing while the navigation is locked, no disabled tab. applyInteraction(key) and applyInteraction(ListString keys) run them in order and return takeLLMSnapshot() of the element after them; the map is read again before each step, so a sequence can use what an earlier step made possible. A key that is not offered ends the sequence with an IllegalArgumentException that names what was done and what the element offers (what was done stays done); an action that throws is reported the same way.

Only harmless moves. An interaction is something the user could do with one click and undo with another: open a section, select a tab, open the dialog to add something. Never one that changes, saves, deletes, sends, generates, logs out or closes a dialog that may hold unsaved work. There are no generic interactions: each element decides. Today DesktopWorkspace / PhoneWorkspace (open-section:label, through WorkspaceLLMSupport.openSections), AdminPart, UserPart (so the phone settings too), ManuscriptDialog and PhoneManuscriptDialog (open-tab:label, through LLMInteract.tabs), and the lists of books, models and protocols, desktop and phone (open-dialog:button text, through LLMInteract.dialogButtons(buttons), which presses the button the way a click does; it is offered only while the button is shown and enabled and no dialog is open, since an open dialog blocks the page and a second one would stack on it). A part that is a table says so with WorkspaceLLMSupport.describeTable(models, grid, addButton) (the number of rows and what the button does, nothing of the rows). Keys use the labels the user reads, which is what the model sees in the states. A dialog is put into the page only when the response is about to be sent, so dialogButtons runs those pending executions right after the press: the result of the interaction already shows the dialog.

The snapshot carries them. LLMSnapshot also has interactions (key to description) and the live element, so LLMSnapshot.interact(path, keys) finds the element by the same path the model read ([n] numbering included) and applies the keys to it. toMarkdown(true) / read(path, max, true) list them under the state of the node (Interactions:); without the flag they are left out, which is what the model gets while the setting is off. Hidden and inactive elements offer nothing. The element is only valid on the thread of the page.

What the model gets back is the whole page after the moves (HelpAssistantWidget.interactNow: apply, then read the page with interactions), because a move can change something other than the element (a section opens a dialog elsewhere).
Plugins add interactions to their own LLMInteract components the same way; getInteraction in an extendable class carries @PublicAPI. Keep to the rule above.

UiStateSource has read(path, deep, withInteractions, done), interact(path, interactions, done) and readProblems(count, done); HelpAssistantService.ask appends HelpPrompts.INTERACTIVE to the prompt when the model has the function, so that an edited prompt cannot lose its rules.

l: What went wrong: the problem log
p: When a user says that something failed, the model calls read_last_errors(count) (HelpTools, bound for everybody) to read what the application showed them. Four pieces:

UiProblem / ProblemLog (bound). A problem is (id, time, kind, message, detail); kinds are EXCEPTION (error dialog), INFERENCE (a failed request to a provider), VALIDATION, ERROR and WARNING (notifications). The ProblemLog of the session lives in SessionPoint.getProblems(), holds the last 20 and is synchronized. The same message told twice within two seconds is one problem and the more specific kind stays (the code that failed records INFERENCE with its exception, then the notification that shows it records ERROR). UiProblem.clean makes the text safe for a model: one line, what looks like a key, a token or a password replaced by [removed], cut at 400 characters; detail is the chain of the exceptions (class and message, four deep), never a stack trace.

UiProblems (utils) is the recorder. UIUtils.showError, internalServerError, inferenceError and showValidationErrors call it, and so does every Notification.error / warning (the central place: the text the user is told is the text recorded), and StoryGenerationListener.onInferenceError (new in GenerationListener, a default that calls onSimpleError; InferenceStep calls it for a provider failure). It reaches the log through the Vaadin session, where Main (after login) and the widget attach it, not through the SessionPoint bean: notifications are shown from ui.access(...) on threads that have no HTTP request, where the scoped bean can not be resolved. Nothing is recorded before it is attached, and recording never throws.

The browser keeps the last three. For the unexpected failures (EXCEPTION, INFERENCE) it also pushes the problem as JSON to the sessionStorage of the tab (JavascriptLibrary.rememberProblem, key marginalia.problems), which survives a reload and a new session. readLastErrors merges both copies by id, newest first (UiProblems.merge), reading the browser's through JavascriptLibrary.readRememberedProblems (a round trip, so the widget answers the continuation in its callback; HelpAssistantWidget.problemsText renders it). What the storage holds is the user's, so anything that does not parse is skipped.

Form problems are not here. What is wrong with the form that is open comes with the screen (Problems with the form, above); the log has the messages the user was told when they tried to save (the generic validation failed warning, or showValidationErrors's text).

The widget also keeps the links of an answer from leaving the application (JavascriptLibrary.openLinksInNewTab: a click handler on the messages, noopener) and stays usable above a dialog (JavascriptLibrary.keepOnTopOfDialogs): a dialog and its curtain are in the top layer of the browser, over the button and the panel, so while one is open (and again whenever another opens) the widget's children become manual popovers, shown after it (CSS .help-root [popover] puts the popover defaults back and moves them to the left, away from the buttons a dialog has in its bottom right corner). The server accepts their events: strict modality does not block this widget.

Marginalia has almost no hand-written frontend code, but three components draw with a JavaScript library that Vaadin doesn't ship: a tree, a chart and a graph. This page documents them, how they get their library, and how to add another one. Plugins can use all three; a plugin can't bring a library of its own (see below).
The Character Tracker plugin (relationship map).
The connector is a small ES module that imports the library, exports a function that draws into an element and registers it as window.name.
The Java class is a Div annotated with @NpmPackage (the library, downloaded by the Vaadin frontend build) and @JsModule (the connector in src/main/frontend).

The Java method sends the data as JSON to JavascriptLibrary.name(element, json), which runs window.name(element, JSON.parse(json)) with the component's element. All scripts the application runs are static methods of JavascriptLibrary (User interface); a component never calls executeJs itself.
The script is queued by Vaadin until the element is attached, so a component may get its data before it is shown (e.g. in the constructor of a dialog).

The nodes are laid out in rings around the center (the concentric layout): the center in the middle, its neighbours on the first ring, theirs on the second and so on, with the distance counted in edges, ignoring direction; nodes the center can't reach are on the outermost ring. A double click (or double tap) on a node arranges the graph around that node, animated, in the browser - there is no round trip to the server. The user can drag nodes and pan and zoom the view. The component fills its parent (graph-view style, at least 300px high), so give the parent a size, e.g. a VerticalLayout with setSizeFull() and setFlexGrow(1, graph) in a dialog; it follows later size changes (a resizable dialog) with a ResizeObserver.

Theme colors of the lines and labels are read from the Lumo variables when the graph is drawn and passed through a canvas, because the browser may compute a color to a form that Cytoscape can't parse. A theme change after that isn't followed until the graph is drawn again.
ui/widgets/GraphView.java, frontend/graph-connector.js. npm package cytoscape. It draws what a tree can't: nodes that are connected in a cycle or to several others.

l: Adding a component for another library
p: Add the Java class (a Div) with @NpmPackage(value = package, version = ^x.y.z) and @JsModule(./name-connector.js). The Maven build downloads the package with the rest of the frontend; the first build after adding one is slow.

Write src/main/frontend/name-connector.js: import the library, export renderName(element, config) that destroys what it drew into element before, and set window.renderName = renderName. Take colors from the Lumo variables rather than hard-coding them.
Add the static method to JavascriptLibrary (element.executeJs(if (window.renderName) { window.renderName($0, JSON.parse($1)); }, element, json)).
If the element needs a size or a positioning context, add the rule to shared-styles.css and its name to CssStyles (both with the same name).
Mark the class @Extendable and give each public method @PublicAPI, run mvn test -Dtest=PublicAPISignatureTest and paste what it prints (Extendable hooks).
Note it here, in Project structure (components, frontend files) and in the changelog.

A plugin can create TreantTree, ChartJs and GraphView like any other Vaadin component: they are classes of the application, and their library comes with the application's frontend bundle. What a plugin can't do is add an npm package or a JavaScript module to that bundle - it is built with the application. Libraries for plugins therefore have to be added here, as a component. The only frontend resource a plugin can add is CSS (UI extensions, ExtensionHasCss); plugins run their own small scripts with executeJs.

A Marginalia plugin (the user interface calls them extensions) is an OSGi bundle - a JAR with a few extra manifest headers - that Marginalia loads at runtime, without a restart. A plugin can add menu items, tabs, panels and settings to the user interface, keep its own data on books, story parts, lorebooks and user settings, call the model, and take part in generation.
This part of the developer guide explains how plugins work and how to write one. It assumes you can build Marginalia from source (Building from source) and know a little Vaadin Flow (User interface).

Code that runs before and after any method of an instrumented UI class, with access to its arguments, local variables and fields, and the possibility to replace the return value.

Hooks are attached by class and method name and read local variables and fields by name. Renaming a method or a variable in the application silently disables the part of a plugin that used it (a warning is logged). Build plugins from the same source tree as the application they run in, and test them after every update. Marginalia itself verifies the decorators of an extension before it starts it and refuses ones that ask for classes, methods, arguments, locals or fields that don't exist.

This page covers what every plugin needs: the Maven project, the bundle activator, the MarginaliaExtension and how Marginalia loads, starts and unloads it.
A plugin is an ordinary Maven project with bundle packaging:
Use your own package. The bundled plugins live under com.github.enerccio.marginalia.extensions.name; a third-party plugin should not.

c:
myplugin/
├── pom.xml
└── src/main/java/com/example/marginalia/myplugin/
    ├── MyPluginActivator.java     BundleActivator - registers the extension
    ├── MyPluginExtension.java     MarginaliaExtension - registers hooks, cleans up
    ├── model/                     data classes stored as JSON in attributes (optional)
    ├── service/                   plugin logic, @Configurable (optional)
    └── ui/                        Vaadin components (optional)

p: The easiest start is to copy the pom.xml of marginalia/plugins/chaptermarker and change the coordinates and the package names. The bundled plugins inherit their version from the repository's parent POM (parent with marginalia-parent); a plugin of your own outside the repository drops that parent and gives its version itself. The important parts:

Everything from the application is provided. Marginalia runs the bundle with boot delegation for all packages (see Class loading), so the bundle sees exactly the classes and libraries of the running WAR. Bundling your own copy of Vaadin, Spring or Gson would create a second, incompatible copy of their classes.

Versions must match the application. Take the Vaadin, Gson and commons versions from marginalia/pom.xml. Compiling against a different Vaadin version than the one that runs usually works until it doesn't.
Import-Package imports nothing. The single negated entry stops bnd from generating Import-Package headers - they are not needed with boot delegation and would make the bundle fail to resolve.

AspectJ weaves Spring's AnnotationBeanConfigurerAspect into the plugin's classes, so a plugin class annotated @Configurable gets its @Autowired fields injected from the application's Spring context, like the application's own UI classes (AspectJ weaving). Without it, those fields stay null.
Libraries the application doesn't have must be embedded in the bundle (Embed-Dependency, commented out in the Reviewer's pom.xml) or shaded. Keep this to a minimum.

Build with mvn package; the result is target/artifactId-version.jar. The application must be installed in the local Maven repository first (mvn install -DskipTests in marginalia/), and reinstalled whenever you change classes the plugin uses.

c:
<packaging>bundle</packaging>

<dependencies>
    <!-- the application's classes, installed by `mvn install` in marginalia/ -->
    <dependency>
        <groupId>io.github.enerccio</groupId>
        <artifactId>marginalia</artifactId>
        <version>1.5.0</version>
        <classifier>classes</classifier>
        <scope>provided</scope>
    </dependency>
    <!-- plus, all `provided`: org.apache.felix.framework, vaadin-core, and any library
         of the application you use directly (gson, commons-lang3, font-awesome-iron-iconset...) -->
</dependencies>

<build>
    <plugins>
        <!-- maven-compiler-plugin, release 25 -->
        <!-- aspectj-maven-plugin with spring-aspects as aspect library - needed for @Configurable -->
        <plugin>
            <groupId>org.apache.felix</groupId>
            <artifactId>maven-bundle-plugin</artifactId>
            <version>6.2.0</version>
            <extensions>true</extensions>
            <configuration>
                <instructions>
                    <Bundle-SymbolicName>${project.artifactId}</Bundle-SymbolicName>
                    <Bundle-Version>${project.version}</Bundle-Version>
                    <Bundle-Activator>com.example.marginalia.myplugin.MyPluginActivator</Bundle-Activator>
                    <Import-Package>!com.example.marginalia.myplugin.*</Import-Package>
                    <Export-Package>com.example.marginalia.myplugin.*</Export-Package>
                </instructions>
            </configuration>
        </plugin>
    </plugins>
</build>

p: The bundle's activator registers one MarginaliaExtension as an OSGi service. That's all it should do - Marginalia discovers the service and calls it:
Only bundles that register a MarginaliaExtension are listed in Admin → Extensions.

onExtensionLoad registers everything the plugin needs: decorators (extensionService.registerDecorator(...), see @Extendable hooks), generation listeners (storyGenerationService.addEventListener(...), see Generation events), cleanup contributors (Extended attributes). It should not build UI - there is no UI at that moment. UI is added later, from decorators, when the user opens the screen the plugin extends.

onExtensionUnload undoes all of it: unregister every decorator and listener, remove the components the plugin added to open screens (Unloading), stop background work. Nothing is removed automatically - a decorator left registered keeps running, from a bundle that no longer exists. The one exception: the data providers registered with IPCService and the tool providers (with their commands) registered with ToolService under the symbolic name of the bundle are removed by the application when the extension is unloaded (Sharing data between extensions).
Annotate the extension @Configurable and inject what you need:

Any bean of the application can be injected - every service in domain/service (Services), Localization, InferenceServices, Configuration, OsgiService... Plugin classes created with new (services, dialogs, forms) can be @Configurable too; the bundled plugins create their service object in the extension (new ReviewerService()) and it is injected the same way.

At startup onExtensionLoad runs without a UI, so UIUtils.internalServerError(...) (which opens a dialog) can't show anything. Throw instead: an exception that escapes onExtensionLoad is logged, onExtensionUnload is called to undo what was registered so far and the bundle is stopped. The other extensions load normally; an upload shows the error to the administrator.

Startup. OsgiServiceImpl listens for the root context's ContextRefreshedEvent, starts Felix with its storage in ~/.marginalia/extensions/org.eclipse.osgi (wiped on every start, so the JARs are always read fresh), installs every *.jar in ~/.marginalia/extensions and starts them. For each MarginaliaExtension service a bundle registered, it calls onExtensionLoad. Each JAR is installed and started on its own: one that can't be installed (not a bundle, a second copy of an installed plugin) or fails to start is logged with its file name and skipped. When the folder holds several versions of one extension (same symbolic name, e.g. an update copied next to the old JAR), only the newest is started; a warning names the skipped JARs, which are moved to extensions/old-versions (not deleted). Before a bundle is started it is verified: the decorators it registers are checked against this version of the application (Verification before loading). An invalid extension stays installed but is not started, and its report is logged. OsgiService.getInvalidExtensions() lists the installed, not stopped bundles that have a .invalid report; the workspaces show them in the red InvalidExtensionsWarning bar (ui.components) at the top (the administrator gets the names as its tooltip, other users a note to tell the administrator). A bundle whose JAR has a jar name.STOPPED flag next to it (see Stopping) is installed but not started either.

Installing at runtime. Admin → Extensions → Load Extension (.jar) writes the uploaded file into ~/.marginalia/extensions (the file name is sanitized: only letters, digits, ., _ and -) and installs and starts it the same way, verification included (OsgiService.installPackage, like uninstallPackage administrators only: AdminGuard.requireAdmin(); an invalid upload throws ExtensionVerificationException with the report). Screens that are already open are not rebuilt: the plugin's decorators run the next time the decorated methods run (the next time the user opens a book, a tab...).

Updating. Uploading a bundle whose symbolic name (or file name) is already installed replaces it: the old one is unloaded as by Unload, uninstalled and its JAR deleted, then the new one is loaded. If the new one fails to install, verify or start, its JAR is deleted and the old one is put back.

Unloading. Unload calls the callbacks registered with bindAttachableComponent, then onExtensionUnload, uninstalls the bundle and deletes its JAR and its verification reports (OsgiService.uninstallPackage). Bundles that failed to start are listed too (state Installed or Resolved) and can be unloaded the same way.

Stopping. Stop (OsgiService.stopExtension, administrators only) creates the jar name.STOPPED flag file, unloads the extension like Unload does (bound callbacks, onExtensionUnload) and stops the bundle; the bundle stays installed and is listed with the state Stopped (isStopped). Start (startExtension) verifies it, starts it and deletes the flag; when that fails, the flag stays. The flag survives restarts. Uploading a replacement of a stopped extension deletes the flag, and Unload deletes the flag too.

Shutdown. When the application stops (the root context closes), every extension is unloaded the same way - bound callbacks, onExtensionUnload, the activator's stop - and the framework is stopped. Still save data as you go: a killed process runs none of this.

An extension should not use LoggerFactory (its lines are mixed with everything else and the administrator cannot see them next to the extension). OsgiService.createLogger(bundle) returns an org.slf4j.Logger that writes to its own file, jar name.log in the extensions folder (sidequery.jar.log), which administrators read in Admin → Extensions → Log:

The usual SLF4J API: {} placeholders and a trailing throwable (logged with its stack trace). TRACE is dropped, DEBUG and above are written. Each line has the time, level, thread, logger name (the symbolic name by default) and the message. The line is also chained to the application log (logger extension.name, same level, so the level settings of the application apply - the release build logs at INFO and keeps story content out of its log, so don't log story text above DEBUG).

The logger is thread safe and can be kept; the file is opened for every line, so nothing stays open after the extension is gone. A file over 2 MB is moved to jar name.log.old (replacing the previous one).
OsgiService.readLog(bundle, maxBytes) and clearLog(bundle) (administrators only) read the end of the file and delete it. The log is deleted with the extension when it is unloaded.

Code that is not created by the extension class (components made by new, services) needs the logger too: pass it on (Lore Generator gives it to its service) or keep it in a static holder that is set in onExtensionLoad and reset in onExtensionUnload, with LoggerFactory as the fallback before and after (Side Query's SideQueryLog).
The class org.slf4j.Logger comes from the application (boot delegation); if your bundle lists its Import-Package explicitly, include org.slf4j.

OsgiService reports single extensions that are loaded or unloaded to ExtensionListeners, for code that has to react to the extension set - the application itself uses it to keep the styles of extensions in the pages (Styles of a plugin):
extensionLoaded(bundle, extension) is called after onExtensionLoad returned. An extension whose load failed is never reported (and not as unloaded either); it is unloaded again as before.
extensionUnloaded(bundle, extension) is called after onExtensionUnload, for every extension that was reported as loaded: Unload, an update that replaces the bundle, the shutdown of the application.

The methods run on the thread that loads or unloads (an administrator's request, the startup), with no UI session. Change a UI through ui.access(...). An exception is logged and doesn't stop other listeners or the loading.

Listeners get no events for extensions that are loaded already. Subscribe first, then read getLoadedExtensions(); an extension loaded between the two is seen twice, so handle repeats (CssRegistry.attach does).

Optional interfaces. Besides MarginaliaExtension, the extension class can implement ExtensionHasCss (styles put into every page, see Styles of a plugin) and ExtensionHasLocalization (languages for the UI: OsgiServiceImpl registers the returned LocalizationBundles in Localization right after onExtensionLoad returned and removes them when the extension is unloaded; see Example plugin).
The older ExtensionObserver (addSubscriber) reports the start and stop of the whole framework, including the pauses during an upload or unload.

Felix is started with org.osgi.framework.bootdelegation=* and the framework class loader as the bundle parent, which is the web application's class loader. Every class a bundle asks for is therefore looked up in the application first: Marginalia's own classes, Vaadin, Spring, Hibernate, Gson, everything in WEB-INF/lib. The consequences:
Plugins use the application's classes directly - no imports, no service lookups, instanceof and casts work.
A plugin can't override or replace a library of the application, and can't use a different version of one.

Plugins don't see each other's classes through imports either; if two plugins need to cooperate, do it through shared data (attributes) or through the application's components. A plugin that uses the objects of another one (which may be missing, or unloaded and installed again) finds it among OsgiService.getLoadedExtensions() by the name of its class and calls it by reflection, taking the types it needs from extension.getClass().getClassLoader(). Do not import its packages (Import-Package, DynamicImport-Package) or name its classes in your code: the wiring is to one revision of the other bundle, so after it is unloaded and installed again your bundle keeps the old classes and does not recognize the new objects, and the JVM remembers a class reference that failed to resolve (NoClassDefFoundError), so a reference used while the other bundle was missing keeps failing after it is installed. For tools for the model use ToolService instead, no reflection is needed (Sharing data between extensions).

The plugin's own classes are loaded by the bundle's class loader, so the class names you pass to registerDecorator must be those of the application's classes; a plugin's own classes are never instrumented.

Most of what a plugin does starts with a decorator: an object whose onMethodEnter and onMethodLeave run before and after a method of an application class. Any method of a class annotated @Extendable can be decorated, private ones included, and the decorator can read the method's arguments and local variables and change what the method returns. This page explains how that works and how to use it. The signature of every such method is declared in the source with @PublicAPI, which is what plugins can rely on.

RuntimeInstrumentationInitializer installs a ByteBuddy agent into the running JVM when the Spring context starts. The agent transforms every class annotated @Extendable whose name starts with com.github.enerccio - classes loaded later when they are loaded, classes already loaded by retransformation. Only method bodies change; the class keeps its fields and methods (disableClassFormatChanges), which is what makes retransformation possible.
ExtendableMethodVisitor rewrites every method that is not a constructor, not static and not synthetic (lambda bodies are synthetic). In pseudo-code, an instrumented method looks like this:
This runs on every call, whether a decorator is registered or not. That's why @Extendable is on UI classes, which run at human speed, and not on services or entities.

Names come from the class file: parameter names from the MethodParameters attribute (the application is compiled with -parameters), local variable names from the local variable table (preserveAllLocals). If either is missing, arguments are called arg0, arg1... and locals varslot.

What counts as a change. Renaming or retyping an argument or a local variable, adding or removing one, changing the return type, renaming or removing the method, or moving it to another class (a decorator registered for the old class and name is never called) can break a plugin. Adding a method does not, and neither does changing the body in a way that keeps the arguments, the locals and what they hold. For each change that can be seen:
instrumented is the object whose method runs (this).

Class name is the binary name of the class that declares the method: nested classes use $ (ManuscriptStoryPart$ChatMessageCard). A method inherited from a superclass is reported under the superclass, for all subclasses; a subclass's own methods under the subclass. The class itself must be @Extendable - the annotation is not inherited, and nested classes need their own.
Method name only: all overloads of a method share its decorators. Check the arguments (hasMethodArgument(name, type)) if you need to tell overloads apart.
Several decorators on the same method run in the order they were registered, for enter and for leave.
A decorator registered for a class or method that doesn't exist is accepted and never called - check names carefully. Verification refuses to load an extension that does this.

Decorators are global: they run for every user and every session. Use the arguments and fields to decide whether to act. The current user is the session-scoped User bean, injected as in services (The current user) - on the UI thread it resolves to the session's user.

What the body of the method returned, whatever the decorators did. Only in onMethodLeave. Primitives come boxed, but ask for the primitive type (int.class) like for arguments.

A decorator of a method that returns a value can replace the value in onMethodLeave. The decorators of a method form a chain in the order they were registered, sharing one current value:

getOriginalReturn is always what the body returned, getCurrentReturn starts as the same value and is whatever the last setCurrentReturn set. A decorator that only wants to add to the result reads the current value, so it keeps what the decorators before it did; one that wants to start over reads the original.
When the last decorator is done, the caller of the method receives the current value. If nobody set one, the method returns what its body returned.

The value must fit the declared return type of the method (a subtype is fine, null is fine for objects); for a primitive return type pass the matching wrapper (setCurrentReturn(5) for int), not null. A value that does not fit is refused with a ModCompatibilityException (a warning in the log, as for the other errors), the current value stays and the method is not affected.
Type checks of the getters are against the declared return type: getOriginalReturn(CharSequence.class) works for a method that returns String, Integer.class does not work for int.

The return value exists only after the body returned. In onMethodEnter, for a void method and when the method throws, hasReturn() is false and the getters and the setter are refused. A decorator cannot swallow an exception or turn a return into one, and the body always runs (What a decorator can't do).

The mutable objects a method returns (a component, a list) can be changed without replacing the value; replace it when you need a different object, or the value is immutable (String, numbers, Optional).

What a method returns is read by its caller, and every plugin that replaces it is now a part of that. A change of the declared return type of an @Extendable method is a change of its public API, and a plugin that replaces the value with a type that no longer fits is refused at run time.

The getters and the reflective calls throw a ModCompatibilityException (a private RuntimeException subclass of ExtensionServiceImpl) when a name doesn't exist or the type doesn't match. ExtensionServiceImpl catches everything a decorator throws, so a failing decorator never breaks the decorated method or the other decorators:
in onMethodLeave, a ModCompatibilityException is logged as a warning: Mod 'decorator class' skipped on class.method: Required component variable 'sidebarBtn' was not found ...;
anything else, and anything in onMethodEnter, is logged as an error with the stack trace.
That makes a renamed variable a log line, not a crash - but also easy to miss. When you work on a plugin, watch the log.
Skip the method. The body always runs, with its arguments as they are after onMethodEnter. What it returns can be replaced afterwards, and so can what it built (a local variable or field) or saved.
Replace the result of a method that throws, or throw instead of a return: a decorator can read the exception in onMethodLeave but it is always rethrown.

.valid: the extension is started. .invalid: it is not - at startup the bundle stays installed, not started (state Installed or Resolved), the report is logged as an error and Admin → Extensions shows an Invalid button that opens it. An upload that is invalid is rejected like one that fails to start: its JAR is deleted, the replaced version is put back and the report is shown to the administrator. A report is reused only while it is newer than the JAR and newer than the application (the later of the creation and modification time of the WAR; of the folder it is unpacked to or of the classes when it runs unpacked or from the IDE). Prefer arguments and fields over locals, and locals over walking the component tree.

p: Use one top-level key per plugin, named after the plugin's package, and put a JSON tree of your own model classes under it. The bundled plugins all follow this pattern:
Rules:
Save through the entity's service - save(...), not saveWithoutEvent(...). See How attributes are stored for why.

Load before you change. Entities held by the UI are detached copies, and the one you got from a decorator may be older than the database. Reload it (service.find(entity) or find(id)), change the attributes, save it, and use the returned object from then on. Saving an old copy overwrites changes made since - to the plugin's data and to the rest of the entity. Lorebook VCS's saveVCSData is a good template:

The same goes for the plugin's own data: when several components edit parts of one JSON tree, each change should re-read the stored tree, change only its part and save it (Lorebook VCS's updateEntryData), not save a copy it loaded earlier.
Version your data. There are no migrations; if the format changes, read old formats too (a version field in your JSON tree makes this easy) and never fail on data you don't understand.

Keep it small. The whole JSON object is serialized on every save of the entity, and some entities are saved often - a story part is saved up to every 250 ms while it's generated. Megabytes of history in a part's attributes slow generation down. Lorebook VCS stores the history once per lorebook, not per entry, for this reason.
c: Lorebook fresh = lorebookService.find(lorebook); fresh.getAttributes().add(LorebookVCSData.KEY, gson.toJsonTree(data)); Lorebook saved = lorebookService.save(fresh);

p: Per user: settingService.getOrCreate(UserSetting.class) returns the current user's settings; store under your key, save with settingService.save(userSetting). To add the settings to the Settings screen, see Extending the UI → Settings panels.
Whole installation: AppSettings the same way, only administrators should change it.
The application itself uses attributes too. Don't use these keys:

Template variables set by macros (setvar, setglobalvar...) - local ones on the part, global ones on the book.
attributes is not a column. The entity has one extendedContent column (bytes, UTF-8 JSON), and ExtendableEntityListener converts between the two:

On save (JpaExtendableRepository.save) it builds one JSON object: each @ExtendedAttribute field of the entity under its field name, as a string, and each key of attributes with the prefix attributes_.
On load (@PostLoad) and after every save it fills the fields and attributes back from that JSON.

The column is gzipped when the content is 256 bytes or more (ExtendableEntity.setExtendedContent; getExtendedContent returns the plain JSON). Rows saved before that are still read and are compressed when the entity is saved again (the application migration ExtendedContentMigration does it for all of them). Code that reads the column with SQL gets bytes that are not JSON.
The column of a story part looks like this:
Two things follow from this:
saveWithoutEvent (used by backup restore, which writes extendedContent directly) does not serialize: changes to attributes saved that way are lost. Always use save.

The _fulltext column that is written next to extendedContent is built only from the application's @Fulltextable fields (see Domain model). A plugin's attributes are not in it and can't be added to it.

@ExtendedAttribute is the application's own way of adding fields to an entity without a migration - many fields of ChatMessage, Manuscript, Protocol and the settings are stored like this. It works for String, the numeric types, boolean, Date and enums, stored as strings (dates as ISO-8601 instants in UTC). @ExtendedAttribute(inject = true, injectPrefix = ...) on a JsonObject field spreads its keys with that prefix, which is how attributes itself is declared; a field of any other type (POJO with nested objects and lists, a list) is converted with Gson, an object spread the same way, a list or scalar stored under the plain prefix. This is for application code: a plugin can't add fields to an entity class, it uses attributes.

If your data refers to another entity, store its uuid (or id). The Cleanup page of the administration purges soft-deleted rows (Domain model), and it knows only the references the application declares (@CleanupReference) - ids inside a plugin's attributes are invisible to it. Two consequences:

A deleted entity your data points to can be purged. Always handle a reference that resolves to nothing or to a deleted entity. Reviewer falls back to the book's provider when the configured one is missing or deleted:
If a reference must keep its target alive, or must be cleared when the target is purged, register a CleanupService.CleanupContributor:
EntityKey uses the root entity class of a hierarchy (AI, not OpenAICompatible). Cleanup runs for the whole installation, not for one user - don't use currentUser in a contributor.
When resolving anything that came from data the user can edit or import, use findForUser(uuid) so that one user's data can't point a plugin at another user's entity.
c: AI configuredAi = aiService.find(setting.getSelectedAiId()); if (configuredAi != null && !configuredAi.isDeleted()) { return configuredAi; } return aiService.find(manuscript.getAi());

cleanupContributor = new CleanupService.CleanupContributor() { @Override public void collectReferences(Set<CleanupService.EntityKey> candidates, CleanupService.BlockSink sink) { // during Analyze / Purge: block candidates the plugin still references for (Long aiId : idsOfProvidersMyPluginUses()) { CleanupService.EntityKey key = new CleanupService.EntityKey(AI.class, aiId); if (candidates.contains(key)) { sink.block(key, "used by My Plugin"); // shown as the reason on the Cleanup page } } } @Override public void beforePurge(Set<CleanupService.EntityKey> purged) { // in the purge transaction, before the rows are removed: drop references to them } }; cleanupService.registerContributor(cleanupContributor); // onExtensionLoad cleanupService.unregisterContributor(cleanupContributor); // onExtensionUnload

p: Plugins add to the user interface from decorators: when a method that builds part of a screen runs, the plugin's decorator finds the component it built and adds to it. This page collects the patterns the bundled plugins use. Read @Extendable hooks first, and User interface for the conventions of the UI code.

Every screen below exists twice: the desktop class and its phone twin (ManuscriptStoryPart and PhoneManuscriptStoryPart and so on), and a decorator only runs for the class it was registered for. Register it a second time for the phone class to support phones, or leave it out and the extension simply adds nothing there, see The phone twins.
Find the component - a field, a local variable or an argument of the decorated method.

Add only once. Many methods run more than once for the same component (refresh(), UserPart.refresh...), so mark the component with ComponentUtil.setData(component, key, value) and check the mark first. Prefix the keys with your plugin's package (KEY + .menuItem, see Extended attributes) - the components are shared with the application and every other plugin.
Remember what you added, so that onExtensionUnload can remove it (Unloading).

l: Menu items on a story part
p: Use the menu registry below: an item of the menu of a part (☰ on a card) is a StoryMenuItem.card(..), with its sub menus, its state worked out each time the menu opens and a row in the key bindings. It works on the desktop and the phone story tab alike. Reviewer registers its Review sub menu this way (ReviewerExtension).

The older way still works: decorate ManuscriptStoryPart$ChatMessageCard.createMenuItems (called when the menu of the card is opened for the first time, not when the card is created, after the registry items were added) and add to the hamburgerMenu field; the card's message field is the part. Such an item has no shortcut row, no key hint and you have to remove it yourself on unload. To update items each time the menu opens, decorate refreshSummaryMenuItems, which the card runs each time the menu is about to open. It can also run before the menu was ever opened: the items are not created then, so check what you read from the menu for null. The card replaces its message with the saved copy whenever the part is edited, so read the field again in the click listener rather than capturing it when the menu is built.

The bottom bar of the story editor has a menu bar with the Summaries item and the settings item (⚙). It is built by small methods of ManuscriptStoryPart that get the bar as an argument (bar), so decorate one of them on leave:
Method
Add to
populateMenuBar(bar)
The bar itself - a new item next to the summaries and the settings item. The method is empty and runs after the application's items were added.
createCogsMenuItem(bar)
The settings menu: the local variable cogs is its MenuItem, add to cogs.getSubMenu() (an item of the registry is better: it gets a key and no cleanup).
The menu bar is built once per story editor, so it needs no marker. Read currentManuscript when the item is clicked, not when it is built - the story editor loads other books into the same instance.

Instruction Exporter is the small example of the settings menu: it adds Export instructions to cogs.getSubMenu() and copies the text with navigator.clipboard.writeText (plugins keep their own scripts).

SummariesDialog (the overview of the summaries, opened from the Summaries item) has a menu bar above its grid, with the item Search and Replace of the application in it. Decorate populateMenuBar(bar) on leave and add items to the argument bar. A new dialog (and menu bar) is created every time the overview opens, so the decorator runs for each of them. The dialog's fields (manuscript, treeGrid) are reachable by reflection; to reload the grid after your tool changed the summaries, close and reopen the dialog, or call its private refresh() with callReflectiveMethod.

Changes to summaries should go through SummaryService (updateSummaryText, removeSummary, createMetaSummary): it keeps the token counts, the hashes of the summaries and the meta summaries that merged them consistent. In particular, don't edit the text of a summary a meta summary stands in for (shown under it in the overview) - its text is part of the hash of the meta summary and it would be dropped as outdated.

l: A tab next to the story
p: ManuscriptStoryPart.renderStoryContent() redraws the message cards and the chapter outline every time the story is redrawn (opening the book, after a generation, after a delete); the leftBar tab sheet with the story outline is created once, so the selected tab survives a redraw. The method runs many times, so check for your tab first. Side Query adds its tab on leave:
The tab dock (and so the plugin's component) lives as long as the story part, a redraw does not recreate it.

leftBar is a TabDock (ui.widgets; since 1.3.0, before it was a VTabSheet): on the desktop the user can drag its tabs into panels of their own, stacked or side by side, and add/remove find the tab wherever it is now. Since 1.5.0 the story itself is a tab of this dock (the id story), so the dock is the whole editor and the user may put the story and your tab in any arrangement; a tab the saved layout does not know still lands in the first sheet, the sidebar of a new book. A tab that is not the selected one of its sheet is hidden and its content disabled (the sheet does that), so do not expect events from your component then; leftBar.select(id) shows a tab. Give the tab a stable id of your own (add(id, caption, content), not the localized caption): the layout the user made is saved with the book by these ids, and a tab added later or after the extension was off lands where the user left it. add(caption, content) uses the caption as the id. Since 1.6.0 every tab has a minimize button, and a minimized tab is an icon in the bar of the dock: a circle with one or two letters, made by TabDockIcons. add(id, caption, letters, content) gives the letters of your tab (SQ); without them they are the initials of the caption. A minimized tab stays in the dock (its content is alive, only not in a sheet); leftBar.select(id) restores it, isMinimized(id), minimize(id) and restore(id) do what they say, and setMinimizable(id, false) takes the button away from a tab. The ids of the minimized tabs and the side of the bar are in getLayout() (minimized, dock), so they are saved with the book like the rest of the arrangement. The ids chapters (the outline), lorebook (the read only lorebook preview, desktop only) and story (since 1.5.0) belong to the application; a tab with the same id would replace them. Remove the tab with leftBar.remove(view). The phone drawer has a TabDock too, but with the detaching off.
Find the layout and insert at a position relative to a known child. Lorebook VCS puts its panel above the lorebook header that LorebookView.create() builds:

A component created once for a view must not hold on to things that change in it: LorebookView stays the same when the user picks another lorebook, so a panel bound to the lorebook it was created with ends up acting on the wrong one. Look the current value up when it's needed (lorebookView.getCurrentLorebook()), or hook the method that switches it.

A grid the view keeps in a field can get more columns. Lore Generator adds a button to every row of the lorebook entries after LorebookView.create() has built the grid, and keeps the column to remove it on unload:

The row's item is the entity itself; read the context that is not part of it (the selected lorebook) from the view when the button is clicked, as above. A dialog the button opens is an ordinary component of the plugin: it can call the model with InferenceService.stream (put LLMAttachments on the user message to send images or files, see Services) and must update the UI through ui.access(...) and UIPushGuard.
The decorator can change any component the method built. Chapter Marker relabels the sidebar button of a part:
If more plugins change the same component, they run in the order they were loaded and the last one wins - append or prefix rather than replace where you can.

Shortcuts work in the desktop layout only (the phone twin of the story has none). Register an action with a default key; it is listed in Settings → Keyboard shortcuts, where the user can change or clear the key, and the handler runs when the key is pressed in the open story tab (not while a generation runs). The handler gets the component of the story tab.

Prefix the id with the plugin name. A key without Ctrl/Alt/Meta fires only when no text field has the focus; avoid keys the browser keeps (Ctrl+N/T/W) and Alt with a letter (types a character on a Mac). Unregister in onExtensionUnload (ShortcutRegistry.unregister(id)); the stored key of the user stays for when the plugin is back.

c:
ShortcutRegistry.register(new ShortcutAction("myplugin.summarize",
        loc -> "Summarize the last part",      // the name in the table, in the language of the session
        "Ctrl+Shift+y",                         // canonical key combination (KeyCombo), null for none
        storyTab -> summarizeLastPart(storyTab)));

l: Menu items of the story editor
p: 1. Get the registry. The extension class is @Configurable, so inject it like any service:
2. Choose the menu and the callback. What the callback gets depends on the menu:
3. Describe when it shows. All of these are optional and are asked again each time the menu opens (and after an item of the settings menu ran):
4. Sub menus. An item that only holds other items has no callback; its items name it with parent(key) (any depth). Reviewer:

5. Keys. Every item with a callback is an action of Settings → Keyboard shortcuts (the id is menu.key or the actionId you gave) from the moment it is registered, with defaultKey or without. A key of a card or text item acts on the part that is being edited, else the part that holds the text selection, else the last part, and on the last part when the item is not visible or enabled for the chosen one (the same predicates decide). A tools item needs no part. Shortcuts work on the desktop only. Pick a default that the browser does not keep (Ctrl+N/T/W, Alt with a letter on a Mac) or none.

6. What happens on unload and reload. unregisterAll(owner) removes the items from the registry and from the key bindings table. Menus that are open keep the Vaadin items they were built with, but an unregistered item is retired: it is hidden the next time its menu is refreshed (a part menu when it opens, the settings menu after any of its items ran or the story tab is entered) and it runs nothing. Registering the same key again (a reloaded extension) replaces the item. New menus, and part menus that are opened for the first time, have the items registered at that moment; a menu that was built before your extension loaded does not get them until the story is opened again.
A parent must be registered before its items; an item whose parent is missing (or not shown on the phone) is left out. Items appear in the order of registration, after the application's.
a row in Settings → Keyboard shortcuts (a default key, or none) and the key of the user shown next to the item,

A tools item can be a check box: .checkedWhen(story - story.isShowGeneratedDiff()) (the action switches whatever the predicate reads; a ticked item is refreshed after the action ran). .actionId(myplugin.summarize) gives the item the id of its key binding when it is not menu.key (keep it when you rename the item and the user has a key stored), and .hintAction((story, card) - id) shows the key of another action (the Edit item shows the key of saving while the text is edited).

The label is also the name of the action in the key bindings table, so make it say what the action does.
