StoryEditor is the story tab (the desktop or the phone one): getCurrentManuscript() (the book it shows now, read it when the action runs, the tab loads other books into the same instance), openSearchReplaceDialog(), openExportDialog(), toggleBookStyles()... StoryCard is the card of the part the menu is of: getMessage() (the ChatMessage, the card replaces it with the saved copy, so read it each time), isEditing(), isLast(), and the actions of the part (toggleEdit(), swipe(), branch(), annotatePart()...). The callback runs on the UI thread of the user, in a request, as any click listener.
StoryMenuItem.card(key, label, action)

StoryMenuItem.tools(key, label, action)
sub menus whose items come and go,
text, visibility and enabled / ticked state that are worked out each time the menu opens, so an item can depend on the part,

The first argument is the owner (use the bundle's symbolic name); the key of an item (myplugin.export) identifies it, so prefix it with your plugin's name. Registering a key again replaces the item. Instruction Exporter is the whole of this example.

The hooks createCogsMenuItem and createMenuItems stay for plugins that add other things than items (a decorated method can do anything), and what a decorator adds directly is not managed by the registry. Test your items without a browser as the application does (StoryMenuRegistryTest): registry.definition(kind, phone, bindings).build(new ContextMenu(), loc, story, () - card) returns a BuiltMenu whose items (get(key)) can be inspected and clicked with stub implementations of StoryEditor and StoryCard.
the item on the desktop and the phone story tab with one definition (.phone(false) for desktop only),

Three menus of the story editor are filled from the StoryMenuRegistry (ui.menu): the settings menu (⚙ at the bottom, StoryMenuItem.tools), the menu of a part (☰ on a card, StoryMenuItem.card) and the right click menu of the text of a part (long press on a phone, StoryMenuItem.text). Registering an item instead of decorating a method gives you:

c:
StoryMenuItem.card("myplugin.summarize", loc -> "Summarize with notes",
                (story, card) -> summarize(card.getMessage()))
        .icon(VaadinIcon.NOTEBOOK::create)                       // a new Icon per menu
        .defaultKey("Ctrl+Shift+y")                              // KeyCombo text, null (the default) for no key
        .visibleWhen((story, card) -> card.getMessage().getId() != null)
        .enabledWhen((story, card) -> !card.isEditing())
        .contextLabel((loc, story, card) -> card.isLast() ? "Summarize (last part)" : "Summarize")   // the text in the menu
        .phone(false)                                            // not on the phone

p: The Settings screen (UserPart) has an Extension Settings tab with an Accordion in the field extensionSettings, empty unless plugins add to it. The bundled plugins use two decorators:

Changes in the panel's fields are tracked like the application's own: any value change outside of UserPart.refresh (and its decorators) locks the workspace navigation until the user saves or discards. Fill the form in the refresh decorator, not later (e.g. from a background thread), or the loaded values count as changes.

Saving on enter lets the application's own settingService.save(userSetting) store the plugin's values too. Note that save() returns early when the application's own fields don't validate - then the plugin's values are not stored either.
Plugin dialogs and components are ordinary Vaadin classes in the bundle. Annotate them @Configurable to inject services. Follow the application's conventions (User interface → Conventions).
What plugins can't do:

Add frontend resources. The browser side of Marginalia is one bundle built with the WAR. A plugin can use every Vaadin component and add-on the application already uses (Vaadin core components, the FontAwesome icons, Viritin's VTabSheet...), but @CssImport, @JsModule, @NpmPackage and add-ons with their own web components don't work from a plugin. Style with the classes of CssStyles (addClassName(CssStyles.TEXT_SECONDARY)), which the application's shared-styles.css defines. A style only your plugin uses goes into a CSS file in the bundle's src/main/resources that the application puts into the page for you (Styles of a plugin), with its class names as constants in the plugin. Use getStyle() only for a value known at runtime. Charts are the exception: the application's ChartJs widget (ui.widgets) draws any Chart.js configuration given as JSON, so a plugin can show a chart without a frontend module of its own.

Add localization keys. Localization knows only the application's L keys. A plugin translates the texts of its own UI with a PluginLocalizationBundle (Texts in several languages). A plugin can also add a language for the application's texts, see Example plugin → Chinese localization.
Add routes. Routes are registered when the servlet starts. Use dialogs and tabs instead.

A plugin can't add keys to the L enum, so the texts of its UI are the English sentences themselves. PluginLocalizationBundle (package extensions) turns one into the text of the language of the current session (Localization.getCurrentLanguage()): localized(message) returns the translation, and the English message when the language has none, so a language or a text that is missing shows English. The bundled plugins have one subclass each and call it through a static field:
ja and zh are shortcuts for add(Language, message, translation); add other languages the same way (the language needs a bundle in Localization, see the Chinese localization).

A text with values has the String.format placeholders in the key (%s, %d) and the values are put in with formatted(...). When a language needs another order, number the placeholders in the key and in the translation (%1$d turns for the messages %2$d-%3$d). Don't build a sentence from pieces: a language puts the words in another order, write one key for each whole sentence (and one for the singular and the plural).

Look the text up when it is shown, not in a field or a constant: the bundle answers for the language of the session that asks, and a text kept in a field stays in the language of whoever created it. A lambda that is called when a menu is opened (l - T.localized(Export instructions)) is fine.

Without a session (startup, a worker thread that got no request attributes) the default language is used, so the title that a plugin registers in onExtensionLoad (ToolService.registerProvider(..., Name provider, ...)) stays in English; the same holds for annotation values (@CommandParameter(descriptionText = ...)), which must be constants.
Texts for the model (prompts, the descriptions of functions and commands, the error messages of commands) stay in English; only what the user reads is translated.
For words the application has a key for (L.LABEL_CANCEL) the plugin can use loc.getValue(...) instead.

l: Telling the help assistant about your UI
p: The help assistant can read the screen of the user, and, when an administrator allows it, move through it. It sees only the classes that implement LLMInteract (User interface → Letting the help assistant see the UI), so a plugin dialog or panel that does not is not part of what it reads: a dialog of yours is simply absent from the screen.

The element is found under the nearest LLMInteract above it in the component tree, and only while it is visible (a dialog only while it is open). Its path is the names of the elements above it and its own simple class name.

getLLMState is Markdown for the model: say what the user sees and would say themselves (the open tab, a filter, a title). Never the text of a story or a lorebook, a key, a password or an id: the state goes to the administrator's AI, which may be an outside provider.

getInteraction() offers moves the model may make: a map from a key to an LLMInteraction(description, action). Only harmless ones the user could undo with a click (select a tab, open a section), never anything that changes, saves, deletes, sends or generates; none while your UI is locked. LLMInteract.tabs(...) makes the entries for a row of tabs, LLMInteract.dialogButtons(button...) the ones that press a button that opens a dialog (offered only while no dialog is open).

getLLMProblems() is what the model reads to explain why a form can not be saved. The default already lists the visible fields of your component that are invalid (with the message the field shows) or required and empty, by their labels, never their values; override it only for a rule that your save method checks across fields (LLMInteract.super.getLLMProblems() plus your lines). Give your fields labels and mark the required ones, then the model can name them.

To add to a class of the application, decorate its getLLMState (or getInteraction) with getCurrentReturn / setCurrentReturn (see Changing the return value); append to the text and put your entries into a copy of the map. Only the classes that override those methods can be decorated: both workspaces, AdminPart (it exists only for administrators), both story editor dialogs, Main, UserPart and the lists of models, protocols and books (getLLMState, getInteraction) and AIDialog (getLLMProblems); the other elements use the defaults of the interface.

What a user was shown that went wrong is recorded for you: your Notification.error / warning (the application's ui.widgets.Notification) and UIUtils.showError / showValidationErrors / inferenceError write it to the session's problem log, which the model reads with read_last_errors (What went wrong). Say what is wrong in the message (the model gets the text the user saw).
A plugin can't add to the application's stylesheet, but it can ship its own CSS. Implement ExtensionHasCss on the class that implements MarginaliaExtension:

getCss returns the CSS text for a page, or null/blank when the extension has no styles there. The entry point is the root component of the page: Main (the workspace) or Viewer (the reader); both implement ApplicationEntryPoint. The text is usually a resource of the bundle, read once and cached:

Use Lumo variables (var(--lumo-contrast-10pct)) in the rules and keep the class names as constants next to the loader (Side Query: SideQueryStyles and sidequery.css); prefix them with the plugin's name, the page is shared with the application and other plugins.

A plugin can use the application's components that draw with a JavaScript library (TreantTree, ChartJs, GraphView, Character Tracker's relationship map is a GraphView), but it can't add a library of its own, see Custom components.
What the application does. Each entry point owns a CssRegistry (created in onAttach, released in onDetach). For every UI it
adds the style of each extension that is loaded already when the entry point is attached (an extension loaded at startup, or before the user opened the page),
adds the style of an extension that is loaded while the page is open (Admin → Extensions → Load), so it works without a reload,
removes the style again when the extension is unloaded, replaced by a newer version or the application stops.

The CSS goes into a style id=marginalia-extension-css-extension class name element in the document head; the element is replaced if it exists, so nothing is added twice. The registry listens to OsgiService through an ExtensionListener (Extension events). getCss is called once per page and extension and an exception from it is logged and skips only that extension, but it should not do anything expensive.

Don't add the style element from your own components (executeJs in a constructor): the style would not be removed when the extension is unloaded and would be added again for each component. Return it from getCss.

Inside click listeners and other event handlers, catch exceptions and report them like the application does: UIUtils.internalServerError(loc, e) logs and shows an error dialog - pass an injected Localization. Expected problems go to Notification. Failures of the model API (InferenceException) are explained by UIUtils.inferenceError(loc, e) or, as text, InferenceErrors.messageOf(loc, e). Exceptions in decorators themselves are logged by the ExtensionService and don't need handling unless you want to show something.

Decorators run on the thread that called the decorated method. For UI methods that's a request thread holding the Vaadin session lock, so decorators can change components directly and services see the current user.

Anything slow - calling the model, large imports - belongs on another thread, with the same rules as in the application (Background work and push): capture UI.getCurrent() on the UI thread, change components only inside ui.access(...), push with UIPushGuard.push(ui), and wrap service calls that need the current user in the request scope.
InferenceServices.forAI(ai) returns the client for a provider; stream(...) sends a list of messages and calls back as the answer arrives, on another thread. Reviewer's review dialog, shortened:

Name the kind of work. Open an InferenceSession around the call that starts the request, with a kind named like your plugin: try (InferenceSession _ = InferenceSession.open(my-plugin)) { service.stream(...); } (a second argument tells apart runs that do not share a prompt). The service then sends the header X-Session-ID with a hash of the user and the kind, which a server or proxy with a prompt cache can use to keep a cache per kind of work; see Prompt cache and session id. The scope covers only the call itself; a request outside of any scope sends no header.
Call controller.continueInference() after each chunk, or the stream stops after the first one. terminateInference() ends it early.
protocol supplies sampling parameters and the response limit; it may be null.
Fit the prompt into the model's context yourself: TokenLimits.promptTokens(ai, protocol) is the room left for the prompt, service.countTokens(text) (or the cheaper countTokensApprox) counts.

infer(...) is the same call without streaming: the callback gets the whole text once (InferenceResultCallback). With a JSON schema, or a class annotated with @LLMSchema / @LLMField, the provider is asked to follow it and the answer is checked (SchemaCheck) or read into an object (TypedInferenceCallback); stream can pass a schema too, but checks nothing. Both can offer functions to the model.
The stream stops when the token is cancelled or isDead() returns true, both checked between chunks; the callback then gets onCancel().
To change what a story generation sends or receives, don't call the model yourself - register a generation listener like Author's Note does (Generation events).
When a plugin is unloaded, components it added to open screens stay there - with listeners pointing into a bundle that is gone - unless the plugin removes them. There are two ways.

Track and remove - what Reviewer, Side Query, Lore Generator and Lorebook VCS do. Keep the extended components in weak sets (so that closed screens can be garbage collected) and undo the changes in onExtensionUnload:

Bind a callback - OsgiService.bindAttachableComponent(component, callback, extension) registers callback to run when the extension is unloaded, for as long as component is attached (a component that is detached and attached again - moved, in a tab sheet, in a reopened dialog - stays bound):

(osgiService is the one passed to onExtensionLoad, or injected.) The callbacks run before onExtensionUnload, each inside ui.access(...) of its component's UI, so they can change the component directly. A component that is detached when the extension is unloaded runs its callback when it is attached again. Calling bindAttachableComponent for an extension that isn't loaded throws an IllegalStateException.

onExtensionUnload runs on the request thread of the administrator who clicked Unload, but the components belong to every user's open screens. Change them inside component.getUI().ifPresent(ui - ui.access(...)), as above, or with UIUtils.accessComponent(component, () - ...), which does the same and runs the change directly when the component isn't attached. The bundled Reviewer, Side Query, Lore Generator and Lorebook VCS do it this way.

Data in attributes stays after unloading, so loading the plugin again picks up where it left off. If your plugin is uninstalled for good, its data stays in the database (and in backups) - harmless, but say so in its README.

@Extendable hooks change what the user sees; generation events change what the model sees. A plugin registers listeners with StoryGenerationService.addEventListener(...) and the generation calls them at fixed points of the pipeline - with the lore, the summaries, the prompt data, the payload and the streamed answer at hand, all of which the listener may read and replace.

The full list of events, what each one makes available and the rules for listeners are in Generation pipeline → Events for extensions. This page shows how to use them on the bundled Author's Note plugin, which inserts a per-book note into the prompt of every generation.

Before AFTER_PREPARE_PAYLOAD there is no payload (a listener could only change the system prompt or the story text in GenerationProperties), after BEFORE_INFERENCE the request is already on its way.

But how much of the story fits into the context is decided earlier, in step 4 (PrepareContentStep), and the note must be counted there - otherwise a long note pushes the prompt over the model's context. So the plugin also listens to BEFORE_PREPARE_CONTENT and reserves the tokens the note will take, see Reserving tokens.

The note has to end up among the chat messages sent to the model, so it is inserted in AFTER_PREPARE_PAYLOAD: at that point PreparePayloadStep has built the final list of LLMChatMessages and whatever event.setPayload(...) sets is what inference sends. The payload looks like this:
the rendered user prompt with the instructions for this turn

PrePromptData.reservedTokens is the room extensions need for text they add after the budget is computed. Step 4 takes it out of the room for the story: fewer story parts are sent, and when not even the rest of the prompt fits, the generation stops with Contextual limit not sufficient, like for a too long template.

countTokens counts the note with the model of the generation (inferenceServices.forAI(event.getAi()).countTokens(...), which is not always the book's model) and adds 100 tokens for the message headers, like the budget does for every story part. 0 when the note is off.
Add, don't overwrite. Several extensions may reserve tokens in one generation: setReservedTokens(getReservedTokens() + mine).

Reserve in time. PrePromptData exists from AFTER_STATIC_TEMPLATE_DATA; the budget reads the reservation during BEFORE_SUMMARIES' continuation. BEFORE_PREPARE_CONTENT is the natural place - lore and the rendered user prompt are known by then. (A listener replacing PrePromptData in AFTER_STATIC_TEMPLATE_DATA starts with 0.)

Count what you insert. The plugin stores the note it counted in the generation's properties, under its package name, and inserts exactly that one - a note edited while the generation runs can't exceed the reservation.

l: When the size isn't known in advance
p: A reservation has to be made before the payload exists. When what an extension adds depends on the payload itself - on the story parts that made it in, on the final messages - it can skip the reservation and make room in AFTER_PREPARE_PAYLOAD instead: build its text, then remove the oldest story messages (the USER / ASSISTANT pairs right after the system prompt) from the payload until the whole payload fits into TokenLimits.promptTokens(ai, protocol) again. Count with the book's InferenceService and set the shortened list with event.setPayload(...). The two can be combined: reserve an estimate, trim if the real text is longer.

Points worth copying:
chain.next() in finally. The generation waits until every listener calls it; a listener that throws before calling it would leave the generation hanging.

Listeners are global. The same listener gets the events of every generation of every user. The plugin acts only on data of the book being generated (event.getManuscript()), which belongs to the user who started it.

Reload what the user may have changed. event.getManuscript() is the book as it was when the generation started. The note is edited in the sidebar and saved right away, so loadCurrent reads it again with ManuscriptService.find(...) - services work in listeners, they run in the user's request scope.
Carry state between events in the properties. event.getProperties() belongs to one generation; keys prefixed with the plugin's package don't clash with other plugins.

The prompt of a part is not on the part. The payload and the lore that were built for a part are a MessagePrompt row (MessagePromptService.getBuiltPrompt(message), getBackgroundLore(message)), not a field of ChatMessage any more. A regeneration keeps the row it replaces in the property GenerationProperties.ORIGINAL_PROMPT next to ORIGINAL_MESSAGE; cleanup puts it back when generation ends before any text arrived.
Replace, don't mutate. The listener builds a new list and calls event.setPayload(...). Another listener may have set an immutable list, and the new list makes it obvious what the plugin sends.
Don't break the generation. A failure is logged and the story is generated without the note.
Keep the system prompt first. Some providers accept a system message only at the start, so the depth is clamped to keep the note after it.

Extensions are separate bundles that should not import each other's classes (one can be unloaded and installed again while another keeps running). There are three ways to work together anyway:
You want
Use
to offer text about a book or a story part to whoever wants it (and to use what others offer), without knowing who they are
IPCService
to offer tools for the model (functions it can call, and the same as commands) that the user chooses in a Tools dialog
ToolService
to use one particular extension and what it can do (objects, lists), if it is installed
a direct call
IPCService lets extensions offer data to each other as text, through callbacks registered by a key. The application can use it too.
There are two kinds of providers:
Kind
Callback
Asked with
About a book
ManuscriptPluginData.getDataFor(Manuscript, Bundle caller, String callerIdentifier)
getManuscriptData(...)
About a story part
ChatMessagePluginData.getDataFor(ChatMessage, Bundle caller, String callerIdentifier)
getChatMessageData(...)
A callback returns the text, or null / blank when it has nothing. It may throw: the exception reaches the caller.
Register in onExtensionLoad, with @Autowired IPCService in your @Configurable extension class:

Use the symbolic name of your bundle as the identifier. When an extension is unloaded the application removes all providers of bundle.getSymbolicName(). A provider registered under another identifier must be removed with unregisterAll(identifier) in onExtensionUnload.
Registering a key again replaces the provider and keeps its place in the order.
The key is part of what other extensions store (Side Query remembers the sources the user checked), so don't rename it.

c:
ipcService.registerManuscriptProvider(
        bundle.getSymbolicName(),   // bundleIdentifier: who offers it
        "outline",                  // providerKey: stable, callers remember it
        "Arc outline",              // providerName: what the user sees
        (manuscript, caller, callerIdentifier) -> service.outlineText(manuscript));

p: getChatMessageProviders() and getChatMessageData(...) are the same for story parts. Asking for a provider that is not there (any more) returns null instead of throwing, since extensions come and go at any time; list the providers again when you show them to the user, and call them on the thread you are on (the callback runs there, so the session and transaction are yours).

The callback gets the caller's bundle and identifier, so a provider can decide what to give to whom. Nothing is checked by the service itself: a provider gives the data of the book it is handed, so it must only be handed books the caller may read.

ToolService lets an extension offer a suite of tools - functions the model can call - to every dialog that runs the model with tools (the generators of the Lore Generator and of the Arc Outline), and the same suite as commands for the command bar and the agents. Neither side imports the other and nothing is found by reflection: the types that cross are the ones of the application (FunctionSet, ToolSelection).
Implement ToolProvider and register it in onExtensionLoad, with @Autowired ToolService in your @Configurable extension class:

Items restrict the suite: the Name generator has one for each category of names. functions gets the ids that are checked (and still offered by items()) and returns functions that know only those - the provider does the restricting with its own types, usually a small class that implements its @LLMFunction interface around the real implementation (NameProviderToolProvider.Restricted). A suite without items is on or off; items is then empty. items() is asked on every use, it may change while the application runs. An item id is saved by the user's choice: keep it stable.
ToolItem(id, label): the id is what is saved, the label what the user sees.

defaultHint is a short text for the model, "when and how to call these": the caller adds the hint of each suite the model gets to its prompt. The user can write their own in the dialog; theirs replaces the default.

commands() is a suite of @Command methods (Commands). The service registers it with CommandService together with the provider and removes it with it, so the extension does not call registerCommands / unregisterCommands itself, and the command bar, the agents and the dialogs with tools have one source and one human name.

The provider is identified by the symbolic name of the bundle and the key. When an extension is unloaded the application removes all providers of that bundle and their commands (OsgiServiceImpl); registering a key again replaces the provider and keeps its place in the order. A function name must not be used by two suites a user can check together: resolve fails with the names of both providers.

c:
toolService.registerProvider(
        bundle.getSymbolicName(),   // bundleIdentifier: who offers it
        "names",                    // providerKey: stable, callers save it with the choice of the user
        "Name provider",            // the human name, the title of the section in the dialog
        new NameProviderToolProvider(lists, registry));

p: A dialog needs three things, and ToolSelectionButton does the first two:

ToolSelection is what the user chose: for each provider (bundle/key) the checked item ids, enabled for a suite without items, and the user's hint. Keep it in your settings (the Lore Generator also keeps it with each lore entry it generated). A provider that is not installed (any more) or an item that is gone is ignored by resolve; a provider that throws is logged and left out.
ToolSet holds the combined FunctionSet (null when nothing is on) and the hints; ToolSet.NONE for a dialog that gives the model no tools.

The button opens ToolSelectionDialog: one section for each suite with a filter field of its own, see UI. Call refresh() when a dialog that stays open may have lost or gained a suite (it also refreshes when it is attached).

c:
ToolSelectionButton tools = new ToolSelectionButton();           // hides itself while no suite is installed
tools.setValue(settings.getTools());                              // a ToolSelection, null for none
tools.addValueChangeListener(settings::setTools);                 // save it, it is plain JSON (Gson)
...
ToolSet set = toolService.resolve(tools.getValue(), new ToolRequest(bundle, MyService.class.getName()));
inference.stream(payload, protocol, set.functions(), callback);   // null when the user chose nothing
prompt += "\n\n" + set.hint();                                    // the hints of the suites the model got

l: Reading what an older version saved
p: The Lore Generator and the Arc Outline used to save the name categories with the prefix of their source (Generator: , Provider: , none meant the generator) and two hints, and found the name extensions by reflection. Each of them has a small LegacyNameTools that turns those into a ToolSelection for the suites name-generator/names and name-provider/names, once, when the settings are read (migrateLegacyNameTools); what is saved next has only the new form. Do the same when you change what your settings keep.

When an extension needs more than text from another one and ToolService is not what it wants, it calls the other extension's own methods. (The Lore Generator and the Arc Outline did this for the name extensions before ToolService existed; the technique is the same for anything else.)

l: Do not import the other extension
p: The obvious way - depend on the other plugin in the pom.xml and import its packages - is the wrong one. A bundle that imports the packages of another bundle is tied to the classes of that bundle: when the other extension is unloaded (Admin → Extensions, an update, a restart of the framework) and loaded again, the importing bundle keeps the old classes, and an extension installed after yours is not seen at all, its classes are other ones. So the bundle does not import them (pom.xml has no dependency on the other plugin), and nothing of it appears in the Import-Package of the manifest. The other extension is found at run time and used by reflection.
OsgiService.getLoadedExtensions() lists the extensions that finished loading (LoadedExtension(bundle, extension)), so the other extension is found by the name of its class:
The rules the bundled code follows:

Only types both sides know cross the border: the JDK and the application (ListString, FunctionSet, Manuscript...). Your bundle can't name a class of the other one. When you need the other extension's own interface, load it with its class loader (extension.getClass().getClassLoader().loadClass(name)) and, if you must implement it, wrap the real object in a java.lang.reflect.Proxy of that interface.

Look it up on every call. Keep no reference to the extension, its classes or its Method objects: they would keep an unloaded extension alive. A missing extension is a normal answer (null), not an error: a dialog asks when it opens and hides the feature when there is none. A screen that stays open can follow the loading and unloading with OsgiService.addExtensionListener (the listener is held weakly, keep a reference to it).

One class touches the other extension (with the class names and the method names as constants), so that a change on the other side breaks one place and the reflection is not spread over the code. Report a failed call with an exception that says what is missing; the caller decides what to show.
Selections and settings are yours: keep what the user chose in your own settings and pass it each time; leave out what the other extension no longer has.

An extension that wants to be called gives its MarginaliaExtension class a few public methods that use only JDK and application types. There is no compiler between the two, so treat the class name, the method names and their signatures as a contract: keep them stable, say so in the README of the plugin, and when you must change them, change the callers in the same commit. The offering extension does not need to know who calls it. (The Name generator and the Name provider had categories(), newFunctions() and functions() for the bridges; they are gone, their suites are offered through ToolService.)

Arc Outline offers its outline as two sources about a book, so the user chooses how much the caller gets: arc-outline / outline (the arcs with their states, descriptions and chapters) and arc-outline / outline-with-notes (the same with the note of every arc and chapter).

Side Query lists all providers: the button with the plug icon above a tab opens a popover with a checkbox for each. Checked book sources are added to the system message after the lorebook; checked story part sources are asked for each story part in the Chat Logs range and put after the text of the part. The checked sources are stored in the options of the tab, a source that is gone is skipped until it comes back.

A plugin can bring a model API of its own. The user then creates an AI of the type Extension, chooses the provider of the plugin in the AI dialog, and the AI works like an OpenAI-compatible one: books use it, it is shared and limited, its usage is counted. The bundled Google Gemini plugin is the worked example, Anthropic Claude a second one.
Piece
What it is
AIType.EXTENSION
The type of such an AI. Stored as an ordinal like the others (1), so it must stay the last value.
ExtensionAI (ais_extension)

An AI subclass with one column, extensionId. Everything else the provider needs lives in getSettings(): the object under the key extensionId of the dynamic attributes, so there is no migration for it and it travels with the AI.
ExtensionAIFactory
What the plugin registers: its getExtensionId(), a getName() for the user, createInferenceService(ExtensionAI) and createForm(ExtensionAI).
ExtensionAIForm
The settings of the provider in the Per Type Settings tab of the dialog: getComponent(), validate() and apply(ExtensionAI).
InferenceServices
registerExtensionFactory / unregisterExtensionFactory, getExtensionFactory(id) and getExtensionFactories(), and forAI(ai), which asks the factory of an ExtensionAI.
The extension id is stored in every AI of the provider and never changes: use the symbolic name of the bundle (the Google plugin uses google-genai).
Register the factory in onExtensionLoad and take it back in onExtensionUnload, like the other registrations (see Plugin basics):

createForm is called by the AI dialog each time the user picks the provider (and when an existing AI is edited), with the ExtensionAI being edited, or a new one that only has the extension id. The form reads the AI's getSettings() and builds its fields (a FormLayout is the usual root; use @Configurable(preConstruction = true) to get Localization into the constructor). The dialog:
calls validate() before it saves or tests, and does not go on when it returns false - the form tells the user why (a notification);

calls apply(ai) on the AI it saves, and on a throw-away copy (a deep copy of the attributes with the values of the dialog, no id) when the user clicks Test Connection, which runs testConnection() of the service the factory creates for the copy. A form that lists models (a Refresh button) can create a service for such a copy itself and close it afterwards.

The general settings of the AI (name, context and response size, jailbreak, reasoning) stay with the dialog; the service reads them from the AI (getMaxContext(), getEnabledReasoning(), getReasoningEffort()...) and the protocol (TokenLimits).

The attributes are not encrypted. Keep an API key with inferenceServices.protectSecret(key) (AES with the installation key, the same as the API key column of an OpenAI-compatible AI) and read it with revealSecret, which returns null for a key from another installation. Never show a stored key: disable the field and offer a Reset button, as the bundled forms do.
Agents

Call AILimitService.check(ai, promptTokens, responseTokens) at the start of stream and infer, in the caller's thread: it throws InferenceException (NOT_AVAILABLE, LIMIT_REACHED) when an administrator's limit for the user forbids the request.

Call InferenceServices.currentSessionId() once, in the caller's thread, when the request starts (the InferenceSession the caller opened is that thread's) and send a non-null answer in the header InferenceSession.HEADER (X-Session-ID) with every round of the request; the Anthropic plugin puts it on the request params, the Google plugin in the HttpOptions of the call. It is a hash of the user and the kind of work that a server or proxy with a prompt cache can use, and ignored by one that does not. The factory hands inferenceServices::currentSessionId to the service.

Call UsageService.record(ai, prefill, generated) once per request, whichever way it ends, with the numbers the API reported (otherwise your own estimate - TokenizerService.countTokensApprox). It needs the user: capture ThreadCopyRequestAttributes.create() in the thread that calls stream/infer and run the recording in InRequestScope.
Callbacks

countTokens is called very often (every part of the prompt): do not make a request for it per call. TokenizerService.countTokensApprox is local. A provider with real tokenizers (several, or a different one per URL) overrides ExtensionAIFactory.createTokenizerResolver() and calls TokenizerService.countTokens(ai, text) from countTokens. The TokenizerResolver gives each of its AIs a TokenizerKey (TokenizerKey.of(id) or TokenizerKey.of(id, secret), which keeps only an HMAC fingerprint of the secret; AIs with an equal key share the tokenizer that worked) and the TokenizerStrategy list to try for it. It is asked for the AIs of the provider only, once per registered factory. countTokens is also called inside read-write transactions (they hold the database write lock): TokenizerService counts approximately there, a provider that does not use it must not make a slow request in countTokens.

createInferenceService(ai) returns an InferenceService. InferenceServices.forAI calls it once and keeps the service in the AI (ExtensionAI.getInferenceServiceFactory() remembers which factory made it), exactly as for an OpenAI-compatible AI. Saving the AI in the dialog clears the cache (setAiType), so new settings reach the next service. Read the settings in the constructor: the service is not rebuilt per request.
Errors

Fail with InferenceException and the right Type (authentication, rate limit, context overflow...): the application has a localized text for each and InferenceErrors.describe adds the provider's message. Anything else is shown as an internal error.
Functions
Limits

Read UnmeteredScope.isActive() once, in the caller's thread, when the request starts. When it is true the application asks on its own account (the help assistant with an AI that is not shared or has no Apply limits): skip AILimitService.check and do not call UsageService.record for that request, however many rounds and threads it takes.
Session id

stream hands chunks one at a time: call onChunk(controller, type, text) and wait for controller.continueInference() before the next, then onCompletion(). ChunkType.REASONING is the thinking, shown apart from the answer. Check callback.isDead() and the CancellationToken between chunks and end with onCancel(). Cut a blocked read short by cancelling the HTTP call when the token is cancelled (the Google plugin does it with an OkHttp interceptor).

The core calls a service for many things (the generation, summaries, other plugins), so implement all of InferenceService that your API can do and throw UnsupportedOperationException for the rest, as the defaults do. What a service has to take care of itself, because nothing above it does:

The runner of an agent asks with InferenceService.round(payload, protocol, functions, callback): one request, the text, the reasoning and the calls the model wants made handed to onRound (they are not called) with a RoundUsage (tokens, and a RoundStats of what is known: the cache, the reasoning, the time, why it ended; -1 or null for what the provider does not tell). The default throws UnsupportedOperationException, so a service that does not implement it can not be given to an agent.
Tokens
Unmetered requests
Usage

When a FunctionSet is passed, offer its definitions, run the calls the model makes with FunctionSet.call(...) (asynchronously, in the request scope), report each with onFunctionCall, ask again with the results, up to MAX_FUNCTION_ROUNDS. See callFunctions in the Google plugin.

A plugin that is not a provider can still bring a tokenizer for the AIs of the type OpenAI-compatible (a custom endpoint, a model whose vocabulary tiktoken does not know). Implement ExtensionTokenizer (getId, getName, countTokens(TokenizerKey, String), optionally accepts(TokenizerKey)) and call TokenizerService.registerTokenizer in onExtensionLoad, unregisterTokenizer in onExtensionUnload.

The tokenizer is listed in the Tokenizer selector of the AI dialog (TokenizerService.getChoices, id ext:id) and is used by the AIs whose user chose it (OpenAICompatible.tokenizer, an extended attribute; null is automatic). Nothing is ever sent to it for an AI that did not choose it.
It sees the TokenizerKey only: key.id() is the normalized endpoint and the model (http://host:8080#model), the API key and the other settings of the AI never reach it.
accepts(key) is only a suggestion: the dialog preselects the first accepting tokenizer when the user creates an AI and has not chosen one. Existing AIs are never changed by it.

An exception from countTokens makes the application count by the local estimate for that call. It is called often and in the middle of the work, so keep it quick. Inside a read-write transaction TokenizerService does not call it at all (it counts approximately, the transaction holds the database write lock).
When the plugin is unloaded, the AIs that chose it keep the choice (the dialog shows it as not loaded) and count by the local estimate until it is loaded again.
A plugin that provides AIs does not use this: it counts in its InferenceService, or gives the application its own resolver with ExtensionAIFactory.createTokenizerResolver() (see Tokens above).

l: When the plugin is not loaded
p: AIs are rows in the database: the AI of an unloaded plugin stays in the list (AITypes.label shows its provider name, or Extension: id) and works again when the plugin is loaded. In between:

InferenceServices.forAI(ai) returns null and drops a service cached from the unloaded plugin; so it does when the plugin was loaded again meanwhile, because the cached service was made by the old factory: the next call asks the new one.

forAIOrThrow(ai) throws InferenceException of the type EXTENSION_UNAVAILABLE ("The extension that provides this AI is not loaded...") and is what the generation steps and the summaries call. Code that has a sensible fallback (the token count in StorySupport) keeps using forAI and its null.
The AI dialog opens such an AI with a notice instead of the form, saves the general settings and leaves the settings of the plugin untouched.

Unregistering does not stop the services that exist. Close what they hold in onExtensionUnload (the Google factory keeps its services in a weak set and closes their clients) and let a closed service fail with EXTENSION_UNAVAILABLE.

AIDialog offers the type Extension only while a factory is registered (or when the AI being edited is one). The type of an existing AI cannot be changed, because the type decides the entity class. For the type Extension the dialog shows a Provider selector - preselected when only one plugin provides AIs, read-only when editing - and, under it, the form of the chosen provider and the Test Connection button. The methods that do this (addExtensionSettings, currentExtensionAI, testExtensionConnection...) are @PublicAPI like the rest of the dialog.
ApiException and IO failures as InferenceException.
Bundle start; the extension registers GoogleGenAiFactory and closes it on unload.

Cancellation. The SDK hides its HTTP call. Every request carries a header with the id of the run, an OkHttp interceptor stores the Call under it (and removes the header before the request leaves), and the CancellationToken cancels that call, so a generation stops at once even if Google is slow to send the next chunk.
Class

google-genai, "Google Gemini"; creates the services and keeps them (weakly) to close their clients. Its createTokenizerResolver() gives the AIs a TokenizerKey (google-genai#endpoint#model + the API key fingerprint) and one strategy that asks the service of the AI for countTokensOnline; GoogleGenAiInferenceService.countTokens goes through TokenizerService.countTokens, so the application's estimate takes over inside write transactions. The service remembers the answers (by the hash of the text) and stops asking Google for a minute after a failure.
GoogleGenAiActivator, GoogleGenAiExtension
GoogleGenAiErrors
GoogleGenAiFactory
GoogleGenAiForm
GoogleGenAiInferenceService
GoogleGenAiMessages
GoogleGenAiSettings
marginalia/plugins/google-genai uses the Google Gen AI Java SDK:
Role

stream, infer, round (one request for an agent: not streamed, the calls are handed back and not made), function calls, JSON schema (responseJsonSchema), usage, limits, thinking (ThinkingConfig: a level for gemini-3*, a token budget for the others), safety settings, cancellation.
The fields, Refresh for the model list, validation, apply.

The payload as Gemini Contents: leading system messages are the system instruction, system messages later in the conversation become user messages, neighbouring messages of one role are one content, the results of the calls of one message are one content.
The settings of an AI (apiKey encrypted, model, baseUrl, requestTimeoutSeconds, maxRetries, safetyFiltersOff) read from ExtensionAI.getSettings().

Thought signatures. Gemini 3 refuses the next round of a function call unless the model's previous answer comes back with its thought signatures. The service therefore keeps the model's own Content (with the signature parts, without the thinking summaries) and puts it in front of the results of the calls, instead of rebuilding the turn from the LLMToolCalls.
Two things in it are worth copying:

l: Packaging a library only the plugin needs
p: The SDK is not a dependency of the application. The plugin's pom.xml lists it as a normal dependency and embeds it:

maven-bundle-plugin puts the JARs inside the bundle and adds them to Bundle-ClassPath. The framework is started with org.osgi.framework.bootdelegation=* and the application's class loader as the parent, so a class the application has wins over an embedded copy (the bundle looks in its own JARs only for what the application does not have). Hence:

libraries the application ships already (OkHttp, Jackson, Kotlin, Gson, slf4j, jspecify) are exclusions of the SDK and provided for compiling - the SDK then runs on the application's versions (OkHttp 4.12, Jackson 2.22), which must stay compatible with the ones the SDK was built for;
nothing is imported (Import-Package lists only the negated own package), so no package of an embedded library has to be exported by the application;
the JAR is large (about 14 MB: the SDK, Guava, Protobuf, google-auth).

A provider that sends the story to a service somebody else runs should say so where the administrator and the users read: the README of the plugin (and its user page) states that the story text, the lore, the summaries and the files of agents go to Google's servers, under Google's terms, and that sharing such an AI sends the text of everybody who uses it.

The plugin has unit tests for the pure parts (GoogleGenAiMessagesTest, GoogleGenAiErrorsTest, GoogleGenAiSettingsTest); the core has ExtensionAIFactoryTest, ExtensionAICrudTest, ExtensionAIGenerationTest and AIDialogExtensionTest with a fake factory, which is the way to test your own provider's contract without a plugin.

c:
<Embed-Dependency>*;scope=compile|runtime;inline=false</Embed-Dependency>
<Embed-Transitive>true</Embed-Transitive>
<Import-Package>!com.github.enerccio.marginalia.extensions.googlegenai.*</Import-Package>

p: marginalia/plugins/anthropic uses the Anthropic Java SDK and has the same classes as the Google plugin (AnthropicActivator, AnthropicExtension, AnthropicFactory, AnthropicSettings, AnthropicForm, AnthropicInferenceService, AnthropicMessages, AnthropicErrors). It is packaged the same way: the SDK (anthropic-java, about 36 MB with the model classes) is embedded, and what the application has (OkHttp, Jackson, Kotlin, the JSON schema generator, slf4j) is excluded. Only the OpenTelemetry API and Standard Webhooks, which the SDK needs and the application does not, come along. Where it differs from the Google plugin:
Cancellation needs no interceptor. The SDK closes the HTTP call when the StreamResponse is closed, also while another thread waits in a read, so the CancellationToken closes the stream of the run.
Everything is streamed, infer and round too (the SDK refuses a long non-streamed request); the pieces of a round are shown through InferenceRoundCallback.onChunk while it is written.

Signed thinking. The next round of a function call has to carry the thinking blocks of the answer with their signatures. Inside one request the service sends the whole Message back (ContentBlock.toParam()); an agent rebuilds its history from the calls, so the blocks are encoded into the LLMToolCall signature of the first call (AnthropicMessages.encodeThinking) and put back in front of the text when the history is sent again.

No sampling parameters. The API version the SDK sends refuses temperature, top_p and top_k; the protocol's values are ignored. Thinking is adaptive with a summarized display for Claude 4.6 and later, a token budget for the earlier models (AnthropicInferenceService.BUDGET_THINKING), and output_config.effort carries the effort. With reasoning off no thinking parameter is sent, because some models refuse disabled.

Conversation shape. System messages in the middle become user messages; results of calls come first in their user message; the payload has to start and end with the user, because the models after Claude 4.5 refuse a prefill. Anything else is an InferenceException of the type BAD_REQUEST thrown before the request is sent, nothing is added to the prompt.

Tests. AnthropicServiceTest runs the real SDK against FakeAnthropicServer (a JDK HttpServer that streams scripted server-sent events): chunks, usage, the request bodies, the function loop with signed thinking, infer with a schema, round, the error statuses, and a stalled stream that is cancelled. That is the way to test a provider without an API key.

This page builds a small plugin from scratch - Bookmarks, which lets you bookmark story parts - and then walks through three bundled plugins: Chapter Marker, the smallest one that changes the UI, Author's Note, which changes the prompt sent to the model, and Chinese localization, which adds a language and no code besides the texts. Together they use everything from the previous pages: a bundle, decorators reading arguments, locals and fields, data in attributes, generation listeners, and cleanup on unload.
What it does:
every story part's menu gets a Toggle bookmark item,
bookmarked parts are marked with ★ in the story sidebar,
the bookmark is stored on the part, so it's kept in backups and copied by Branch Story.
The Bookmarks example: a bookmarked part in the sidebar and the Toggle bookmark menu item
The plugin compiles against the application's classes, installed in the local Maven repository:

c:
mvn -N install                  # in the repository root: the parent POM the application's POM refers to
cd marginalia
mvn install -DskipTests

p: Copy marginalia/plugins/chaptermarker/pom.xml and change:

groupId to com.example.marginalia, artifactId to bookmarks, and replace the parent (the plugin is outside the repository) with a version of its own, e.g. 1.0.1; the dependency on marginalia then needs the version of the installed application instead of ${project.version},
Bundle-Activator to com.example.marginalia.bookmarks.BookmarksActivator,
Import-Package to !com.example.marginalia.bookmarks.* and Export-Package to com.example.marginalia.bookmarks.*.
Keep the rest - the provided dependencies, the AspectJ plugin (for @Configurable) and the bundle plugin. See Plugin basics → pom.xml for what each part does.

bookmarks/
├── pom.xml
└── src/main/java/com/example/marginalia/bookmarks/
    ├── BookmarksActivator.java
    └── BookmarksExtension.java

p: It only registers the extension:

This example decorates createMenuItems to show the technique; for a menu item of the story editor prefer the StoryMenuRegistry (see UI extensions), which also gives the item a keyboard shortcut and needs no cleanup.
How it works:

Two decorators. menuDecorator runs after ChatMessageCard.createMenuItems() - the card runs it when its menu is opened for the first time (not when the card is created, so the cards of a long story stay cheap), so every menu that is opened gets the item. sidebarDecorator runs after ManuscriptStoryPart.createSidebarButton(msg, orderId, dbId), which renderStoryContent() calls for each part of the branch.

Reaching the components. The menu is the card's field hamburgerMenu; the sidebar button is the local variable sidebarBtn of createSidebarButton, the part is its argument msg. Both names are checked before use (hasLocalVariable) or fail with a logged warning if the application changes.
Adding once. ComponentUtil.setData(menu, MENU_ITEM_KEY, item) marks the menu; a second call for the same menu does nothing.

Data. The bookmark is one boolean under the plugin's key in the part's attributes. The click listener reads the card's message field at click time and reloads the part (chatMessageService.find(id)) before changing it, because the card's copy may be stale (Extended attributes).

Redrawing. After saving it calls the story part's private renderStoryContent() through callReflectiveMethod, reaching the outer ManuscriptStoryPart through the inner class's this$0 field. The redraw runs createSidebarButton again, so the sidebar decorator adds the ★.

Unloading. Decorators are unregistered; menu items are removed from the tracked menus inside each menu's own ui.access(...), because they belong to other users' sessions (Extending the UI → Unloading). Sidebar buttons lose their ★ on the next redraw.
Errors. onExtensionLoad runs without a UI, so it throws instead of opening an error dialog; Marginalia logs the error and unloads the extension again.

With Chapter Marker installed too, both plugins decorate createSidebarButton, and decorators run in the order the plugins were loaded. Bookmarks prefixes the text, so it works after Chapter Marker; Chapter Marker replaces the text of chapter parts, so the ★ of a bookmarked chapter is lost when Chapter Marker runs second (and when the part is edited).

Load target/bookmarks-1.5.0.jar in Admin → Extensions and open a book (books that were already open need to be closed and opened again). Open a part's menu, choose Toggle bookmark - the part's sidebar entry gets the ★.

If nothing appears, look in the log for Mod 'com.example.marginalia.bookmarks.BookmarksExtension$...' skipped on ... (a name that doesn't exist) or Unhandled exception in extension .... The lines of the extension itself (here log.error(Cannot toggle bookmark, e)) are in Admin → Extensions → Log of the extension, see Logging.

c:
cd bookmarks
mvn package                     # target/bookmarks-1.5.0.jar

p: Show the bookmarks in a tab of their own: decorate renderStoryContent() and add a tab to leftBar, like Side Query (A tab next to the story).
Put bookmarked parts into the prompt: register a generation listener, like Author's Note (Walkthrough: Author's Note, Generation events).

marginalia/plugins/chaptermarker turns the story sidebar into a table of contents: a part whose text contains a Markdown heading is shown as 5. Chapter 3: The Harbour, highlighted. It has two classes and no data of its own - the heading is part of the story text.
ChapterMarkingActivator is the same as the Bookmarks activator. ChapterMarkingExtension registers two decorators in onExtensionLoad.
Labelling the sidebar - after ManuscriptStoryPart.createSidebarButton(msg, orderId, dbId):
It remembers the button's original text, the order and the part's uuid on the button (ComponentUtil.setData(...)), then sets the chapter title and style if the part has a heading.
Following edits - after ManuscriptStoryPart$ChatMessageCard.autosaveAndSwapToMarkdown(), which saves an edited part:

It finds the sidebar button whose stored uuid matches the edited part and relabels it - or restores the original text when the heading was removed. The data stored on the button in the first decorator is what makes this possible without rebuilding the sidebar.
Unloading unregisters both decorators. Labels already changed stay until the story is redrawn, which is acceptable here: they're just text.
What to take from it:
arguments, locals and fields are all used, each with the right accessor;
primitive arguments are read with the primitive type;
a fallback for the local variable keeps the plugin working if the variable is renamed;
component data (ComponentUtil) carries state from one hook to another.

The other bundled plugins build on the same pieces: Reviewer and Side Query add menu items, tabs, settings panels and call the model (Extending the UI); Lorebook VCS stores larger data in a lorebook's attributes (Extended attributes); Lore Generator adds a button to every row of the lorebook grid and streams a generation from the model into a dialog; Author's Note, below, changes the prompt of every generation.
Adds the tab on leave of ManuscriptStoryPart.renderStoryContent() (like Side Query) and registers the listener.
AFTER_PREPARE_PAYLOAD comes when the list of chat messages for the model is complete; what the listener sets is what is sent:
AuthorsNoteData
AuthorsNoteExtension
AuthorsNoteService
AuthorsNoteView

BEFORE_PREPARE_CONTENT comes before the generation decides how much of the story fits into the context. The listener loads the note, keeps it in the generation's properties and reserves its tokens, so the story gets less room:
build a new payload and setPayload(...) it instead of changing the list you got.
chain.next() in finally - the generation waits for every listener;
Class
Does
Generation events explains the payload, the choice of the events and reserving tokens in detail.
Hooking into generation - onExtensionLoad registers two listeners next to the decorator and keeps the registrations:
listeners are global, so act only on the data of the book being generated;
Loads and saves the data, counts the note's tokens, inserts the note into a payload.

marginalia/plugins/authorsnote sends a per-book note to the model with every generation: an Author's Note tab next to the story outline edits it, a generation listener inserts it into the prompt. It shows the one thing decorators can't do - change what the model gets.
pass state from one event to the next in event.getProperties(), under your package name;
reserve the tokens of what you add (PrePromptData.reservedTokens) before the budget is computed, and add to the reservation instead of overwriting it;
The note: on/off, the text, a private scratchpad, the insertion depth and the role. Stored in the book's attributes under the package name.
The sidebar tab with a token estimate of the note; every change is saved right away.
Unloading unregisters both listeners besides removing the decorator and the tabs - a listener left registered would keep changing the prompts of every user.
What to take from it:

marginalia/plugins/chineselocalization adds Simplified Chinese to the language selector of the workspace. It is the smallest possible plugin - no decorators, no UI, no data - and shows the third optional interface of an extension besides ExtensionHasCss: ExtensionHasLocalization.

The pom.xml is the one of the other plugins without what the plugin doesn't use: it needs only the application (classes classifier) and the Felix framework, both provided, and the bundle plugin - no AspectJ, since there is no @Configurable class, and no Vaadin.
The extension implements MarginaliaExtension as always - both methods stay empty, there is nothing to set up - and ExtensionHasLocalization:

Marginalia calls getLocalizationBundles() right after onExtensionLoad and registers the bundles in Localization; when the extension is unloaded they are removed again. Nothing else is needed: the language shows up in the LanguageSelector of every workspace the next time it is attached, and a user who picks it is shown the whole UI in it after the page reloads.
The bundle extends LocalizationBundleBase: loadMessages() fills the texts with setValue, the other methods describe the language.
What to take from it:

a language code is the identity of a bundle: only one bundle per code exists. A second one is refused (and logged) - an extension can add languages but not replace the English texts or the Japanese ones of the application;

a bundle doesn't have to be complete: a key it lacks is shown in the default language, and the application logs a warning listing the missing keys when the bundle is registered. A plugin built for an older version keeps working when the application adds keys;

the placeholders (%s, %d) of a text must match the English text in number and order of their types, the application formats the text with them. Copy LocalizationBundleEN as the start and translate in place;
the bundle is created in getLocalizationBundles(), and the texts are looked up when needed, so a plugin's own user interface that uses Localization gets the right language without more work;
unloading the plugin makes sessions that used its language fall back to the default one - nothing is lost, the user's setting stays and works again when the plugin is loaded.
To try it, build and load it like any plugin (Build and load): in Admin → Extensions load chineselocalization-1.5.0.jar, then pick 中文（简体） in the language selector.

p: Marginalia's tests are integration tests first: most of them start the real Spring XML configuration against a throwaway SQLite database and talk to a fake OpenAI-compatible server. They need no network, no model and no API key, and they run in CI on every push and pull request. This page explains the test infrastructure and how to add tests.

Spring caches the application context, and with it the database, for the whole test run. All test classes that use MarginaliaTestBase share one SQLite database. Write tests so that they don't depend on what else is in it:
create the data a test needs in the test, with uniqueName(...) for anything looked up by name;
assert on the entities you created (contains, doesNotContain), not on totals (hasSize);
operations that work on the whole database (cleanup, database backups) must only assert on their own data - see CleanupServiceTest.
When a test really needs an empty database or changes global state, mark it with @DirtiesContext. The next test then gets a new context with a new folder and database:

The first context of a JVM costs about 20 seconds (Spring, Hibernate, Flyway; measured as the start of one test class on the first machine of the table, a context built later in a warm JVM should cost less), so use it sparingly.

Each context gets its own folder under target/test-home/ with the database, data, backup and extension folders. They are not deleted after the run, so you can open a test database with any SQLite tool after a failure. mvn clean or deleting target/test-home removes them.

test/llm/MockLLMServer is a small OpenAI-compatible server on 127.0.0.1 with a random port, built on the JDK's HttpServer. One shared server lives for the whole test JVM (MockLLMServer.shared()); each test gets its own scenario with its own base URL, http://127.0.0.1:port/scenario-id/v1. A provider created with createAI() points to the test's scenario, so tests never see each other's requests or answers.
It answers:
Endpoint
GET /models
The scenario's model list (default mock-model; change with llm.models(...)).
POST /chat/completions
Streaming (server-sent events) and non-streaming chat completions.
Chat completions are answered in this order:
queued responses - llm.enqueue(...) or llm.reply(text), one per request;
the responder function - llm.respondWith(request - ...), if set and it returns a response;
the fallback - llm.fallback(...);
otherwise HTTP 500 no response programmed.
MockLLMResponse builds one answer:

waitFor(latch) is the tool for "while generating" states: the request is received, the pipeline waits for the stream, and the test can stop the generation or inspect the state before releasing the latch.

The openai-java client retries 408, 409, 429 and 5xx responses. A queued error response is consumed once per attempt, so enqueue it several times (or use fallback) when a test expects the error to reach Marginalia. The server closes the connection after every response, so a retry never reuses a stale pooled connection.

c:
MockLLMResponse.text("Hello world")                        // one content chunk
MockLLMResponse.chunks("Hel", "lo").chunkDelay(ofMillis(50))
MockLLMResponse.split(longText, 20)                        // chunks of 20 characters
MockLLMResponse.text("answer").withReasoning("thinking")   // reasoning chunks first
MockLLMResponse.text("answer").withReasoning("...").reasoningField("reasoning")  // instead of reasoning_content
MockLLMResponse.text("cut").finishReason("length")
MockLLMResponse.error(429, "slow down")                    // OpenAI-style error body
MockLLMResponse.chunks("a", "b", "c").disconnectAfter(2)   // stream ends abruptly
MockLLMResponse.text("answer").usage(120, 8)               // token counts in the last chunk (only if asked for)
MockLLMResponse.text("late").waitFor(latch)                // held until the latch is released
MockLLMResponse.toolCall("add", "{\"a\":1}")               // the model calls a function; .andToolCall(...) adds one

The instruct tests check the bytecode that makes @Extendable methods extensible (see Plugin development):

ExtendableMethodVisitorTest transforms fixture classes from instruct/fixture/ with instruct/Instrumenter - the same transformation the agent applies, without an agent - and checks that the result verifies, keeps the class schema, behaves like the original and exposes arguments and locals to decorators.
RuntimeInstrumentationTest installs the real agent into the test JVM and checks classes loaded both before and after the installation (fixture/agent/).

ExtensionVerifierTest runs the extension verification on the extensions of fixture/verify/VerifyFixtures (decorators that are valid, ask for things that don't exist, or can't be followed) against the decorated VerifyTarget. Their class files are packed into a JAR on the fly and served by a stand-in Bundle. Decorators must be anonymous classes with the context calls inside them, as in a real extension - a decorator that delegates to a helper class would not be checked.

PublicAPISignatureTest checks the @PublicAPI of every instrumented method of every @Extendable class of the application against the compiled classes (target/classes). It reads them with ByteBuddy's type pool and the local variable table (PublicAPISignatures), so the application classes are not loaded or initialized, and it needs the classes compiled by ajc like the application. A failure names the method and prints the annotation the method needs.

The fixtures are compiled with the same -parameters and preserveAllLocals options as the application; if you change the compiler settings in pom.xml, these tests tell you whether extensions still see names of arguments and locals.

Marginalia is built once as a WAR and then shipped in two forms: a Docker image for servers and a desktop app with its own Java runtime and Jetty. This page describes how each is built, what CI does, and how a release is made. For everyday builds see Building from source.

Where it goes

mvn package in marginalia/ produces target/marginalia-1.6.0.war (see Building the application). The WAR always runs in Vaadin production mode: build-frontend writes the production flow-build-info.json into it, and a development one left in src/main/resources is never packaged (see Development and production mode).
One resource differs between a development build and a release build:
File
Development
Release
logback.xml
src/main/resources/ - com.github.enerccio at DEBUG
src/main/resources-release/ - everything at INFO, no story content in the log

The build decides, not the packaging: IDE runs and mvn jetty:run use target/classes, which has the development file. The WAR plugin adds src/main/resources-release/ to WEB-INF/classes and leaves the development file out, so every WAR from mvn package - the Docker image, the desktop profile, a WAR deployed by hand - logs at INFO.

The user manual is packed too: resources in marginalia/pom.xml copies the Markdown pages of manual/user (no pictures, never filtered) to classpath:/manual/, where ManualService reads them (see Services). The source folder is outside marginalia/, so a build that copies only marginalia/src must copy manual/user as well, as both Dockerfiles do (/build/manual/user); without it the WAR builds, with an empty manual.

The build also needs the Git history: git-commit-id-plugin writes the commit id and the closest tag into git.properties, and the WAR filters them into its build info. Build from a clone, not from a source archive.

creates a Jetty base with the modules server, http, ee11-deploy, ee11-websocket-jakarta, ee11-webapp, ee11-jsp (the WebSocket module is required for Vaadin push);

declares a HEALTHCHECK (every 30 s, 120 s start period): the image has no curl, so bash opens a socket to 127.0.0.1:8080, sends GET /health and the container is healthy when the status line is 200 (the application context is up and the database answers, see Architecture). Docker only reports the state, it does not restart the container;

The app image: Marginalia.app (macOS), Marginalia/Marginalia.exe (Windows), Marginalia/bin/Marginalia (Linux).
The portable folder: bin/marginalia, bin/marginalia.bat, app/, server/, runtime/.

DesktopLauncher is the main class of the app image and of the portable scripts. It depends on the JDK only and starts Jetty in its own JVM by loading start.jar through a class loader, so it never needs Jetty on the classpath and never ends up in the WAR. On start it:
resolves the data folder home/.marginalia (--home sets user.home) and redirects its output to .marginalia/desktop/logs/;
finds server/ next to or above the launcher JAR (jpackage places app content differently per OS);
checks the port (default 8765): if Marginalia already runs there, it just opens the browser; if another program uses it, it picks a free port (unless --port was given);

writes a Jetty base into .marginalia/desktop/jetty-base/ (modules ee11-*, webapps/ROOT.xml pointing to the WAR, a persistent work folder) - so the installation itself can stay read-only, e.g. inside a signed app bundle;
starts Jetty on 127.0.0.1, waits up to three minutes for the start page, then shows the tray icon (or a small window where there is no system tray) and opens the browser.

The JVM options needed by the extension agent (-Djdk.attach.allowAttachSelf=true -XX:+EnableDynamicAgentLoading, plus --enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED for SQLite) are passed by jpackage --java-options and by the scripts in bin/. The scripts add MARGINALIA_JAVA_OPTS. Keep the three places in sync - the desktop.javaOptions property and both scripts. On macOS, -Dapple.awt.UIElement=true keeps the app out of the Dock; it lives only in the tray.
Command-line options are described in Desktop app.

jlink and jpackage only build for the platform they run on, so each operating system and CPU is built on its own machine. CI does this with a build matrix (below). Locally you get only your own platform.

If you add a dependency that needs a JDK module not in desktop.modules (a ClassNotFoundException or NoClassDefFoundError for a java.* / javax.* / jdk.* class in the desktop log only), add the module to the list. jdeps --print-module-deps on the WAR's libraries helps to find it.

The app images are not signed or notarized. macOS Gatekeeper and Windows SmartScreen warn on the first start; the Desktop app page tells users how to get past it. Signing would be added to the jpackage call (--mac-sign, --mac-signing-key-user-name...) and, for Windows, as a separate signtool step in CI.

Each plugin in marginalia/plugins/ is a Maven project with bundle packaging (Apache Felix maven-bundle-plugin) that depends on the application's classes JAR with provided scope. They are built against one exact version of the application:

server.yml builds all the plugins against the freshly installed application and attaches the JARs to the release of a v* tag; the Docker image doesn't contain them (server users put them into data folder/extensions or install them in Admin → Extensions). When you change application classes that a plugin uses (decorated @Extendable methods, UI classes, services), rebuild the plugin and test it against the new application. See Plugin development.

p: marginalia/plugins/Dockerfile is a separate build environment for the plugins, used by servers that build from source (and by anyone without a local JDK/Maven). Its builder stage (Maven + JDK 25, like the main Dockerfile) installs the application into the image's local Maven repository (with -Dvaadin.skip=true: the plugins need only the classes JAR, so the frontend is not built, see Building) and builds every plugin against it; the final stage is a small Alpine image that holds the JARs in /jars. Its command copies them to /output, replacing the *.jar files there, so the compose file (marginalia/plugins/docker-compose.yml, build context ../..) mounts marginalia/plugins/build as /output. The plugins are built one after the other and none of them needs another one installed first (the Lore Generator finds the Name generator at run time, not at build time). The Name generator's build clones the sources of its names from GitHub (the Maven image has git); without network it keeps the tables committed in the repository, see its README:
The JARs are not copied while the image is built, because a bind mount exists only when a container runs.

rebuild.sh (Linux, macOS) and rebuild.bat (Windows) in the repository root update a Docker server: when the upstream branch has new commits they stop the container, git pull, build the plugins as above, copy the JARs into data/extensions (overwriting the installed ones; extensions load on start) and run docker compose up -d --build. --force skips the check for new commits. The two scripts must be kept in step; .gitattributes keeps the shell script on LF and the batch file on CRLF.

docker compose -f marginalia/plugins/docker-compose.yml build
docker compose -f marginalia/plugins/docker-compose.yml run --rm plugins

Version. Set the new version in the parent pom.xml in the repository root and in the parent of the application and the plugin POMs - mvn versions:set -DnewVersion=version -DgenerateBackupPoms=false in the root does all of it (the plugins' marginalia dependency follows ${project.version}). The archive names and the app version shown by the OS come from the POM, not from the tag, so the two must match: for a v* tag the test job first checks that the tag is v + the POM version and fails otherwise, so no archives are built or attached. jpackage on macOS requires a version of the form x.y.z with x ≥ 1.

Database. If the release changes the schema, check that the migrations upgrade a database of the previous release (keep a copy of one around) - FlywayMigrationTest covers only the migrations themselves.

Create the GitHub release for the tag (by hand or gh release create v1.6.0) with the release notes. desktop.yml attaches the ten desktop archives when its matrix finishes, server.yml the WAR and the plugin JARs and pushes the Docker image - whichever finishes first creates the release if it doesn't exist yet (softprops/action-gh-release).

p: The manual is part of the repository: Retype reads manual/ and writes the static site to docs/ (configured in retype.yml). GitHub Pages serves docs/ from the master branch, so the published manual changes when a commit with a new docs/ reaches master. Rebuild and commit docs/ in the same change as the sources - see Building the manual.

Contributions are welcome: bug reports, fixes, new features, extensions, and corrections to this manual. This page describes how to report a problem, how changes are made and what a pull request should contain.
Marginalia is released under the MIT License. By contributing you agree that your contribution is released under the same license.
Open an issue on GitHub. For a bug, include:
what you did, what happened and what you expected;
the version (desktop app archive name, or the commit for a Docker server) and how you run it;
the inference provider type and model, if the problem is about generation (never your API key);
the relevant part of the log - see Where are the logs?. Logs may contain story text; remove what you don't want to share.
Security problems (access to other users' data, login, cookies) should not be reported in a public issue - contact the maintainer privately through GitHub first.
TODO.md is the list of planned work for the first release, ordered by priority. Items marked 🧩 are good candidates for an extension instead of a change to the core.

For anything larger than a small fix, open an issue (or comment on an existing one) first and describe what you plan. Some features belong in an extension rather than in the core - see Plugin development.
Read Architecture and the page about the area you are changing.
Set up the build and make sure mvn test passes on a clean checkout - see Building from source.
Fork the repository and create a branch from master with a short descriptive name (fix-summary-prompt, lorebook-tag-filter).
Make the change, with tests where the area is testable (see Testing).
Run mvn test in marginalia/. If you touched a plugin or classes plugins use, build the plugins too.
Start Marginalia and try the change in the browser - most of the application is UI, which the tests don't cover.
Update the manual if users or developers will notice the change (see Documentation).
Push and open a pull request against master.

CI runs the tests and builds the desktop app on all platforms for every pull request that changes marginalia/ (see Continuous integration). A pull request is merged when CI is green and the change has been reviewed.
Commit messages follow the style already in the history: one line, lowercase, starting with a verb in the imperative, class and method names in backticks, related changes separated by a semicolon:
Common verbs: add, fix, update, remove, refactor, rename, migrate, handle. Mention the issue number when the commit fixes one (... (#17)).

Keep commits focused - one fix or one step of a feature per commit, not a mix of a feature, a reformat and an unrelated fix. Don't commit generated or local files: target/, src/main/frontend/generated/, src/main/bundles/, flow-build-info.json in src/main/resources and .idea/ are ignored by Git for this reason.
